title: Programming Refusal with Conditional Activation Steering
question: Can activation steering be made conditional so that a refusal or behaviour vector is applied only to prompts from a chosen category?
mechanism: h' <- h + f(sim(h, proj_c h)) * alpha * v, where c is a condition vector and v a behaviour vector, both extracted from contrastive prompt sets; proj_c h = ((c.h)/(c.c)) c; sim is cosine similarity; f is a step (binary) threshold on that similarity, so v is applied only when h aligns with c. Multiple conditions are combined by expanding the thresholding function. Threshold, layer and comparison direction are chosen by grid search (Appendix C.2).
training: No weight optimisation (paper: 'all without requiring weight optimization'). Condition and behaviour vectors come from contrastive prompt sets; threshold, layer and comparison direction are picked by grid search over labelled prompts.
setup: Seven chat models (Table 1; Qwen 1.5 Chat 1.8B, Danube 4B and OLMo 7B named in the text); refusal on harmful vs harmless prompt sets; rules such as 'if input is about hate speech or adult content, then refuse'.
numbers: No reliable numeric result extracted: the Table 2 subset is garbled in text extraction (fulltext ~line 410) and the main comparison (Figure 1) is a bar chart with no values in the text. Paper states conditioning 'largely unchanged' harmless refusal rates (Sec 4, around lines 366-372).
limits: No limitations section in the read text. The paper notes the threshold controls the required alignment between input and harm category (Sec 4) and that the threshold must be grid-searched per setting.
evidence_quote: Intuitively, based on how well aligned the hidden state h is with the condition vector c, the function f determines whether to apply the behavior vector

novelty_note.B: Gate is cosine similarity between the current hidden state and a condition vector extracted from prompts, used as a step function on the behaviour vector, with no separate classifier.

title: Contextual Linear Activation Steering of Language Models
question: Can a fixed steering direction be paired with a context-dependent coefficient, so steering strength adapts per input and can differ across spans of one generation?
mechanism: Per block l, a fixed unit-norm direction d_l is extracted from a probe (mean difference, logistic regression or RFM). A learned block-specific sensing vector c_l in R^(k+1) gives the coefficient alpha_{l,t} = c_l . [h_{l,t}; 1], so steering strength varies per block and token. interp: the intervention is h + alpha_{l,t} d_l; the paper's displayed intervention formula was not fully legible in the text extraction.
training: Gradient training of one sensing vector per block: 'we minimize the standard next-token prediction objective on a small dataset of prompt-completion pairs'. Direction d_l comes from a probe fit. Dataset size not read.
setup: 11 steering tasks on four instruction-tuned LLMs (including Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.1-70B, Llama-3.2-1B per Table 7). Tasks include IMDb sentiment, Grandiloquent, GSM8K, MNMT, Repetition, LeetCode, Alpaca, MMLU, JailbreakBench, ToxicChat. Baselines: LAS, ReFT, LoRA.
numbers: Per-task table (Sec 6): Repetition CLAS 93.75 +/- 5.91 vs LAS 58.50 +/- 35.12 (delta +35.25); model not identified in the read excerpt.
Same table: MMLU CLAS 79.50 +/- 14.27 vs LAS 58.50 +/- 20.49 (delta +21.00).
Sec 6: 'CLAS matches LAS on the former but improves substantially on the latter' (sentiment/style tasks vs GSM8K/MNMT).
limits: Abstract scopes the ReFT/LoRA claim to 'settings with limited labeled data'. The paper reports that on simpler sentiment and style tasks CLAS matches LAS, so gains concentrate on complex tasks. The read text does not report a failure analysis.
evidence_quote: To learn the sensing vector, we minimize the standard next-token prediction objective on a small dataset of prompt-completion pairs.

novelty_note.B: Coefficient is an inner product of the hidden state with a learned per-block sensing vector and no separate classifier, so the steering strength acts as a gate computed from the hidden state. The sensing vector itself is gradient-trained, unlike a training-free gate.

title: GAPS: Dimension-Level Gates for Conditional Activation Steering
question: Beyond deciding when to steer, which neurons should a steering vector act on, so that behaviour change costs less capability?
mechanism: Static separability gate: per-neuron AUROC_d between target and source activations; keep neuron d if its deviation from 1/2 exceeds tau_z * sigma_0, with sigma_0 = sqrt((N_src+N_tar+1)/(12 N_src N_tar)) (Eqs 2-3; the text extraction garbles the 1/2 term, read as interp). Dynamic posterior gate: per neuron and per step, Gaussian class-conditional log-densities (means and variances from the contrastive set); steer neuron d only if x_d is more likely under the source than the target (Eqs 4-5, Appendix A). Final mask m_sep * m_post multiplies the steering vector, and the token-level gate g(h) from CAST or DSAS is kept: h <- h + alpha g(h) (m * v).
training: None: the paper describes two training-free gates. All statistics are estimated from the same contrastive activations used to build the mean-difference steering vector.
inference_cost: O(D) elementwise operations per token, 'the same order as the steering-vector addition itself' (Appendix A).
setup: Gemma-3 (4B) and Qwen-3 (1.7B). Toxicity mitigation on RealToxicityPrompts; concept removal over seven OneSeC concepts (football, cloud, baby, church, book, flower, balloon); capability measured by Wikipedia perplexity and MMLU. Token-level baselines CAST and DSAS.
numbers: Abstract: DSAS+GAPS lowers Gemma-3's toxicity rate from 6.52% to 0.48%, 'versus 3.52% for DSAS alone'.
Ablation table (Gemma-3, RealToxicityPrompts, fulltext lines ~500-508): CAST 3.70 and CAST + msep*mpost (GAPS) 2.14 toxicity; DSAS 3.52 and DSAS + msep 2.06.
Abstract: 'Ablations attribute most of the gain to the posterior gate.'
limits: Authors leave a systematic study of prior selection to future work. Scope is two models, two token-level methods and two tasks. Ablations show the separability gate alone is a weaker complement than the posterior gate.
evidence_quote: The dynamic posterior gate mpost detects whether the source (undesired) concept is currently expressed, steering a neuron only when its current activation is more likely under the source than the target concept.

novelty_note.B: Dynamic posterior gate is computed from the current hidden state itself (per-neuron likelihood ratio) and decides whether to apply the steering vector, with no separate classifier.
novelty_note.C: Per-neuron Gaussian likelihood ratio is a diagonal discriminant rule (quadratic discriminant analysis restricted to single neurons); no covariance inverse or whitening is used, so this is a partial match. interp: the closest match to C.

title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
question: Can a steering intervention adapt to input semantics, rather than applying one fixed vector, without any training?
mechanism: Step 1: for each instance and layer, last-token activations of positive and negative outputs are collected (forward of x||y); activation differences from contrastive pairs are aggregated across layers. Step 2: mean difference is binarised to a mask over critical elements (attention heads, hidden states, or FFN neurons). Step 3: at inference the mask is applied to the input activations, scaled by a factor delta, so the change is element-wise and depends on the input. The exact scaling formula (Sec 3.4) was not read.
training: None: training-free. The paper says it 'necessitates only a small number of additional examples (i.e., 150 items)' to build the dynamic steering vector.
setup: LLaMA2-7B-Chat, BLOOMZ-7B, Mistral-7B, Falcon-7B-Instruct; eleven benchmarks: COPA, StoryCloze, NLI, MMLU, SST2, SST5, BoolQ, Winogrande (multiple choice); TriviaQA, ToxiGen, TruthfulQA (generation).
numbers: Sec 1: 'accuracy improvements reaching up to +14.69' over baselines.
Sec 1: needs only 150 additional items to build the dynamic steering vector (no training).
limits: No limitations section in the read text.
evidence_quote: SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM

title: Steering When Necessary: Flexible Steering Large Language Models with Backtracking
question: Can intervention be decided and scaled from the generated content as well as the question, with a backtracking step to fix tokens that already deviated?
mechanism: (1) Heads anchoring: a per-head probe p = sigmoid(theta . x) on the last-token activation of each QA pair; top-k heads by validation accuracy. Steering vector from the probe weights (Probe method; a Prototype alternative uses cosine similarity to positive and negative cluster centres). (2) State tracking: per token, p(x_{i,j}) = (1/k) sum over top-k heads of (1 - p_theta(x)); intervention strength alpha from the probe (interp: alpha = sigmoid of theta.x). (3) Backtracking: step back s tokens and regenerate with steering when the tracked state indicates deviation (exact trigger rule garbled in extraction).
training: Trains per-head probes/classifiers on labelled TruthfulQA QA pairs; no LLM weights are updated. Training-set-size sweep uses 496 (20%) to 2481 (100%) samples (Figure 7b).
setup: TruthfulQA open-ended generation (True*Info) and multiple-choice (MC1, MC2, MC3); six multiple-choice datasets are mentioned in the abstract. LLMs not identified in the read text.
numbers: Table 1 (TruthfulQA): Baseline True*Info 66.50, MC1 33.41, MC2 51.07; Probe (Ours) True*Info 80.56, MC1 48.71, MC2 66.58.
Sec 4: threshold 0.6 causes True*Info to 'drop sharply', attributed to excessive intervention; 0.4 is best for True*Info.
limits: Authors report a trade-off: Info falls as the number of intervened heads and the strength rise, because the model is pushed toward truthful but less informative answers (Sec 4). Threshold 0.6 gives a sharp drop.
evidence_quote: Since intervening after detecting a deviation from the desired behavior is often too late, we further propose the backtracking mechanism

title: Multi-property Steering of Large Language Models with Dynamic Activation Composition
question: How should steering intensity be scheduled over generation when several properties (safety, language, formality) are steered at once?
mechanism: Activation extraction: K=30 pairs of in-context prompts with opposite-polarity answers; at each generation step i the attention-head activations at the last query position give v+_i and v-_i, and Delta_i = v+_i - v-_i. Injection: Attn_{l,h}(.) <- Attn_{l,h}(.) + alpha_i Delta_i for all layers and heads. Schedules: Start (alpha_1 only), Fixed (alpha_i = c), Diminishing (alpha_i decreases linearly to 0 over a range set by val_max), and Dynamic (Dyn). Dyn sets alpha_i from the information gain, a KL divergence between steered and unsteered next-token distributions restricted to a top-p token set (formula partly read).
training: None described in read sections: training-free, with steering vectors from in-context contrastive prompts.
setup: Mistral 7B for all experiments. Properties: unsafe/safe, language (Italian and other languages), formality. Base queries from a 500-prompt English QA set; manual composition sets built from machine-translated Alpaca and similar data.
numbers: No single summary number extracted: conditioning and fluency results are in Figures 4-5 and appendix tables, not read at value level.
Sec 6 (Figure 5 caption): 'Overall, stronger steering intensity is only required on the first few generated tokens.'
limits: Authors state: 'the results we report are based on experiments with one instruction-based model only, namely Mistral 7B', and call for larger, RLHF-aligned model coverage. Manual composition sets use machine-translated data.
evidence_quote: Overall, stronger steering intensity is only required on the first few generated tokens.

title: Fusion Steering: Prompt-Specific Activation Control
question: Can per-prompt, multi-layer activation injection from enriched reference activations improve factual accuracy on SimpleQA questions the base model originally got wrong?
mechanism: Reference activation per layer: h_l = mean of a_{l,t} over token positions of the ground-truth answer and model-generated explanation in an enriched prompt (Eq 1). Shift Delta_l = gamma (h_l - mu_l), with mu_l the mean activation over tokens at inference (Eq 2). Steered activations a' = a + Delta_l (Eq 3), blended a_final = alpha a_steered + (1 - alpha) a_orig, with fusion weight alpha (Eq 4). Layers are split into early (0-8), middle (9-17) and late (18-25) groups, each with its own (alpha, gamma), tuned per prompt with Optuna on token overlap and perplexity.
training: No weight training. A per-prompt Optuna hyperparameter search (gradient-free) over alpha and gamma; the objective uses ground-truth answers, so tuning needs labels. Ground-truth answers are present only at reference capture, not at inference.
setup: Gemma-2-2B-IT with 8-bit quantisation; SimpleQA (500 prompts, of which the 260 graded INCORRECT by the baseline were used); Mistral Small 3.1 as grader. Single NVIDIA T4 GPU.
numbers: Sec 4: segmented steering 25.4% accuracy (66/260) vs 16.2% full-layer and 3.5% baseline.
Sec 4: under the SimpleQA rubric, segmented steering 13.1% CORRECT (34/260) vs baseline 0.0%.
Abstract: 'Under the stricter SimpleQA rubric, segmented steering boosts fully correct responses from 0.0% to 13.1%.'
limits: Authors note: the requirement of ground-truth answers and explanations 'limits the scalability' where curated supervision is rare; reliance on greedy decoding; and possible over-long or unnatural completions when explanation tokens dominate the activation.
evidence_quote: The injection weights are optimized per prompt using Optuna, targeting a joint objective that balances token overlap (factual alignment) and perplexity (fluency proxy).

novelty_note.D: Converts an enriched prompt (question plus ground-truth answer and explanation) into per-layer reference activations that are injected into a question-only prompt. It is not a system prompt, but it does turn in-context content into an activation edit.

title: A Few Neurons Reveal When LLMs Misuse Tools: Sparse Detection and Selective Steering for Reliable Tool Use
question: Can tool-use failures (over-calling, missing, invalid arguments) be detected from a few FFN neurons, and corrected by steering gated on that detector?
mechanism: PRISMS: (1) rank FFN neurons (layer, index) by their contribution to the residual stream; select the top k (k = m = ceil(0.03 N) over N layer-neuron pairs in the reported setup) to form a shared basis S_f per failure mode. (2) Fit an L1-regularised logistic probe within that basis; its support D_f is the sparse detector, giving a risk score per prompt (decisions read at the final prompt token, or before </think>) and per generated call span (validity). (3) Layerwise steering directions are built independently from the full basis, contribution-selected, bidirectional. (4) Detector-gated control: when risk is low the model is unchanged; when high, suppress over-calling, elicit missing calls, and check argument validity before execution.
training: No weight updates. Probes are fit on natural rollouts from each model (R=8 samples per prompt for decision labels, R=16 for validity) with prompt-level label summaries and prompt-disjoint train/validation/test splits (Appendix A.1-A.2).
setup: Six models: Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-3-4B-IT. Tool-use settings with search engines, code interpreters, databases and APIs. Baselines: Healy et al. (2026) for validity and Sun et al. (2026) Probe&Prefill for over-calling.
numbers: Sec 1 (Figure 1 text): pooled over-calling 0.131 -> 0.026 (80% reduction) and capability accuracy 0.689 -> 0.831 (+14.2 points), detector-gated vs unconditional baseline.
Abstract: over-calling and missing reach ROC-AUC 0.98-1.00 before generation on Qwen3; validity 0.86-0.90 from the call span.
Abstract: 1-2 MLP neurons for missing, 2-16 for over-calling, about 128 for validity.
limits: No limitations section in the read text. The authors note that high detectability does not make a neuron causal, which is why intervention is tested separately; validity is monitored only after generation and before execution.
evidence_quote: It leaves unflagged computation unchanged, suppresses predicted over-calling, elicits calls under predicted missing, and monitors argument validity before execution.

novelty_note.F: Steers tool-calling behaviour (suppresses over-calling and elicits omitted calls), gated by a sparse failure detector. interp: the detector is a separate L1 probe, so it is not a flag-B gate.

title: Controlling Tool Use with Heading-Specific Activation Steering
question: Do tool-use decisions have an extractable internal steering direction, and can it suppress or amplify tool calls?
mechanism: For each trajectory i and layer l, hidden states are averaged at '### Reasoning' anchor positions (h_R) and at the anchor of target heading k (e.g., ### Search, ### Code, ### AskUser) (h_k). Sample delta_{k,i} = h_R - h_k; v_k is the mean of deltas over N_k trajectories (Eqs 1-3). Intervention is applied locally at heading-formation steps at a chosen layer l*: activation addition (sign convention: the text says adding v_k suppresses the tool heading; Figure 1 caption says activation addition 'subtracts' the vector) or orthogonalisation of the hidden state against v_k (amplifies tool use).
training: None. Mean differences over structured trajectories: 60 GPT-4o-generated examples (20 each for Math, Time, Intention) used only for vector extraction.
setup: Five open-source instruct models including Mistral-7B, Mistral-Nemo (12B), Mistral-Small (24B), Llama-3.1-8B and Llama-3.1-70B, across three domains (Math, Time, Intention); baseline Tool Prompt. Figure 1 averages tool calls per query over five models.
numbers: Table 1 (Math): Mistral-7B tool calls per query 3.90 -> 0.56 under activation addition; accuracy drops only modestly.
Table 1 (Math): Llama-3.1-8B 1.93 -> 0.35; Mistral-Small 1.55 -> 0.13 (text, Sec 4).
limits: Authors report that suppression is most effective where parametric reasoning suffices and degrades where retrieval or user clarification is needed. Geometry is diffuse and bimodal, not linear, and tool types recruit distinct features with low cross-tool overlap. The relationship between the geometry and the causal effect is left open.
evidence_quote: Orthogonalization projects hidden states to be orthogonal to the suppression vector at tool-heading positions, removing its suppressive component.

novelty_note.F: Steers tool-calling decisions (suppresses or amplifies tool calls) with a heading-anchored steering vector applied at heading-formation steps.
novelty_note.G: Authors report tool-invocation steps align diffusely and bimodally with the suppression vector rather than consistently, and different tools use low-overlap features. interp: this suggests the signal may not be a single clean linear tool-use concept.

title: Minimizing Collateral Damage in Activation Steering
question: Can a steered activation hit its target alignment with less collateral change to non-target features, by accounting for activation anisotropy?
mechanism: Steering with an alignment budget: find activation x with d.x = alpha (post-steering cosine to target direction d) that minimises expected squared collateral change weighted by the empirical second-moment matrix of activations (Sigma_w = E[w(f) f f^T]); solution lies on a latitude of the hypersphere of normalised activations. COAST performs gradient steps on the sphere: grad J(x) = 2 Sigma (x - h), projected onto the tangent space; interp: iterative per-activation optimisation at inference. Proven to converge to the global minimum in the continuous limit. Reduces to SLERP when features are isotropic.
training: No model weights are trained. The steering target is found by iterative optimisation of the steered activation under the fixed budget (interp: per activation at inference).
inference_cost: 'marginal overhead ... e.g., 0.9% to 4% in our experiments' (Introduction); throughput in tokens/s measured in Sec 4.
setup: Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct among others (Table 1 and Appendix C). Tiny benchmarks: tinyArc, tinyGSM8k, tinyHellaswag, tinyMMLU, tinyTruthfulQA, tinyWinogrande; ASR on safety tasks.
numbers: Intro: up to a 30% improvement in Attack Success Rate over Angular Steering, and up to 20% accuracy gain over ActAdd at the same ASR (paraphrase of the Introduction).
Fig 1 (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct): Pearson r between average collateral damage and accuracy of -0.946, -0.944, -0.970 on tinyArc, tinyGSM8k, tinyHellaswag, and r < -0.9 across six benchmarks.
limits: Authors report that existing methods trade steering success against performance; COAST is shown with overhead and tuning sensitivity. Appendix notes that aggressive step sizes may drive the optimisation off the optimal path, which can be resolved with finer hyperparameter tuning (paraphrase).
evidence_quote: We formalize the concept of collateral damage as the expected unintended alignment shift toward non-target directions

title: Could Inference-Time Interventions Preserve Alignment? Safety Cost of Steering Vectors Is Separable and Reducible
question: Can the safety-degrading component of a steering vector be removed while keeping its steering effect and bounding false refusals?
mechanism: v* = v~ * ||v|| / ||v~|| with v~ = v - r r^T v, where r is a learned unit vector (rank-1 in the main experiments). r is optimised by Lagrangian primal-dual updates with three constraints: (i) harmful prompts under v* refuse at least as often as the unsteered baseline; (ii) on effect prompts the output distribution stays close to that under v; (iii) false refusal on benign prompts stays near the unsteered rate.
training: Gradient-based primal-dual optimisation of one direction r per steering vector. No model weight updates. Dataset sizes are in Sec 5, not read.
setup: Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-8B and Qwen-14B (three models); behaviours self-awareness, power-seeking, corrigibility; seven jailbreak scenarios (None, Prefix, Ref.Sup., AIM, GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR).
numbers: Sec 6: steering increases mean ASR across all three models, with worst-case increase 'exceeding 63% on Qwen-7B'.
Sec 6: refusal-direction ablation recovers 'at most 8% on mean ASR'; CAST-optimised vector reduces mean ASR below the unsteered baseline on both Qwen models and 'to within 1% on Llama-8B'.
limits: Authors note the safety-degrading subspace is not fully characterised by any known direction, so the rank-1 approximation is an assumption; the true dimensionality is unknown. Rank-1 is used in main experiments.
evidence_quote: We identify and remove this safety-degrading component, formulating the task as a constrained optimization problem solved through primal-dual updates, subject to preserving the intended steering effect and bounding false refusal.

title: OPIUM: Mitigating Steering Externalities and Over-Refusal via Dual Objective Latent Optimization
question: Can side effects of steering vectors (safety loss from utility vectors, over-refusal from refusal vectors) be removed in activation space without weight updates?
mechanism: Initialise v from a CAA vector v_A (mean difference over contrastive pairs at layer l). Optimise v to minimise L(v) = ||z^v_m(x^A) - z^{v_A}_m(x^A)||^2 + lambda ||z^v_m(x^B) - z^{v_B}_m(x^B)||^2, matching hidden states at a later layer m > l: on behaviour-A prompts to the steered model, on behaviour-B prompts to the unsteered (or safer) reference. v is projected back to the norm of v_A after each gradient step (Algorithm 1).
training: No weight updates. Gradient optimisation of the steering vector only, using 32 benign and 32 harmful held-out prompts; the paper says it 'converges in minutes'.
setup: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Behaviours: Corrigibility and Survival Instinct (CAA multiple-choice, 80 items each); HarmBench DirectRequest (320 prompts, ASR judged by HarmBench Llama-2-13B); over-refusal with FalseReject and OR-Bench.
numbers: Table 1 (Qwen2.5-7B): base CR 56.29, ASR 32.50; refusal vector CR 38.36, ASR 14.06; OPIUM CR 61.32, ASR 27.50.
Table 1 (Llama-3.1-8B): base CR 43.71; refusal vector CR 38.99, ASR 15.31; OPIUM CR 41.01, ASR 20.31.
limits: Authors state: OPIUM is specific to the vector and task used in optimisation, so each new intervention needs a re-run; it assumes the target behaviour and the externality can be separated by the chosen anchors, which 'may fail when they are semantically entangled' (e.g. language steering pushes refusals into the target language). Layer choice for matching has no principled criterion yet.
evidence_quote: Given reference behaviors on two prompt sets, OPIUM optimizes a new steering vector

title: Improving Instruction-Following in Language Models through Activation Steering
question: Can instruction-specific vectors (format, length, word inclusion) be extracted as activation differences and used to steer models to follow those constraints?
mechanism: Difference-in-means on paired inputs: x = base query and x+ = base query plus instruction; at the last input token and layer l, v_l = mean_i (x+_{i,l} - x_{i,l}), u_l = v_l / ||v_l||. Inference: residual stream x~_l = x_l + c u_l (Figure 1), with c the steering strength. Steering can be applied with no instruction in the prompt, or added on top of an explicit instruction.
training: None: difference of means from forward passes only; training-free.
setup: Phi-3, Gemma 2 2B and 9B, Mistral 7B; IFEval (Zhou et al., 2023a) and an augmented version for format, length and word inclusion/exclusion; compositionality and cross-model transfer also tested.
numbers: Sec 3 (Steering Results): 'the instruction-following accuracy without steering hovers around 10%'; with steering 'accuracy improving to approximately 30%' (Figure 3a, inputs without instructions).
limits: Authors report failure cases: when the steering vector does not capture the specific sentence or word required, adherence does not improve (examples in Sec 3-5). Steering can fail to exclude a specified word (e.g., 'step').
evidence_quote: These vectors are computed as the difference in activations between inputs with and without instructions, enabling a modular approach to activation steering.

novelty_note.D: Converts an instruction (as the activation difference between prompts with and without it) into a steering vector that makes the model follow that instruction when it is absent from the prompt (Sec 2.2, Figure 1).

title: Painless Activation Steering: An Automated, Lightweight Approach for Post-Training Large Language Models
question: Can steering vectors be produced automatically from any labelled dataset, with no hand-written prompt pairs or feature labelling, and do they complement weight or prompt post-training?
mechanism: For each evaluation dimension k, build a positive prompt set P+ and a negative set P- (PAS-Full uses correct vs incorrect items; iPAS variants use the model's own chosen answers, Table 1). Steering vector: a*_l(s_t) = mean over P+ of activations at layer l and target location s_t minus mean over P-. Inference: a_l(s_t) <- a_l(s_t) + lambda a*. Layer, strength and target are tuned on validation (Appendix C: layers 8-25; strengths 0.25 to 32).
training: No gradient training of model weights. Vector construction needs forward passes over the labelled training split; the paper says the PAS pipeline 'completes in about 100 seconds'.
setup: Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, Nous-Hermes-2-Mistral-7B-DPO; 18 tasks: bias and sentiment (10), moral preferences (3), alignment (2), intelligence (3); comparisons with ICL, SFT, and RL.
numbers: Abstract: iPAS improves accuracy by 10.1% on Bias, 5.2% on Morality and 34.8% on Alignment.
Intro: steering vectors are 'at least 5000 times more storage-efficient' than post-trained weights; the whole PAS pipeline 'completes in about 100 seconds', whereas RL 'takes hours, if not days'.
limits: Abstract: PAS 'yields no significant gain on Intelligence tasks'. Limitations section discusses theoretical analysis of limits and multi-layer steering (partly read).
evidence_quote: Compute a steering vector a∗ as the mean activation difference between the two prompt sets at a chosen layer ℓ

title: AlphaSteer: Learning Refusal Steering with Principled Null-Space Constraint
question: Can refusal steering be made to leave benign activations essentially unchanged while steering malicious activations toward refusal?
mechanism: Steering map s = Delta h, where Delta is constrained to the null space of benign activations. The null-space projector P is built from the SVD of the benign non-central covariance H_b H_b^T (Sec 3, around lines 281-298). For benign inputs Delta h_b is near zero, so h' = h + Delta h stays near h. For malicious inputs Delta is fit by linear regression so that Delta h_m approximates a refusal direction r. The paper calls Delta 'trainable' while describing this closed-form construction.
training: Construction from forward-pass activations on benign and malicious prompt sets: null-space projection from SVD and a linear-regression fit for the refusal map. The paper also calls Delta 'trainable'; no gradient training is described in the read sections (interp: closed form).
setup: Multiple jailbreak attacks scored by defence success rate (DSR) with GPT-4o; utility benchmarks. Models and attack list are in Table 1 (not read in detail).
numbers: Sec 4.1: the refusal vector alone (+RV) 'can even consistently refuse all malicious prompts, achieving the DSR of 100% in most cases.'
limits: Authors state: 'the effectiveness of AlphaSteer remains unknown on large reasoning models' and 'the effectiveness on larger models remains unknown' (Sec 5).
evidence_quote: it learns to construct a nearly zero vector for steering benign data, with the null-space constraints.

novelty_note.B: Steering vector s = Delta h is computed from the hidden state with a learned linear map, and is near zero for benign inputs, so the map acts as an input-dependent gate with no separate classifier. interp: the gate is the map itself, not a separate score.

title: Function Vectors in Large Language Models
question: Do ICL tasks get represented by a compact vector that can trigger the task on new inputs?
mechanism: Causal mediation: mean task-conditioned activation of each attention head (abar = mean over ICL prompts, Eq. 2); score each head by CIE(a | p~) = f(p~ | a := abar)[y] - f(p~)[y] on uninformative (shuffled-label) prompts (Eq. 3); keep top heads. The function vector (FV) is the sum of selected head outputs at the last token; it is added to the residual stream at one layer of a zero-shot prompt (v_t FV, Eq. 5).
training: none (forward passes and activation patching over ICL prompts; no gradient training reported)
setup: GPT-J, GPT-NeoX, Llama 2 (70B); over 40 ICL tasks (abstract and intro)

title: In-Context Learning Creates Task Vectors
question: Can ICL be understood as compressing demonstrations into a single query-independent task vector that parameterizes a function applied to the query?
mechanism: Split the forward pass into A (demonstrations -> theta) and f (query + theta -> output). theta is the hidden state at the '->' token at layer L, computed with a dummy query x' (e.g. Plum) so theta does not depend on the query. f is a forward pass on the query alone, with attention to the demonstrations blocked, into which theta is patched at layer L. L is chosen on a development set (accuracy peaks at an intermediate layer for all models).
training: none (forward passes only; no gradient training reported)
setup: LLaMA 7B/13B/30B, GPT-J 6B, Pythia 2.8B/6.9B/12B; 18 tasks in algorithmic, translation, linguistic and factual-knowledge categories; single-token outputs
numbers: Across all models, the separated A/f procedure keeps around 80-90% of regular ICL accuracy (Sec. 3 text; exact table not confirmed from extracted text)
limits: Authors list open questions on how the task vector is constructed and how it is used to compute the output. Experiments use single-token outputs only (stated simplification). Patching layer L is a free parameter selected on dev data.
evidence_quote: To make θ independent of the query x, we use a dummy query (x′ = Plum) and use the representation of → at the Lth layer as θ.

novelty_note.D: A task vector built from in-context demonstrations is patched into the residual stream of a later forward pass, so demonstrations become an activation intervention; the paper does not handle system prompts.

title: How Few-Shot Examples Add Up: A Causal Decomposition of Function Vectors in In-Context Learning
venue: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306 (2026), as stated in the paper header
question: How do individual few-shot examples combine into a function vector (FV), and what do attention contextualization and the QK/V pathways contribute?
mechanism: Per-example sub-FV v_i is the FV extracted with attention restricted so the final token sees only example i and the query. The full n-shot FV is fitted as v_FV ~ sum_i w_i v_i by ordinary least squares, with weights w_i shared across a batch of prompts. Injection accuracy Acc_max (max over layer and scale) is the quality score. An uncontextualized ablation removes cross-example attention. A causal decomposition splits the effect into QK-routing and V-update pathways.
training: none (OLS fit of global weights and forward-pass ablations; no model training reported)
setup: Discrete mapping toy tasks; model names and exact task count not recovered from extracted text (appendix not fully extracted)

evidence_quote: The FV extracted under this restricted attention graph is denoted vi

novelty_note.E: Predicts a multi-demonstration FV as a weighted linear sum of per-example sub-FVs before composition, a partial additivity model. It does not predict interference between separately applied patches, so this flag is weak.

title: Training-Free Task Vectors for LLM Behavioral Control
venue: NeurIPS 2026 (40th Conference), as stated in the paper header
question: Can steering vectors be turned into persistent, compositional weight-space edits without any fine-tuning?
mechanism: Steering vector s_l = mean residual difference between positive and negative contrastive prompt sets at layer l (Eq. 1); normalize s-bar = s/||s||_2. For a module W (d x l) with SVD W = sum_i sigma_i u_i v_i^T and expected input mu, TFTV(W, s-bar, mu) = s-bar (sum_i sign(mu^T v_i) sigma_i v_i)^T (Eq. 2), a rank-one matrix. Edit W <- W + alpha * TFTV on a chosen module set (Eq. 3). Property 1: ||TFTV||_F = ||W||_F, so the update matches the weight norm.
training: none (forward-pass statistics on contrastive prompts; completions are filtered by an LLM judge; no gradient training)
setup: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, gemma-4-E2B-it, Ministral-3-14B-Instruct; five traits (incl. evil, hallucination, sycophancy); MMLU and GSM8K for utility
numbers: Exceeds the strongest training-free baseline in trait score in five of six settings 'by 5.57-53.38 points' (Sec. 5.1, text)
Llama MMLU stays within 0.15 points of the base model across settings (Sec. 5.1 text; Table 2)
limits: Authors state that TFTVs do not eliminate the trade-off between trait control and utility, especially under stronger or composed edits. Performance depends on which modules and layers are edited, and automatic selection is left as future work. Misuse risk is noted because edits are persistent.
evidence_quote: TFTVs convert activation steering directions into rank-one weight updates using only forward-pass statistics

novelty_note.A: Builds a rank-one weight edit from a steering direction plus the SVD of the target matrix, with no training; the closed-form construction uses forward-pass means and the top singular vectors.

title: Steer Like the LLM: Activation Steering that Mimics Prompting
question: Can activation steering be made faithful to prompt steering by learning token-specific steering coefficients that imitate the prompt's effect?
mechanism: Prompt steering is written as an additive change to activations, Al|PS = Al + Delta_PS (Eq. 3). Prompt Steering Replacement (PSR) approximates it: Al|AS = Al + alpha * lambda(Al; theta) * z_attr,l (Eq. 7), where lambda(a; theta) = ReLU(a . w + b) is a per-token scalar coefficient on the layer's own activations (Eq. 8) and z_attr,l is a rank-1 direction. S-PSR edits one layer; A-PSR edits all layers sequentially. Parameters (w, b, z) are trained so the steered activations or output log-likelihood match those of prompt-steered runs, using triplets (x, x', y') filtered by judges.
training: yes: per attribute, gradient training of (w, b, z) on prompt-steered response triplets. Persona-Vectors set: 100 positive and 100 negative prompt pairs, 10 sampled responses per prompt; AxBench: 72 training concepts (Sec. 4 text)
setup: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (plus a third model not confirmed from extracted text); Persona Vectors (trait alignment at coherence 80); AxBench; IFEval
numbers: Text claim (Sec. 5, Persona Vectors): A-PSR (MSE) outperforms prompt steering for all three language models, A-ConstMSE for 2 of 3 (table cells not used because column headers are interleaved in the extraction)
limits: Rank-1 PSR is not expressive enough for all IFEval instruction types: for some types the MSE loss barely improves and prompting stays stronger. Log-likelihood training helped where MSE did not. The authors state the work is a first instantiation of the framework.
evidence_quote: the strength of prompt steering interventions varies significantly across token positions

novelty_note.B: The per-token steering coefficient is a learned ReLU probe on the layer's own hidden state (Eq. 8) that scales a steering vector. It is trained rather than a fixed rule, so it is close to B but not training-free.
novelty_note.D: Trains a replacement model so that an activation intervention reproduces the activation effect of a prompt-based steering instruction.

title: Prompt-Activation Duality: Improving Activation Steering via Attention-Level Interventions
question: Why does residual-stream persona steering lose coherence over multi-turn dialogue, and can steering enter through attention so it follows prompt-mediated pathways?
mechanism: GCAD. Extract the system-prompt contribution to attention: Delta^(l) = mean over positive prompts of the cropped attention-delta, sum over system-prompt source tokens of alpha_{t,i} V_i W_o (Eq. 7). Gate per token: c_i = 2 c_base * sigmoid(s * (d_i - dbar)), where d_i is the head-averaged pre-softmax query-key compatibility with mean system-prompt keys (Eqs. 9-10). Update: a_steered = a + c_t * Delta, applied at the attention output of layers 9-19 (c_base = 3.5, s = 1.5).
training: none (contrastive prompt sets are run forward; no gradient training reported)
inference_cost: one extra dot product per head for the gate, according to the paper (Sec. 4)
setup: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; multi-turn persona steering over 60 conversations; 15-trait average; trait and coherence scored 0-100
numbers: On the main multi-turn benchmark, GCAD improves average coherence drift from -18.6 to -1.9 and raises turn-10 trait expression from 78.0 to 93.1 (abstract)
limits: No limitations section was extracted. The paper reports that a trait with a peak at layer 9, outside the GCAD range, still degrades badly under baseline steering (Humorous). Evaluation is on persona traits with model-assigned scores.
evidence_quote: Since di reuses queries and keys already computed by the model, the gate adds only one dot product per head

novelty_note.B: The gate is a centered sigmoid of a query-key dot product computed from the model's own Q and K, with no separate classifier, and it scales the steering per token.
novelty_note.D: Extracts the steering signal from the system-prompt contribution to attention (cropped attention-delta) and re-injects it at the same attention site.

title: One Token Can Be Enough: Bridging Prompting and Activation Steering with Prefix Steering
question: Under what conditions can steering one token reproduce prompt-induced attention outputs, and does a brief intervention at the final prompt token keep control while preserving capability?
mechanism: Prefix Steering: apply an existing additive steering direction (or COAST operator) over a short span of tokens starting at the final prompt token, with no intervention after that span. Theory: under fixed-state attention assumptions, steering one existing token can match the attention-head output of an added prompt token exactly when W^K(h_p - h_tn) and W^K r lie in a matching subspace U, with error growing with distance from that set (Lemmas 1-2).
training: none (difference-in-means directions from forward passes)
setup: Four models and five tasks; OLMo 3 7B for the duration sweep, HarmBench (control) and MMLU-Pro (capability); additive steering and COAST
limits: The authors state that the attention-level match does not determine the best steering strength, because repeated interventions also change later representations. The theory relies on fixed-state assumptions and does not establish equivalence with prompting. No numeric result table was extracted; the duration results are reported in Figure 3 (not read numerically).
evidence_quote: directions and operators over a short span starting at the final prompt token, with no further direct intervention afterward

title: PRISM: Recovering Instruction Sets from Language Model Activations
question: Can a frozen model's activations be decoded into the full set of instructions, constraints and subgoals that steer its response?
mechanism: Activation snapshot H_l = residual-stream activations at selected generated-token positions of a frozen target model (prompt positions excluded). A learned projection maps H_l into the embedding space as a soft prefix to an interpreter that reuses the base weights with LoRA and decodes a bullet list. Training: supervised pretraining, then GRPO where an LLM judge scores coverage and hallucinated bullets, reward R = coverage minus penalties, and the policy update uses group-relative advantages.
training: yes: supervised pretraining on instruction lists, then judge-guided GRPO (RL) on the interpreter; training data includes benign multi-instruction sets and 24,953 public prompt-injection examples (intro/Sec. 3 text)
setup: Target model Qwen3.5-9B (also Gemma and Ministral reporters); benign, constrained, prompt-injection and hidden-objective evaluation sets; judge calibrated with Cohen's kappa

Average reward 0.754 vs 0.532 for the strongest non-PRISM baseline (intro)

evidence_quote: A learned projection maps these states into the model’s embedding space, where they are consumed as a soft prefix by the interpreter

title: Memory Inception: Latent-Space KV Cache Manipulation for Steering LLMs
question: Can reminder or guidance text be held as latent KV slots that attend only at selected layers and heads, instead of being cached at every layer or added as a residual offset?
mechanism: A memory bank B = {(k_m, v_m)} of latent KV slots is encoded from the guidance text. At a selected site, the bank is concatenated with the prompt KV cache (Eq. 2). Sites are chosen by a calibration selector: score a_{l,u} = max_j q k_target / sqrt(d) - max_j q k_ref / sqrt(d) per unit, keep top-k units per layer and top-m layers, with layer gains rho_l. Multi-bank routing is a softmax over bank evidence, with size-normalized log-sum-exp scores (Eqs. 4-5).

inference_cost: KV-storage reduction only: 6.4x in the long-context Llama case and 60-118x in other settings (Table 1 and Sec. 5). Realized latency and VRAM were not measured.

Content-matched KV storage cut by up to 118x (abstract; 60-118x in Table 1)

Authors note the mechanism could be misused for covert behaviour shaping.

novelty_note.F: Routes attention over text-derived banks that can hold retrieved facts, a memory-retrieval use. No retrieval or tool-call decision is steered; the routing is attention-level.

title: First-Order Steering: Translating Weight Adaptation into Activation Steering
question: Can a differentiable model-merging procedure over LoRA adapters be turned into composable activation steering vectors, and which merges make those vectors accurate?
mechanism: For a merged model g(x, s) with steering strengths s, the first-order steering direction for behaviour i is a column of the Jacobian of the hidden layer with respect to s. Composed behaviours add as vectors. The approximation error is bounded by Hessian norms. HeRD-Merging trains per-subset matrices R_S by gradient descent to reduce the mixed-Jacobian and Hessian error terms while keeping merge accuracy.

title: Local Linearity of LLMs Enables Activation Steering via Model-Based Linear Optimal Control

The feature setpoint beta_k* comes from a linear feature setpoint (LFS) procedure; the steering magnitude is adapted from the online-observed feature error v_k^T z_k - beta_k*. title: When Does Activation Steering Change What a Model Computes From?
question: Does a successful activation steering vector recreate the state the model naturally uses, or only bias the output toward the target?
mechanism: Counterfactual register editing: estimate a rank-16 register subspace U from class-conditional mean differences at layer 12 (validation-selected). Edit z~ = z + Pi_U(mu(s~) - mu(s)) at the current-state token, flipping only the hidden bit. Score register agreement R and Counterfactual Update Selectivity CUS on discriminating items. Compare with mean-activation (function-vector-style) steering: transplant the target activation at one layer and scale the steering vector to the natural activation difference.

title: HyperSteer: Activation Steering at Scale with Hypernetworks
question: Can one hypernetwork generate steering vectors for arbitrary steering prompts so steering scales to thousands of prompts and generalizes to unseen ones?
mechanism: A transformer hypernetwork H reads the steering prompt s. The cross-attention variant also reads the residual stream of the base LM on the base prompt x, and an MLP on the final token state outputs Delta_xs in R^d (Eqs. 2-3). Delta is added to the base model residual at layer 20. The hypernetwork is trained end-to-end with the LM cross-entropy of the steered output against AxBench labels (Eq. 4).

title: UniSteer: Text-Guided Flow Matching in Activation Space for Versatile LLM Steering
question: Can one text-conditioned flow over residual-stream activations replace a separate steering direction or module for each behaviour?
mechanism: Train a conditional flow model v_theta(a_t, t, c, l, i) over activations of a frozen LLM, with linear path a_t = (1-t) a_0 + t a_1, a_0 ~ N(0, I), target velocity a_1 - a_0, loss E||v_theta - u_t||^2 (Eqs. 2-4). Editing (flow inversion): partially invert the source activation under the source condition to tau = 1 - lambda, then transport forward under the target condition: a_edit = F_{tau->1}(F_{1->tau}(a_src; c_src); c_tgt). The edited activation is injected back into the frozen LLM. The same model classifies by reconstruction energy.

title: Self-Updatable Large Language Models by Integrating Context into Model Parameters
venue: ICLR 2025 (header states 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025')
question: Can context be integrated into a model's parameters so the model answers questions about it without the context and without extra storage?
mechanism: SELF-PARAM: an original model with the context in its prompt is the teacher. The target model is the same network without the context. Minimize KL divergence between the teacher's and target's next-token predictions over a target sentence set (generated QA pairs from an instruct model plus sentences from the pretraining data). No new parameters are added and no retrieval is used at inference.

inference_cost: zero additional parameters or storage, per the abstract

title: Belief Dynamics Reveal the Dual Nature of In-Context Learning and Activation Steering
question: Do ICL and activation steering both act by updating belief in latent concepts, and can a closed-form model predict their effect?
mechanism: Bayesian account: log posterior odds of concept c given context x are log(p(c)/p(c')) + evidence from the context + a*m, where m is steering magnitude (Sec. 4.3). The prior-odds term is replaced by a constant offset b. ICL evidence accumulates with context length N and with the number of shots, giving a sigmoidal behaviour curve; steering gives a sigmoidal trend in the magnitude. Parameters a, b, gamma, alpha are fitted to averaged behaviour by L-BFGS.
training: none for the model itself; a few scalar parameters are fitted to averaged behaviour with L-BFGS
setup: Llama-3.1-8B (persona-matching: Dark Triad and Moral Nihilism datasets; flipped-label sentiment); Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct analysis

limits: Steering vectors used in practice are not the true concept vectors, so the magnitude-to-effect scale is only proportional. The prior odds b are estimated rather than observed from the concept priors p(c). The model is a predictive account on the tested tasks and contexts.

novelty_note.E: Predicts the context length or steering magnitude at which the behaviour flips, from a closed-form fit, and states that ICL and steering interventions are additive in log-belief space, which would predict the combined effect of two interventions.

title: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
question: Can a steering vector built from contrastive multiple-choice answer pairs, added to the residual stream at inference, shift Llama 2 Chat behaviour on alignment-relevant traits?
mechanism: For a chosen layer L, run each contrast pair (same question; one prompt ends with the behaviour-positive answer letter, the other with the behaviour-negative letter) and record residual-stream activations at the answer-letter token. Steering vector = mean over pairs of (a_L(positive) - a_L(negative)). At inference, add multiplier x vector to the residual stream at all token positions after the user instruction (multipliers 2 and -2 in the sycophancy example, Table 1). Layer chosen by sweep.
training: none for the vector: forward passes over contrast pairs and a mean difference, no gradient training. The packet gives no pair count beyond 'hundreds of diverse contrast pairs'.
setup: Llama 2 7B Chat and 13B Chat (base 7B used for vector similarity/transfer); behaviours include coordination with other AIs, corrigibility, hallucination, myopic reward, survival instinct, sycophancy and refusal; multiple-choice behavioural evals and GPT-4-rated open-ended generation on a 1-10 scale.

title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
question: Is refusal in chat models mediated by a single one-dimensional direction in the residual stream, and can that direction be removed by a simple weight edit?
mechanism: Difference-in-means direction r^(l) = mean activation on harmful instructions minus mean on harmless instructions, per layer l and post-instruction token position; one candidate (layer, position) is selected on validation prompts by bypassing refusal when ablated and inducing refusal when added. title: Refusal in LLMs is an Affine Function

It combines removing the existing component along r (directional ablation) with adding back the chosen offset (CAA).

title: On the Non-Identifiability of Steering Vectors in Large Language Models
question: Is a steering vector uniquely recoverable from behaviour, or do large equivalence classes of behaviourally indistinguishable vectors exist?
mechanism: Local linearisation: o(x,v,alpha) ≈ o(x,0,0) + alpha J_l(x) v, with J_l the Jacobian of output logits with respect to the hidden state at layer l. Any perturbation v_perp in ker(J) leaves the first-order output unchanged. The null-space dimension is estimated by SVD of the activation covariance matrix over the same contrast pairs; equivalence is tested by adding orthogonal perturbations to a steering vector and comparing effect sizes (Cohen's d) using a pre-trained semantic classifier and raw logits.
training: none for the steering vectors (CAA and other extraction methods); the study is analytic plus forward-pass experiments.
setup: Two model families at mid-network layers, five semantic traits; extraction methods including contrastive and PCA vectors; several prompt distributions.
numbers: Results (equivalence paragraph, full text): cosine similarities between the two vectors 'range from −0.54 to +0.32', while 'Cohen's d remains below 0.27 in all conditions'.

limits: Empirical validation covers two models at mid-network layers across five traits; magnitude may vary by model family, scale and layer (Limitations).
The authors do not verify that the SVD-estimated semantic null space coincides with the Jacobian null space (Limitations).
evidence_quote: Empirically, we find that orthogonal perturbations achieve near-equivalent efficacy with negligible effect sizes across multiple models and traits

novelty_note.G: Shows that orthogonal perturbations to a steering vector, which leave the logits unchanged to first order, produce the same behavioural effect, so 'the observed behavioral effect of steering does not localize semantic content to a specific direction' (paper's wording).

title: Endogenous Resistance to Activation Steering in Language Models

title: Understanding Unreliability of Steering Vectors in Language Models: Geometric Predictors and the Limits of Linear Approximations
venue: Master's thesis, Eberhard Karls University of Tübingen (submitted June 2025; arXiv Feb 2026)
question: Why does steering reliability differ across behaviours, and what geometry of the training data predicts it?
mechanism: CAA steering vector from the mean of training activation differences. Diagnostics: (i) directional agreement, the cosine between each training activation difference and the steering vector; (ii) separability of positive and negative activations along the difference-of-means line, quantified by a discriminability index; (iii) separability along the first LDA component and along a logistic-regression direction, used as diagnostics; (iv) convergence of the steering vector across subsamples. title: What Drives Representation Steering? A Mechanistic Case Study on Steering Refusal
question: Through which model components (attention OV vs QK circuits, MLPs) does a refusal steering vector act, and can the vector be sparsified?
mechanism: Refusal steering: difference of mean activations on harmful versus harmless instructions (following Arditi et al.), added as alpha * s at every token position including the prompt. Multi-token activation patching extended to steered generation; edges scored with EAP-IG (edge attribution patching with integrated gradients) by their indirect effect on the steered output. Steering value vector decomposition: the steering vector's contribution through the OV circuit is decomposed per dimension and interpreted. Sparsification keeps the most important dimensions of the steering vector (selection rule not captured from packet).
training: none for the steering vector (difference of means); EAP-IG uses gradients for attribution only.
setup: Gemma 2 2B Instruct, Llama 3.2 3B Instruct and Qwen 3 8B (non-thinking); harmful training data from AdvBench, MaliciousInstruct, TDC2023 and HarmBench; 100 JailbreakBench harmful and 100 Alpaca harmless test prompts.

Contributions item 1: different steering methodologies 'leverage highly interchangeable circuits (≳ 90% overlap)'.
limits: interp: analysis is limited to refusal steering on three models; generality to other behaviours is not tested in the packet.
evidence_quote: indicating that the refusal vector largely ignores the QK circuit

title: A Geometric Account of Activation Steering through Angle-Norm Decomposition
question: Is concept information carried by the angle or the norm of a hidden state, and does the norm matter for steering stability?
mechanism: Decompose hidden state x = r u with u = c s + sqrt(1 - c^2) v, where r is the norm, s the concept direction, c the angular concept score and v the unit direction orthogonal to s. Six steering methods are compared in this framework. The main new one is spherical steering with norm scaling: y = beta r (gamma s + sqrt(1 - gamma^2) v), gamma the target concept score and beta a radial scale; beta = 1 reduces to norm-preserving spherical steering. Probes trained on normalised versus raw hidden states test where concept information lies.
training: Linear probes are trained on hidden states to test concept encoding; the interventions themselves are training-free.
setup: Seven language models from 1B to 70B parameters (including Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct); four concept datasets; evaluation by fold (Figure 2).
numbers: Contributions: 'modest norm increases can reduce perplexity by up to 1.8× without substantially changing the semantic steering effect'.

title: On the Steering Dimensionality of Refusal in Language Models
venue: 40th NeurIPS 2026, Workshop: Interpretability as a Science (per header)
question: How many steering directions (the steering dimensionality) are needed to reliably induce and suppress refusal, and does this differ between safety-triggered and general refusal?
mechanism: Steering subspace V_k from a contrast matrix H of last-token activation differences: top-k PCA components, SVD right singular vectors, or K-means centroids. Additive steering: h' = h + V_k^T alpha_k with per-direction coefficients. Directional ablation: h' = (I - P_k) h, where P_k is the orthogonal projection onto the row space of V_k, written with the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse (eq. 2). A behaviour is t-dimensionally steerable when steering effect grows monotonically up to dimension t and saturates beyond it. Safety refusal contrast uses harmful versus harmless prompts; general refusal contrast instructs the model to write a refusing and an affirming response to the same harmless query.
training: none: PCA, SVD and K-means over contrast activations; the general-refusal contrast responses are generated by prompting the model.
setup: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (the two models named in the implementation details); 3 rollouts per input at temperature 0.6; Qwen3.8-27B used as judge, retaining 200 response pairs.

Results: for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, steerability 'largely saturates beyond a 3-dim steering subspace using K-Means, yet directional ablation remains ineffective across all four evaluation settings' (general refusal).
limits: For Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, directional ablation 'substantially degrades response coherence' (Results); the authors read this as the subspace being entangled with general capabilities, which they say is undesirable.
evidence_quote: Although directional ablation can alter refusal behavior, it also substantially degrades response coherence.

novelty_note.D: For general refusal, the model is instructed to write a refusing response and an affirming response to the same harmless query, and these instruction-driven responses supply the contrast activations for the steering subspace.
novelty_note.E: Measures a dimensional capacity limit (the minimum number of directions one behaviour needs; a 5-dim subspace is insufficient for general refusal); this is per behaviour, not a prediction of interference between separate patches.
novelty_note.G: Reports that the extracted subspace for Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct degrades coherence, which the authors read as the steering signal being entangled with general capabilities rather than the refusal concept alone.

title: The Sharp Directions Are Against You: Curvature Analysis of Activation Steering
question: Why is CAA fragile (anti-steering on many inputs), and can removing the high-curvature part of the steering vector fix it without retraining?
mechanism: Steering Hessian H_steer = d^2 L / dv^2, where L is the next-token cross-entropy of a target token under the steered model, differentiated with respect to the steering vector v. Top-k eigenvectors by |lambda| form the sharp subspace S_k, estimated by Lanczos (m = 40 iterations, full reorthogonalisation) with Hessian-vector products from central finite differences over n = 12 prompts. Sharp removal: v_cleaned = v_CAA - P_{S_k} v_CAA. Proposition 2 bounds the direction change (cosine ≥ 1 - eps) and the curvature reduction kappa_gap = |lambda_1| / |lambda_{k+1}|; default k = 15.
training: none to the model: the Hessian is estimated by finite differences of gradients over a small prompt set (n = 12), and the correction is a one-off projection of the CAA vector.
setup: Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B; four behavioural tasks; 36 token-level conditions (3 models x 4 tasks x 3 layers); open-ended generation over 25 conditions; refusal correction tested on Arditi et al.'s refusal direction (Sec 5.6).
numbers: Abstract: removing the sharp component 'approximately preserves its direction and magnitude (cosine > 0.974, norm reduction < 3% for typical settings) while reducing the vector's directional curvature by up to 12× (median 4× across 36 conditions)'.
Abstract: 'Sharp directions account for only 1–5% of the CAA vector's squared norm'; steering along them 'reverses the intended behavior in every condition tested, with anti-steer rates of 53–100%'.
Abstract: sharp removal 'outperforms standard CAA in open-ended generation across all 25 conditions tested'.
limits: Sharp removal is a post-processing step on the vector; the packet reports no inference-time cost beyond the one-off Hessian estimate.
Target-token robustness: the multi-token contrastive variant has cosine 0.61 with the single-token version (Sec 3.1).
evidence_quote: Removing the sharp component of a steering vector approximately preserves its direction and magnitude (cosine > 0.974, norm reduction < 3% for typical settings)

novelty_note.G: Argues the CAA vector's sharp-direction component acts as noise rather than signal: 'sharp directions act as noise rather than signal: they disrupt coherent behavioral control regardless of steering polarity' (abstract); CAA has the wrong sign on three of four tasks at most layers, so the vector's effect is driven by curvature rather than the intended concept.

title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
question: Where do autoregressive transformers store factual associations, and can one mid-layer MLP be edited to change a single fact?
mechanism: Causal tracing: corrupt the subject tokens with noise, then restore single hidden states from the clean run; mid-layer MLP outputs at the last subject token carry the decisive effect. ROME edits one MLP projection W at layer l*: k* is the subject key at the last subject token, v* is optimized so the layer outputs the new object, and the update is closed form, W_new = W + Lambda (C^-1 k*)^T with Lambda = (v* - W k*) / ((C^-1 k*)^T k*), where C = K K^T is the uncentered key covariance pre-cached from a Wikipedia sample (Eq. 2, Sec. 3.1).
training: No network training. Each edit optimizes only the target value vector v* (Fig. 4 caption: 'value v* is optimized'). C is estimated once from a sample of Wikipedia text (Appendix E.5; sample size not extracted). The paper states the method edits a single fact at a time.
setup: GPT-2 XL on zsRE (10,000 records; compared against FT, FT+L, KE, KE-zsRE, MEND, MEND-zsRE) and on the authors' CounterFact dataset of counterfactual assertions.
numbers: Table 1, zsRE on GPT-2 XL: ROME Efficacy 99.8 (+/-0.0), Paraphrase 88.1 (+/-0.5), Specificity 24.2 (+/-0.5); unedited GPT-2 XL Efficacy 22.2 (+/-0.5).
Sec. 3.4 human evaluation: evaluators are '1.8 times more likely to rate ROME as more consistent with the inserted fact' and rate ROME '1.3 times less likely to be more fluent than the FT+L model'.
limits: Edits are directional: 'The iconic landmark in Seattle is the Space Needle' is stored separately from the reverse statement, so both need two edits (Sec. 5).
Edits one fact at a time and is 'not intended as a practical method for large-scale model training' (Sec. 5).
Human evaluators rated ROME text as somewhat less fluent than FT+L (Sec. 3.4).
Logical, spatial and numerical knowledge were not investigated (Sec. 5).
evidence_quote: In a convolutional network, Bau et al. solve this using an optimization, but in a fully-connected layer, we can derive a closed form solution:

novelty_note.A: Closed-form rank-one update of one MLP projection computed from key and value vectors taken from forward passes, but applied to a single fact rather than a behaviour.
novelty_note.C: The pre-cached covariance inverse C^-1 sets the update direction (C^-1 k*); it is not used as a gate or steering direction.

title: On the Limitations of Rank-One Model Editing in Answering Multi-hop Questions
question: Does editing one fact with ROME support multi-hop reasoning, and does spreading the same edit over several layers help?
mechanism: Redundant Editing: run ROME independently at several MLP layers (the 5th to 20th, e.g. layers 5, 8, 11, 15, 17, 20) and load all edited MLP layers into one model, so the same fact is stored at several depths. Each per-layer edit uses ROME's rank-one update, which Sec. 3.2 writes as Delta W = (k_s^T k_s)^-1 k_s^T (v_o* - W k_s), with k_s the subject activation and v_o* the desired output, both taken from forward passes. Layer combinations are chosen by sweeping, and the paper stops at 6 layers because COUNTERFACT language metrics start to fail.
training: No gradient training of the model is described. The paper inherits ROME's editing procedure and does not restate how v_o* is obtained.
setup: GPT-J-6B; MQuAKE 2-hop questions (2HQ) with single-hop edits; COUNTERFACT for specificity and naturalness metrics.
numbers: Abstract: 'improve accuracy on 2-hop questions by at least 15.5 percentage points, representing a 96% increase over the previous single-edit strategy'.
Sec. 5 (configuration 5,8,11,15,17,20): 'a 15.5 percentage point (96.3%) multi-hop accuracy gain compared to the vanilla single edit strategy'.
limits: Trades off specificity and language naturalness on COUNTERFACT; configurations beyond 6 layers show clear failures (Table 3 caption).
Overfitting: when hop-1 is edited, models sometimes prefer the edited hop-1 answer over the correct 2HQ answer (overfitting analysis, Table 4).
Analysis does not extend to other editors (fine-tuning, representation editing), other architectures, 3+ hop questions, or simultaneous multi-hop edits (Sec. 9).
evidence_quote: Redundant Editing strategy: insert copies of a same approach designed to edit both shallow and deep MLP

title: Unified Concept Editing in Diffusion Models
question: Can one closed-form edit of text-to-image cross-attention weights erase, debias and moderate many concepts at once without degrading unrelated generation?
mechanism: UCE updates the key and value projections W of cross-attention layers. With edit concepts c_i mapped to target vectors v_i* and preserved concepts c_j kept at W_old c_j, the closed form (Eq. 7) is W = (sum_i v_i* c_i^T + sum_j W_old c_j c_j^T)(sum_i c_i c_i^T + sum_j c_j c_j^T)^-1. The paper says this generalizes TIME and MEMIT. Debiasing (Alg. 1) keeps one vector per attribute value, adjusts its magnitude alpha <- eta (R_curr - R_des) on each iteration, and moves a concept to the preserve set once its ratio is within 0.05 of the desired ratio.
training: None: the paper states the edit is a closed-form solution and 'edits the model without training'. Debiasing uses an iterative loop over alpha that re-measures generated-image ratios (Alg. 1) rather than gradient training.
setup: Stable Diffusion cross-attention weights; erasure of up to 100 artist styles, debiasing of 35 Winobias professions, and nudity moderation on I2P prompts; COCO-30k for fidelity; Winobias and I2P for bias and safety metrics.
numbers: Joint-debiasing paragraph: 'a gender ratio deviation of 0.27 versus 0.22 for the gender-debiasing model and 0.67 for the original Stable Diffusion'.
Table 1 caption: 'Our method can erase upto 100 concepts while performing similar to pre-trained SD on COCO-30k dataset.'
limits: Removing over 500 artists degrades general image generation even with preservation terms (Discussion, before the Conclusion): the authors say 'a critical mass of artists is needed'.
Intro reports that in prior work debiasing one concept affects others; the authors claim their procedure eliminates this mutual effect.
interp: word-level composition effects, e.g. 'successful person' becoming 88% male of 100, are an example the paper gives of biases that per-attribute edits may not cover.
evidence_quote: Our method adopts that concept-erasure approach, and we benchmark against the previous state-of-the-art.

novelty_note.A: A low-rank closed-form edit of existing cross-attention weights, computed from text-encoder embeddings, that changes a behaviour (erasure, debiasing, moderation) rather than a single fact.
novelty_note.E: Reports an empirical capacity limit: erasing more than about 500 artists degrades general generation even with preservation terms.

title: LEACE: Perfect linear concept erasure in closed form
question: Is there a closed-form, minimal-distortion way to make a representation linearly unable to predict a concept, and can it be applied at every layer of a language model?
mechanism: Theorem 4.2: with W = (Sigma_XX)^(+1/2) (the whitening transform) and Sigma_XZ the cross-covariance, the minimal-distortion affine erasure is P* = I - W^+ P_{W Sigma_XZ} W, where P_{W Sigma_XZ} = (W Sigma_XZ)(W Sigma_XZ)^+ is the orthogonal projection onto the column space of W Sigma_XZ, and the bias is b* = E[X] - P* E[X]. Concept scrubbing (Alg. 1) fits (P, b) on the hidden states at each layer, applies x -> P(x - mu) + mu, and passes the edited states to the next layer.
training: None gradient-based: the paper says LEACE 'does not require gradient-based optimization' and needs only covariance statistics, which can be computed in a streaming fashion. Scrubbing caches hidden states for training (up to 500GB in the authors' runs); recomputing them instead raises compute from O(l) to O(l^2) (Sec. 6.1).
setup: Pythia 160M to 12B and LLaMA 7B to 30B, erasing part-of-speech information from the input of each transformer block (Pile and RedPajama samples); BERT embeddings for gender bias in profession prediction.
numbers: Sec. 5: LEACE 'is around 2 orders of magnitude faster' than RLACE and does not require gradient-based optimization.
Sec. 5 (BERT): 'profession-prediction accuracy of 77.3% on the projected embeddings (compared with 79.3% over the original embeddings)'.
limits: Only linear concept erasure is studied; the authors 'conjecture that it is intractable to nondestructively edit X' against a general nonlinear adversary (Sec. 7).
Scrubbing caches hidden states for training (up to 500GB in the authors' runs); recomputing them instead raises compute from O(l) to O(l^2) (Sec. 6.1).
SAL, the full-rank baseline, causes larger perplexity increases than LEACE (Table 1).
evidence_quote: Instead, we would like to erase all linear information about a concept in the activations at every layer, which we term concept scrubbing.

novelty_note.C: Uses the whitening transform (Sigma_XX)^(+1/2) and a cross-covariance projection to remove a concept; it is an erasure of a feature rather than a gate or steering vector.

title: Controlling Language and Diffusion Models by Transporting Activations
question: Can inference-time activation steering match the optimal-transport map between source and target activation distributions, preserving those distributions, and control LLMs and diffusion models?
mechanism: Linear-ACT: for each activation coordinate, a univariate affine map T(a) = omega a + beta fitted from sorted samples A and B of source and target activations, with omega = sum_i a~(i) b~(i) / sum_i (b~(i))^2 and beta = m_b - omega m_a (Def. 3.1, using recentred sorted values). Strength lambda interpolates (1 - lambda) a + lambda T(a); lambda = 1 is full transport. A transport support limits maps to in-distribution activations. Mean-ACT and several prior steering vectors are shown to be special cases (Sec. 3.3, Table 1).
training: None gradient-based: the map is 'recovered in closed form' from sorted sample values (Def. 3.1). The sample size for each experiment is not extracted from the text read.
inference_cost: Reported as no computational overhead at inference time, because the map can be composed with the adjacent linear layer (Sec. 3.1, Appendix A).
setup: Gemma2-2B and Llama3-8B on RealToxicityPrompts (1000 prompts; toxicity, perplexity on 20k Wikipedia sentences, MMLU) and on TruthfulQA; SDXL and FLUX for style control and concept negation.
numbers: Sec. 4 (toxicity, Table 2): Linear-ACT achieves 'up to 7.5x reduction in toxicity on Gemma2-2B and 4.3x on Llama3-8B' with minimal impact on PPL and MMLU.
Sec. 4 (TruthfulQA, Table 3): 'increases MC1 by roughly 5% for Gemma2-2B and by almost 8% for Llama3-8B' at lambda = 1.
limits: No limitations section for Linear-ACT was found in the read text; Table 2 shows a small PPL increase and MMLU drop in some settings (e.g. MMLU 51.3 (-1.8) for Post-LN).
interp: per-coordinate univariate maps do not model correlations between activation dimensions (a reading of Def. 3.1, not a stated limitation).
