title: AROMA: Autonomous Rank-one Matrix Adaptation
question: Can LoRA rank be grown automatically, layer by layer, to use far fewer parameters than fixed-rank LoRA or AdaLoRA?
mechanism: Dual-loop rank-one growth: each module starts at rank zero and adds one rank-one LoRA component at a time. The inner loop trains the current rank-one component (Delta W = sum_i B_i A_i) until an inner convergence criterion is met; the outer loop adds components until an outer criterion stops growth. Optimizer states are reset between components to keep subspaces independent (Sec. 4, Fig. 2).
training: Gradient-based fine-tuning with Adam: RoBERTa-base on GLUE, and LLaMA3-8B on commonsense170K. Automatic termination in the MRPC example occurs at 1600 to 2400 steps (Fig. 1 caption).
setup: RoBERTa-base on GLUE tasks compared with full fine-tuning, BitFit, adapters, LoRA r=1/8/16 and AdaLoRA; LLaMA3-8B on commonsense170K evaluated on ARC, OBQA, SIQA, PIQA, BoolQ and others.
numbers: Intro: AROMA uses '<10% of the parameters required by LoRA r=8 and AdaLoRA r=8 without prespecified rank'.
GLUE table (RoBERTa-base): LoRA r=8 1.34M parameters, average 85.43; full fine-tuning 125.0M parameters, average 85.40.
limits: Not yet tested in multimodal applications, and scalability to LLMs above 100B parameters is not validated (Limitations section).
Uses gradient-based training, so it does not reduce the training cost that closed-form methods target.
evidence_quote: Workflow of AROMA. For each module, AROMA trains rank-one matrices sequentially with a dual-loop architecture.

title: Keys to Robust Edits: from Theoretical Insights to Practical Advances
question: Why do locate-and-edit methods fail robustness tests (paraphrased or shuffled subjects, long context), and can disentangled keys fix this?
mechanism: Analysis: a fact's key (the MLP input used by ROME-style editors) is compared in a whitened space; the paper shows that keys for rephrased or shuffled subjects diverge, and that unrelated entities overlap (key collisions). REP (Robust Edit Pathway) adds an adapter to the key: k_hat = f_gate(k) * f_proj(k) + k (Eq. 3). The projection is trained with an aggregation loss that pulls same-subject keys toward the target key k* under the C^-1 whitened inner product (Eq. 4), plus a consistency loss (Eq. 6, L = L_agg + alpha L_consistency). At test time a token-level gate threshold tau decides whether the projection is applied.
training: Gradient-trained adapter (projection and gate) on keys of the same subject; the paper states REP 'requires additional training steps to learn the adapter parameters'. Training sizes are not extracted.
inference_cost: Not quantified; the authors state REP adds computational overhead compared to direct editing methods (Sec. 9).
setup: ROME, MEMIT, R-ROME and EMMET on LLaMA2-7B, Mistral-7B and Qwen2-7B, using CounterFact and ZsRE; robustness tests of paraphrased subjects, shuffled subject tokens and long context.
numbers: Abstract: REP 'improves success rate over robustness tests by up-to 66.4% while maintaining the success rate unaffected'.
Table 1 (EMMET row) contains the entry '82.7+66.4'; the abstract attributes the up-to 66.4-point gain to REP on robustness tests.
limits: Single-fact editing only; interrelated or continual edits are left open (Sec. 9).
Requires additional training of the adapter, adding overhead (Sec. 9).
Only locate-and-edit methods are studied; other editors are not covered (Sec. 9).
evidence_quote: Figure 2: Overview of REP. Left: Key concept visualization; Right: Architectural design of the adapter.

novelty_note.C: Whitened-space similarity under ROME's covariance inverse decides which keys match, a covariance-inverse metric rather than a gate or steering direction built from discriminant analysis.
novelty_note.G: Shows key collisions: 'Michael Jordan' and 'Kobe Bryant' overlap in the whitened space, so the similarity signal reflects relatedness rather than the intended fact.

title: WISE: Rethinking the Knowledge Memory for Lifelong Model Editing of Large Language Models
question: Can lifelong model editing satisfy reliability, generalization and locality together, if edits are stored in a side memory rather than in the main weights or in retrieved activations?
mechanism: A side FFN value matrix W_v' holds the edits while the main W_v stays frozen. A routing indicator Delta_act(x) = ||A(x) (W_v' - W_v)||_2 (Eq. 3), computed from the layer's activation A(x), is trained with a margin loss (Eq. 5) so that edit inputs score above beta and irrelevant inputs below alpha. The threshold epsilon is the smallest edit score seen so far; at inference the side memory is used if Delta_act(x) > epsilon, otherwise the main memory (Eq. 6). Continual edits are split into shards in distinct parameter subspaces and merged into one shared side memory (WISE-Merge) without conflicts (Sec. 2.3).
training: Gradient-based: each shard's side memory is trained with the autoregressive loss plus the routing loss L_a (Sec. 2.3); the main model is not updated. Edit counts go up to T=1000 in Table 2.
inference_cost: Reported: WISE-Merge adds 'constant additional costs (0.64% extra parameters and 4% extra GPU VRAM)'; WISE-Retrieve inference time rises by 'about 7% after 3K edits' (inference-time analysis).
setup: LLaMA-2-7B and Mistral-7B on ZsRE QA, hallucination and out-of-distribution sets, with sequential edits T = 1, 10, 100, 1000; baselines ROME, MEMIT, MEMIT-MASS, FT-EWC, MEND, DEFER and GRACE.
numbers: Table 2 (ZsRE, LLaMA-2-7B, T=100): WISE Reliability 0.90, Generalization 0.81, Locality 1.00, Average 0.90; ROME at T=100 Average 0.16.
Table 2 (LLaMA-2-7B, T=1000): WISE Average 0.83 vs GRACE 0.67 and MEMIT-MASS 0.65.
limits: Side-memory retrieval has room for improvement to reach the oracle (Table 6).
WISE-Retrieve's inference time grows with the number of edits (Fig. 6).
Because edits live in a separate side memory, users can discard them without modifying the main LLM (Limitations and Broader Impacts).
evidence_quote: We only edit the knowledge in the side memory and train a router to decide which memory to go through when given a query.

novelty_note.B: The routing indicator Delta_act(x) is computed from the layer's own FFN activation with no separate classifier and selects between two weight branches per input; it routes a trained weight edit rather than a steering vector.

title: $μ$KE: Matryoshka Unstructured Knowledge Editing of Large Language Models
question: Does unstructured (long-form) knowledge editing with window-by-window updates break dependencies between early memory edits and later output tokens, and can a Matryoshka objective fix it?
mechanism: Locate-and-edit computes working-memory updates delta_i at selected layers for each window, then maps them to weights with constrained optimization. The Matryoshka objective L_mu is a weighted mean in which each working memory is trained against all later target tokens, so gradients flow from later tokens back to earlier memories; adaptive coefficients lambda_{i,j} balance window terms according to the affinity of their gradient directions (Sec. 3.2-3.3).
training: Gradient-based: working memories and weight shifts are optimized with gradient descent; edit batch size 1 and decoding temperature 0.001, following AnyEdit (Sec. 4). No training-data size is extracted.
setup: Two LLMs on five unstructured-editing benchmarks, compared with AnyEdit and locate-and-edit baselines such as MEMIT and AlphaEdit (model names not extracted).
numbers: Abstract: 'µKE improves edit efficacy by up to 12.33% over state-of-the-art methods'.
Results (Table 1): 'up to 12.33% with the original question and 10.5% with the paraphrased question of absolute improvement' in BLEU over AnyEdit.
limits: The locate-and-edit optimization is coupled to fixed learning rates and step counts; adaptive coefficients only partly address this (Limitations).
Existing benchmarks lack annotations of fine-grained knowledge units within long targets, limiting evaluation (Limitations).
evidence_quote: This memory update objective targets a series of condensed representation shifts (partially) covering the corresponding subsequent edit target in the sequential update process.

title: MELO: Enhancing Model Editing with Neuron-Indexed Dynamic LoRA
question: Can model editing satisfy edit success, locality, generality and sequential editing together, with high efficiency, by adding a small LoRA block per edit batch and indexing it in a vector database?
mechanism: Training: each edit batch is learned in a fresh, non-overlapping LoRA block of partial rank p, updated by W_B^t <- W_B^t - eta grad L[f(X_e^t; W_B^t W_A^t), Y_e^t] (Eq. 8-9). Inference: the last hidden state h_l of the input is the key K_q, matched to the nearest cluster centre in a vector database. If K_q falls within that cluster's radius, the LoRA block recorded for the nearest stored key is activated; otherwise no block is applied. Cluster radii expand under explicit rules when an edit falls just outside them (Sec. 3).
training: Gradient descent on LoRA blocks only, per edit batch (learning rates in Table 1: 1e-3 for BERT, T5-Small and T5-Large, 1e-4 for GPT2-XL). No retraining of the base model. Data: SCOTUS, zsRE and a hallucination set.
inference_cost: Not quantified; the paper states MELO 'requires the least trainable parameters and computational cost' among the compared editors.
setup: BERT on SCOTUS (Fairlex), T5-Small and T5-Large on zsRE, GPT2-XL on hallucination correction; baselines LoRA, MEND, SERAC, CMR, ROME, GRACE.
numbers: Table 2, MELO row: '0.96 0.92 0.72 0.98 0.97 17.45 1.04 2.66' (the column grouping is garbled in the text extraction; the table reports locality, edit success, generality and perplexity/ARR metrics).
limits: No limitations section was found in the read text. interp: the radius and cluster rules are hand-set hyperparameters (Table 1).
evidence_quote: Each batch of edits is learned in a set of LoRA blocks located in different layers

novelty_note.B: A nearest-neighbour lookup on the last hidden state with no separate classifier decides which LoRA block to apply; the gated object is a trained low-rank block rather than a steering vector.

title: ORBIT: Training-Free Multi-Attribute Behavioral Steering via Orthogonal Subspace Rotation
question: How can several behavioural attributes be steered at once without training, when summed steering vectors cancel and dominate each other?
mechanism: Per attribute k: a 2D plane (b1 = contrastive mean direction, b2 = first PCA direction of paired differences, orthogonalized against b1). Signed projection s_k = h . b1_hat and zero-margin gate g_k = max(0, -s_k) (Eq. 2-3), so aligned tokens are untouched. Gate-weighted aggregate target r = sum_k g_k b1_hat (Eq. 4). Planes are merged by SVD into one orthonormal joint subspace, and the in-subspace component is rotated norm-preservingly toward the target while the orthogonal component is unchanged. An optional additive boost is scaled by the same gates (Eq. 9).
training: None: training-free, using contrastive activation pairs to form each attribute's direction; no classifier training. Joint success rates are in Appendix F.1.
setup: Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen-2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B; TraitFactory (13 traits, 20 topics) and ToneBank (5 tones); GPT-4o-mini judge (0-10) and a coherence score; baselines CAA, K-Steering, MAT-STEER and MSRS.
numbers: Table 1, ToneBank, Llama-3.2-3B, K=2: unsteered judge 5.06 (coherence 90.8); CAA 5.72 / 86.2 with geometric gain +0.44; K-Steer 4.91 / 83.8 with -0.12; ORBIT 5.94 / 88.0 with +0.81.
limits: Relies on approximately linear attribute representations; attributes with nonlinear or entangled representations may not be captured by one direction (Sec. 9).
Suppression of attributes is demonstrated only in a limited setting; a systematic study of mitigating multiple undesirable behaviours is left to future work (Sec. 9).
evidence_quote: Continuous gates from signed projections determine pass-through, single-trait, or joint steering

novelty_note.B: The gate g_k = max(0, -s_k) is a signed projection of the hidden state onto each attribute axis, with no separate classifier, and it decides per token whether and how much to steer.
novelty_note.E: Section 3.4 characterizes geometric failure modes of naive additive steering (norm dominance and pairwise angular conflict), and the introduction argues that the chance of pairs with substantial negative cosine similarity rises as attributes are added.

title: ARM: Role-Conditioned Neuron Transplantation for Training-Free Generalist LLM Agent Merging
question: Can a training-free merge of agent experts keep role-critical behaviour, such as tool-call formatting, by selecting a backbone and transplanting role-salient MLP neurons?
mechanism: Role-conditioned saliency s_{l,j}(M; b, r) is the expected per-role mean MLP activation over calibration trajectories (Eq. 2). Backbone selection uses an Activation-Overlap Score: the overlap between the candidate backbone's top-k% role-salient neurons and the expert's, per benchmark. Neuron transplantation copies a small top-k% set of donor MLP neurons from the expert into the chosen backbone, protecting neurons salient for other benchmarks.
training: None: the abstract states that 'without gradient-based optimization' ARM improves cross-benchmark generalization. A calibration set is used for activation tracing.
setup: Qwen3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B expert pools on WebShop, OfficeBench, tau-bench, OS and other agent suites, plus out-of-domain benchmarks; baselines Task Arithmetic, TIES and Model Stock.
numbers: Sec. 4: 'the overlap rate drops from 61% to 41% on Qwen3-8B, and from 50% to 43% on Qwen2.5-7B' with role-conditioned tracing versus role-agnostic tracing.
limits: Requires homologous expert checkpoints with the same architecture and tokenizer; does not apply to heterogeneous families or black-box APIs (Sec. 6).
Activation-level diagnostics for multi-turn agent behaviour remain under-explored (Sec. 6).
evidence_quote: Without gradient-based optimization, ARM improves cross-benchmark generalization while enjoying efficiency.

title: Ability Transfer and Recovery via Modularized Parameters Localization
question: Where are abilities stored in LLM parameters, and can an ability be transferred or recovered by moving only the parameters of activation-selected channels?
mechanism: Channel identification: feed the same inputs to the ability model and the base model, average activations over answer tokens per output channel, and rank channels by the activation difference Delta a_i; the top p% form an ability mask M_act. Masks from several ability models are aggregated into one unified mask. The task vector Delta theta = theta_abl - theta_trg (task arithmetic) is applied only to the rows the mask selects, followed by a lightweight fine-tuning step (Sec. 4.1-4.3).
training: Activations and masks come from forward passes. Post-transfer fine-tuning is gradient-based, on the same ability datasets (about 1500 instances per ability in the text read). No training-cost totals are extracted.
setup: A Qwen2.5-Math-7B model pair for multilingual mathematics (MetaMathQA translations) and science (MegaScience translations, 11 languages); compared with task arithmetic, TIES and DARE.
numbers: Abstract: 'ability-related activations are highly concentrated in a small set of channels (typically <5%)'.
Table 1: overlap of top-1% activation-difference channels across abilities for Qwen2.5-7B Math-Instruct vs. Instruct (values not extracted).
limits: No limitations section was found in the read text (interp: results are reported on one model pair).
Post-transfer fine-tuning improves compatibility, so the transfer alone is not sufficient for the best reported scores (Sec. 4.3).
evidence_quote: select the top p% to form an activation-based ability-specific mask

title: Probe-Free Low-Rank Activation Intervention
question: Can an activation intervention that needs no probe improve truthfulness, by pushing activations of one layer toward the region of desirable answers?
mechanism: FLORAIN models desirable answers for each question as an ellipsoid with centre mu_q, a shared covariance Sigma^-1 (an LDA-style assumption) and radius rho_q; under Mahalanobis distance the projection onto the ellipsoid has an analytical form (Thm. 4.1). The intervention in the heads of one layer is a sample-wise nonlinear low-rank map; its parameters minimize the distance between the modified activations and the projection, with alpha weighting local (question-specific) against global (overall) directions. Training uses scaled gradient descent with the inverse covariance as preconditioner (Sec. 4).
training: Gradient-based: parameters of the low-rank map are fit by (preconditioned) gradient descent on activations of desirable and undesirable TruthfulQA answers. Sample sizes are not extracted; the paper notes the ellipsoid estimate is sensitive to small training sets (Limitations).
inference_cost: Claimed, not measured: intervening in one layer 'provides conditions for parallelization to reduce inference intervention time' (Sec. 1).
setup: Llama-7B, Llama3-8B and Llama2-chat-13B on TruthfulQA (generation and multiple-choice), and Alpaca and Vicuna on instruction-tuned tasks; baseline ITI.
numbers: Table 1, Llama-7B: unintervened True*Info 21.15; ITI 26.52; FLORAIN 31.46 (True 34.72, MC1 31.76, MC2 47.43, CE 2.21, KL 0.09).
limits: Depends on the scale of the training dataset; with few samples the mean and covariance estimates are biased (Limitations).
The optimization is nonconvex and the first-order algorithm may converge to local minimizers (Limitations).
evidence_quote: we propose to use preconditioned gradient descent, the scaled convex combination

novelty_note.C: The projection uses a Mahalanobis distance with a shared inverse covariance Sigma^-1, as in linear discriminant analysis, to define the target region for steering.

title: On Task Vectors and Gradients
question: Why does task arithmetic work, and when is merging single-epoch task vectors as good as merging converged ones?
mechanism: Full-batch GD with step eta on task t: the one-epoch task vector tau_t = theta_t^(1) - theta_base = -eta grad L_t(theta_base), so the sum of task vectors equals one GD step on the summed multitask loss with effective step alpha*eta. For k>1 epochs the deviation from joint training is a second-order term O(eta^2), with explicit 2-norm bounds for feed-forward networks that assume bounded weights and activations with bounded derivatives (Sec. 2-3).
training: Gradient-based fine-tuning of vision models on seven benchmarks; the analysis is of full-batch GD and the paper gives no training-cost totals.
setup: Seven vision benchmarks (including SVHN and DTD) with task arithmetic and merging of one-epoch versus converged fine-tuned models.
numbers: Sec. 2.1: the gradients from the first 5 epochs maintain a high cosine similarity (> 0.8) with the first epoch's gradient (Fig. 3b).
limits: The theory is for full-batch GD, while the empirical setting uses SGD-style finetuning (Sec. 2).
The multi-epoch error bound is second order and depends on the stated boundedness assumptions (Sec. 2-3).
evidence_quote: We show that under standard gradient descent, a task vector generated from one epoch of finetuning is exactly equivalent to the negative gradient of the loss, scaled by the learning rate.

title: Composable Interventions for Language Models
question: How do knowledge editing, model compression and machine unlearning interact when applied in sequence to the same language model, and do general-purpose metrics measure composability?
mechanism: An intervention phi is a tuple: operator omega(f, gamma) producing a new model, strength hyperparameters gamma, a loss, and a criterion kappa in [0,1]. Order-free error (Eq. 1) is the area above the maximum of two curves, one per application order (i then j, j then i), swept over gamma_i: integral of 1 - min(kappa_i(phi_j(phi_i(f, gamma_i))), kappa_i(phi_i(gamma_i)(phi_j(f)))), with the maximum criterion value taken as 1; smaller is more composable. Order sensitivity (Metric 2) measures how much the combined success depends on the order of application. Implemented in a unified codebase over existing editing, compression and unlearning methods. The paper defines metrics and measures them; it proposes no new intervention.
training: The framework adds no training. The composed interventions are optimization-based (each operator omega 'aims to minimize loss', Sec. 2.1); their data sizes are not in the read text.
setup: Editing, compression and unlearning methods on recent LMs; Llama-3 8B appears in the Table 1 summary (full text). Benchmarks are in Sec. 4, not in the packet.
numbers: 417 different compositions (Abstract)
limits: Packet omits the limitations section. The paper reports that general-purpose post-intervention performance is a poor proxy for composability and calls for new multi-objective interventions; it does not propose one.
evidence_quote: Interventions are more composable if they achieve high performance when applied in either order.

title: PermDoRA -- Understanding Adapter Interference in Language Models: Limits of Parameter-Space Geometry
question: Is adapter interference when composing DoRA adapters driven by linear parameter-space geometry, so that orthogonality-aware Riemannian merging should beat Euclidean averaging?
mechanism: DoRA splits each update into magnitude and direction: Delta W_i = B_i A_i, V_i = Delta W_i / ||Delta W_i||_F, m_i = ||Delta W_i||_F (Eq. 1). A user's authorized manager adapters are flattened into one adapter. Euclidean composition (Eq. 3): average the effective updates, then truncated SVD to rank r. Riemannian composition (Eq. 4): normalized directional average v = sum_i v_i / ||sum_i v_i||, magnitudes averaged, then SVD refactoring. Diagnostics test angular alignment and orthogonality of the adapter updates as predictors of composition performance.
training: Yes. Backbone frozen; a shared baseline adapter is trained; each domain manager is trained with task loss plus an EWC penalty, lambda/2 sum_j F_j (theta_j - theta_base_j)^2 (Eq. 2). Training-set sizes are not in the packet.
inference_cost: The paper claims inference cost does not scale with the number of authorized domains, because one flattened adapter is used; no measured figure in the packet.

novelty_note.E: Tests whether pre-composition geometry statistics (angular alignment and orthogonality of adapter updates) predict composed performance, and reports they are weak predictors.

title: When Do Task Vectors Interfere? Mapping the Validity Boundaries of Weight-Space Composition
question: When is the functional (output-distribution) interaction between two task vectors non-additive, and does it depend on the prompt distribution and the prompt format?
mechanism: Surface theta(alpha, beta) = theta_0 + alpha*Delta_a + beta*Delta_b on a 7x7 grid, alpha, beta in {0.2,...,1.2}, where Delta are LoRA-merged or full fine-tuning displacements. Additive counterfactual in logit space (Eq. 2): l_add = l_{alpha,0} + l_{0,beta} - l_{0,0}; p_add = softmax(l_add) (Eq. 3). Per-prompt interaction (Eq. 4): JSD(p_{alpha,beta}(.|x), p_add(.|x)). The interaction ratio divides the averaged numerator by the averaged JSD from the base p_{0,0} (Fig. 1 caption), per seed, then averages seeds with equal weight; uncertainty by hierarchical bootstrap over seeds and prompts.
training: Yes for the task vectors: each is a LoRA or full fine-tune of the base for one task (data sizes not in packet). The interaction measurement itself is inference-only.
setup: Five model settings from 0.5B to 8B in two families, LoRA and full fine-tuning (Abstract); Qwen2.5-1.5B calibration; Llama-3.1-8B cross-family audit over three tasks; prompt strata code, math, instruction, safety, summarization; EvalPlus pass@1 for code.
numbers: Abstract: code prompts under the training-format wrapper, the interaction contrast 'collapses ... from +6.9 to +0.3 points'
Abstract: 'an untrained chat template leaves it intact (+12.5)'
Abstract: 'all eight preregistered sign predictions held' on unseen task pairs
limits: Additive counterfactual is a valid reference only for additive composition; TIES first-order effects are shown only descriptively. Full fine-tuning audited only at 0.5B; Llama covers three tasks. pass@1 inherits the wrapper blindness. Not a universal merging-performance predictor and not a safety guarantee.
evidence_quote: The numerator and denominator are averaged separately over prompts and the 36 interior points before forming a seed-level ratio of expectations.

novelty_note.E: Predicted the sign of pairwise interference ordering for unseen task pairs before their adapters existed; 8/8 held (preregistered, paper's own test).
novelty_note.G: interp: the paper reports that the contrast is gated by a denominator effect in the readout rather than a change in the underlying interaction (companion causal study cited in the paper), so the measured signal tracks the serialization wrapper.

title: Non-Interfering Weight Fields: Treating Model Parameters as a Continuously Extensible Function
question: Can catastrophic forgetting be avoided structurally by storing knowledge as a continuous function of a capability coordinate and locking the region each task occupies?
mechanism: Frozen Mistral-7B. Each module holds Nb=16 low-rank bases (A_b in R^{dout x r}, B_b in R^{r x din}, r=8). A coordinate z_{t+1} = tanh(W_p GRU(h_t, z_t)) is computed from mean-pooled hidden states, z in [-1,1]^64. A 3-layer MLP weight field F_theta: R^64 -> R^{L x Nb} gives per-layer gating logits; top-k=8 softmax gating selects bases; y = W_base x + (alpha/r) sum_{b in top-k} w_b A_b B_b x. After a task: fit a Gaussian (mu, Sigma) to its coordinates, boundary tau at the 95th percentile, sample M=256 anchors a_j inside the region, snapshot S_j = F_theta(a_j); lock loss L_lock = (1/M) sum_j ||F_theta(a_j) - S_j||^2. L_sep pushes new coordinates away from committed regions. Total L = L_NLL + lambda_lock L_lock + lambda_sep L_sep + lambda_budget L_budget.
training: Yes. Backbone frozen; the coordinate module, weight field and adapter bases are trained with next-token NLL plus lock, separation and budget terms, sequentially per task. Dataset sizes not in the read text.
inference_cost: Two-pass forward (coordinate pass, then gated pass; Fig. 1 caption); 8 of 16 bases active per module; 323M trainable parameters on a 7.24B frozen backbone (Fig. 1). Overhead not measured as latency.
setup: Mistral-7B; sequential Task A (instruction following) then Task B (code generation).
numbers: Table 3 (perplexity, Task A after A+B): Full FT sequential 3.85 -> 7.14 (+85.5%); LoRA sequential 4.21 -> 5.89 (+39.9%); LoRA separate 4.21 -> 4.21 (0%); NIWF 4.35 -> 4.35 (0%), Task B 4.62
limits: Packet omits the limitations section. Internal tension: the text says the lock is enforced 'with zero tolerance, not through a weighted penalty' but also says it is enforced through an MSE loss with weight lambda_lock (interp: in practice a soft penalty on anchors). Bases can saturate and need expansion (Sec. 6.2). Results are on one two-task protocol.
evidence_quote: The constraint is enforced at specific anchor points with zero tolerance, not through a weighted penalty.

title: RIZZ: Routing Interactions to Near Zero-Interference Zones for Continual Adaptation of Black-Box Agents
question: Can a frozen black-box LLM adapt online to nonstationary task streams using only routed external memory, verifier-gated writes and budgeted prompt compilation, without cross-task interference?
mechanism: Stream of (x_t, y_hat_t, r_t) where r_t in [0,1] comes from a deterministic verifier (e.g. fuzzy ratio). A router assigns each query to a memory branch using output-shape guards, function and application labels, embedding-based snapping and Jaccard de-duplication; branches are created, reused or merged. Retrieval gathers branch-local, global, graph-structured and working-memory context, compiled into a bounded prompt under a fixed context budget. Writes happen only on verified outcomes: successful examples are stored, procedural rules are reweighted by helpful and harmful use, failures become anti-templates, redundant branches are pruned or merged.
training: None for the base model, which is never updated. Adaptation is memory writes gated by the verifier; no gradient training is described.
inference_cost: Table 1 (Claude Haiku 4.5, $1/M input, $5/M output): StreamBench cost $7.37 for RIZZ vs $7.99 for Frozen; TRACE cost $12.79 for RIZZ vs $7.51 for Frozen.
setup: Claude Haiku 4.5 as the frozen model (main); gpt-4o-mini and gpt-5.1 in Table 4; StreamBench, TRACE, LongMemEval-S and tau-Bench.
numbers: Table 1, StreamBench: Frozen 0.6013 -> RIZZ 0.6339 (+3.3 pp)
Table 1, TRACE: Frozen 0.6369 -> RIZZ 0.7060 (+6.9 pp)
Table 4, LongMemEval-S with Haiku-4.5: Frozen 0.270 -> RIZZ 0.670 (+40.0 pp)
limits: Gains need recurring local structure; sparse or procedurally heterogeneous streams leave too few verified examples per branch. The frozen model can only express what it already can. Persistent memory adds privacy, poisoning and extraction risks, and branch storage is not a privacy mechanism. ACE* collapses on StreamBench and TRACE (marked context-window collapse).
evidence_quote: At inference time either offline or online, RIZZ routes the input, retrieves branch-conditioned memory under a fixed context budget, calls the frozen model, verifies the output, and writes back only when feedback justifies doing so.

novelty_note.F: A router selects a memory branch and retrieves branch-conditioned memory per query, which steers memory retrieval; the paper does not steer tool calls.

title: Predicting and Repairing Merge Collapse in Large Language Models
question: Can a destructive merge of fine-tuned specialists' task vectors be predicted from the weights before evaluation, and repaired without data?
mechanism: Task vectors tau_k = theta_k - theta_base with merge scale s_k. Per coordinate, total power P = mean_k (s_k tau_k)^2 splits into signal S = (mean_k s_k tau_k)^2 and interference I = P - S = Var_k(s_k tau_k) (Eq. 1). A pre-merge interference score is built from I under a working noise model; destructive merges exceed a threshold (1.9e-3, Table 4 caption). PRISM averages the task vectors first, then soft-thresholds each layer at the universal threshold lambda_l = kappa * sigma_l * sqrt(2 log n_l), kappa = 1.0, where sigma_l is set from the layer's interference (sqrt symbol lost in extraction). A floor keeps a share of coordinates. A gate on the cancellation share rho of interference applies soft thresholding only when rho >= tau_g; otherwise the plain average is returned.
training: None. Data-free: 'without data or tuning' (Abstract). The score needs only the weights and minutes of CPU time (Intro).
inference_cost: Merge-time only: PRISM is linear time with no SVD (Sec. 1). Score computation takes minutes of CPU time (Intro).
setup: 22 merge configurations from four model families, up to eight specialists per merge; Qwen2.5-7B coefficient sweep; Llama-3.1-8B (K=3) and Mistral-7B (K=2) in the gate analysis; continued-pretraining Qwen2.5-1.5B specialists on Japanese web text and biomedical abstracts.
numbers: Prospective test: 12 of the 14 predictions made before evaluation were correct (Sec. 4)
Table 4: naive averaging falls 18.4 and 14.4 pp below the base on R1-Distill+Coder and Math-PRM+Coder, while PRISM stays within 0.5 pp
Intro: the score flags 5 of 7 destructive merges and none of 15 harmless ones
limits: Sign-conflict statistics are anti-predictive. Shrinkage helps destructive merges but can forgo the plain average's gain on harmless ones, hence the gate. Threshold scale and pretraining titration are reported as robust but are on a limited set of families.
evidence_quote: The power that averaging removes equals the variance of the task vectors across specialists, our measure of interference.

novelty_note.E: A pre-merge interference score computed from the weights predicts which merges collapse before they are built (5 of 7 destructive flagged; 12 of 14 prospective predictions correct).

title: GRAM: Group-wise Rank-Aware Model Merging via Subspace Alignment
venue: NeurIPS 2026 (conference named in page header; status not stated)
question: Does grouping tasks by the principal-angle geometry of their update subspaces before SVD merging reduce subspace interference in data-free merging?
mechanism: Per layer, task vector Delta W_i = U_i Sigma_i V_i^T (compact SVD, Eq. 3). Objective (Eq. 4): partition T tasks into K groups and give each merged matrix rank at most r, minimizing the sum of per-task reconstruction errors. Grouping: Grassmannian k-means++ on chordal distances between left singular subspaces (data-free). Within each coalition: SVD-based merge with a greedy adaptive rank allocator that pools singular values across members under the global rank budget. The paper states that per-task projection error is governed by the principal-angle alignment term (1 - cos^2 theta) between each task and the shared subspace.
training: None for the merge (data-free; only fine-tuned weights). The task models are fine-tuned upstream (LoRA on Flan-T5, vision fine-tunes, Qwen2-7B medical LoRAs).
inference_cost: Stores K merged models instead of one (K=2 in the experiments): 'a marginal increase in storage for a targeted, significant reduction in subspace interference' (Intro).
setup: GLUE with Flan-T5-Base and Flan-T5-Large (LoRA r=16, K=2); 8-task CLIP vision; Qwen2-7B-Instruct with four English/Chinese medical LoRAs.
numbers: Sec. 5.2, Flan-T5-Base GLUE: GRAM 83.8% average, +2.1 over TSV-Merge (81.7%)
Sec. 5.2, Flan-T5-Large GLUE: GRAM 88.7%, +0.9 over TSV-Merge (87.8%)
limits: Assumes task identity is known at inference (task-aware deployment, Intro). Requires storing K models. Packet omits the limitations section.
evidence_quote: Crucially, GRAM is entirely data-free: the pipeline operates exclusively on the fine-tuned weights, requiring no source data, activations, or calibration sets at merge time.

novelty_note.E: interp: principal-angle alignment of task subspaces is used as a pre-merge predictor of per-task projection error for a shared-basis merge, and to choose the partition before merging; it is not a capacity limit.

title: On Fairness of Task Arithmetic: The Role of Task Vectors
question: How does task arithmetic with one global scalar coefficient affect group fairness (DPD, EOD) relative to full fine-tuning and LoRA?
mechanism: theta(lambda) = theta_0 + lambda * Delta theta (Eq. 2): a single scalar applied uniformly to all inputs and subgroups. Subgroup-specific task vectors are merged. lambda is chosen by training accuracy (Fig. 1 caption). A theoretical bound links lambda to DPD and EOD (Sec. 5.1, App. C; body not in the packet).
training: Yes for the source models: FFT and LoRA fine-tuning per task or subgroup produce the task vectors (data sizes not in packet). Applying the task vector needs no further training.
setup: LLaMA-7B on hate speech (described as LLaMA-2-7B in the limitations); DistilBERT and Qwen2.5-0.5B on Civil Comments toxicity; ViT-Base/16 on UTKFace age; metrics DPD and EOD.
numbers: Fig. 1 caption: optimal lambda = 0.8 for the gender setting and lambda = 0.5 for the race setting (chosen by training accuracy)
limits: A single global scalar cannot capture multidimensional fairness constraints. Single sensitive attribute per task. Limited classification tasks; no frontier API models. Effectiveness may depend on dataset and subgroup structure.
evidence_quote: This keeps the intervention interpretable but cannot capture richer multidimensional fairness constraints.

title: Whoever Started the Interference Should End It: Guiding Data-Free Model Merging via Task Vectors
question: Can data-free merging reduce linear-layer interference by minimizing output disagreement with each expert, using the task vectors as a stand-in for the unavailable inputs?
mechanism: Layer-l interference for task i (Eqs. 3-5): J_i = E_x ||(theta_m - theta_i) x||^2 with delta_i = tau_m - tau_i. Since inputs are unavailable, the paper argues the task vector of a linear layer approximates a linear subspace of its input, and substitutes surrogate inputs: random tau_i^random ~ N(mu_i, sigma_i^2) from the task vector's mean and std, or random sub-vectors of tau_i (Eqs. 22-24). Loss (Eq. 23, as extracted): sum over tasks of (tau_m - tau_i)^T tau_i^random divided by ||tau_i||_F. The merged task vector has a closed form (Eq. 20 per the full text) with a regularization coefficient; no rescaling coefficients are used.
training: None. Data-free: no additional data, extra storage or rescaling coefficients (Intro).
inference_cost: None added at inference (merged weights). Merge cost: 'about 8 minutes and 4 GB of GPU memory' for ViT-L/14 (computational-efficiency paragraph; section not confirmed).
setup: Vision and language merges, including ViT-B/32 and ViT-L/14 (CLIP) on multi-task sets; benchmark details are not in the packet.

Abstract: outperforms mainstream test-time adaptation merging by 3.3%
about 8 minutes and 4 GB of GPU memory for ViT-L/14 (section not confirmed)

Derivation assumes Lipschitz continuity and a small learning rate with a limited number of iterations (Sec. 3.2). title: Merge to Learn: Efficiently Adding Skills to Language Models with Model Merging
question: Is parallel train-then-merge (train a skill model separately, then add its task vector to a general model) a cheaper alternative to continued finetuning or retraining for adding new skills?
mechanism: Task arithmetic: tau_D = theta_D - theta_pre (Eq. 1); theta_final = theta_G + omega * tau_D (Eq. 2), with omega chosen on held-out data or by heuristic. Heuristic without held-out data: the mixture weight is proportional to the share of training steps devoted to the new skill. WiSE-FT variant: tau_CFT = theta_CFT - theta_G with theta_final = theta_G + omega * tau_CFT (Eqs. 5-6). Linear interpolation is also compared.

Intro: PTM reduces exaggerated refusals by '30–80%'

title: Signal in the Noise: Polysemantic Interference Transfers and Predicts Cross-Model Influence
question: Do semantically unrelated SAE features that interfere in activation space produce predictable steering effects, and do those patterns transfer from small models to larger instruction-tuned models?
mechanism: Pre-trained Neuronpedia SAEs (32,768 features) on GPT-2-Small and Pythia-70M. Interference scale I_l(i,j) = cos(d_hat_i,l, d_hat_j,l) between l2-normalized SAE decoder directions (Sec. 2.1). Semantic relatedness S(i,j) = cosine of text-embedding-3-large embeddings of GPT-4o-mini glosses. Features grouped by agglomerative clustering. Four intervention foci: feature-direction steering, token-gradient steering, prompt injection with top-activating snippets of interfering features, and neuron masking or amplification. Vulnerability is the shift in the next-token distribution. Interference patterns from the small models are used to steer Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct.
training: None for the method: the SAEs are pre-trained by Neuronpedia. Token-gradient steering uses gradients with respect to input tokens; no weight training is described. Tuning details are in App. I.2.
setup: Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small with Neuronpedia SAEs (480 target features from GPT-2-Small and 180 from Pythia-70M); transfer to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct.
numbers: Appendix comparison: intervention effects 'increase by approximately 10×–100× in GPT-2-Small and 100×–1000× in' under the weighted-overlap metric, versus about the 10% level for direct latent-space manipulation (section not confirmed; text near Figure 5)
limits: Effects depend on the evaluation metric: weaker under the default metric, pronounced under weighted overlap. Post-hoc annotation explains only a minority of interference cases. SAEs are available for only two small models. Limitations of SAEs are discussed in App. P.
evidence_quote: We define the interference scale between two SAE features fi,ℓ and fj,ℓ at layer ℓ as the cosine similarity between their activation-space directions

novelty_note.E: The cosine interference scale between SAE feature directions identifies semantically unrelated features that will interfere with a target, before the intervention is run.
novelty_note.G: The steering effect on a target feature is produced by interfering, semantically unrelated features that share activation directions, so the signal reflects something other than the intended concept; the paper's central finding.

title: Disentangling Steering Vectors
question: Can a difference-in-means steering vector be decomposed into semantically consistent constituent directions, and does removing an unwanted constituent give the intended steering?
mechanism: DiffMean v = mean of token activations on the positive set minus mean on the negative set (Eq. 1, global token mean). Steering Vector Dissection: (1) collect activations for positive and negative datasets; (2) pair each positive activation with its nearest negative by nearest-neighbour search and take differences as instance-level steering vectors; (3) train a sparse autoencoder on these differences, f = sigma(W_enc x + b_enc), x_hat = W_dec f + b_dec (Eqs. 2-3); (4) interpret and filter basis vectors with an ensemble of three LLM judges. Removal: v_DiffMean-reject = v - <v, v_reject> v_reject on normalized vectors (Eq. 13).
training: Yes, for the SAE trained on steering-difference vectors (data sizes not in packet). No weight updates to the LLM. LLM judges are used for filtering.
setup: Qwen2.5-7B (layers 13 and 20) and Llama3.1-8B (layers 15 and 23); PubMedQA (domain) and PKU-SafeRLHF (behaviour); StrongREJECT for steering evaluation; SVD-based baseline in Sec. 7.
numbers: Table 6, Qwen2.5-7B L13: StrongREJECT original 0.018, DiffMean 0.057, DiffMean-reject 0.352 (delta CI [0.277, 0.390])
Table 6, Llama3.1-8B L15: original 0.015, DiffMean 0.014, DiffMean-reject 0.084
limits: Interpretation-based filtering depends on LLM judges. Table 6 covers four model-layer pairs. Steering with DiffMean only fails to raise compliance in three of four pairs, and the removal gain is largest in earlier layers. The term 'disentanglement' is used loosely (footnote 1).
evidence_quote: Steering with the unsafe DiffMean vector does not reliably increase compliance: in three of four model–layer pairs it leaves the StrongREJECT score at or below that of the unsteered model.

novelty_note.G: The unsafe DiffMean vector's intended effect is cancelled by rejection components it contains; removing them raises the StrongREJECT score in the earlier layers (Table 6).

title: Concept Heterogeneity-aware Representation Steering
question: Can representation steering be made input-adaptive by modelling source and target activations as Gaussian mixtures and transporting between clusters, instead of one global difference-in-means shift?
mechanism: Cluster source and target activations (k-means; equal-covariance Gaussian components). Discrete OT between clusters with Gaussian Bures-type costs (Eq. 5), solved by Sinkhorn-type scaling of a kernel matrix, giving plan P. Local steering vectors v_ij = b_j - a_i weighted by P_ij. Input-dependent gate over cluster centroids (Sec. 3.2): k(x, a_i) = exp(-||x - a_i||^2 / (2 sigma^2)), sigma the median squared distance from x to centroids; p_hat(i|x) = sum_j P_ij k(x,a_i) / sum_{m,n} P_mn k(x,a_m); the steering map is the p_hat-weighted combination of cluster-level shifts. CHaRS-PCT (Sec. 3.3) keeps the top principal directions u_k of the plan-weighted covariance of the local vectors, alpha_ijk = u_k^T (v_ij - v_bar).
training: None: clustering, OT and the kernel gate are computed from activation samples; no gradient training is described.
setup: Instruct LLMs from 3B to 32B (Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-3B/7B/32B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma2-9B); jailbreak attack success rate (ActAdd and DirAbl interventions); tinyBenchmarks utility; toxicity mitigation; image style steering.

limits: Equal covariance within OT-matched clusters and k-means are simplifying choices the authors say may not be optimal; a diagonal-covariance variant (App. E.6) did not improve results. Kernel bandwidth is set by a heuristic.
evidence_quote: Figure 1. PCA (left two) and t-SNE (right two) visualizations of last-token representations for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B- Instruct, colored by k-means clustering.

novelty_note.B: The gate p_hat(i|x) is a kernel weighting of distances from the hidden state x to cluster centroids, with no separate classifier, and it sets how much each cluster-level shift is applied to x.
novelty_note.C: interp: the general Gaussian OT map (Eq. 2) involves covariance matrix powers with -1/2 exponents, but the final method uses equal-covariance translations, so the covariance term appears only in the derivation (diagonal-covariance variant App. E.6 not shown to help).

title: Personalized Steering of Large Language Models: Versatile Steering Vectors Through Bi-directional Preference Optimization
question: Can a steering vector be optimized so that it directly changes the generation probabilities of contrastive preference response pairs, rather than being the mean activation difference of contrastive prompts?
mechanism: A single-layer steering vector v is added to the activations at layer L. Data are regular preference pairs (q, r_T, r_O), not multiple-choice prompts. Algorithm 1: initialize v_0 = 0; each iteration samples a batch of pairs and a direction d drawn uniformly from {-1, +1}; response likelihoods are computed under the steered model A_L(q) + d v_t; v is updated by a DPO-inspired objective that raises the target response and lowers the opposite one (the exact loss is garbled in extraction). Strength is set by the multiplier on v, and vectors can be summed (v_Power + v_Wealth).
training: Yes: the steering vector alone is optimized by gradient-based preference optimization on contrastive preference pairs; LLM weights are frozen. Dataset size not in the read text.
inference_cost: One vector addition at one layer; the authors restrict to one layer to reduce steering cost (Conclusion).
setup: Llama-2-7b-chat-hf for persona steering (power-seeking, wealth-seeking, corrigible-less-HHH, hallucination); Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 in the appendix; transfer across LoRAs.
numbers: Table 6, Llama-2-7b-chat, power-seeking: v_Power at multipliers -1 / 0 / 1 gives 1.2 / 1.67 / 2.38
Table 6, power-seeking with v_Power + v_Wealth: 1.18 / 1.67 / 2.67
limits: Single-layer design; multi-layer steering is left to future work (Conclusion). Evaluation is on open-ended behaviour scores. Packet omits the main comparison and evaluation sections.
evidence_quote: Due to the consideration of reducing the steering cost, here we design our steering vector to only affect a single layer in the transformer.

title: Orthogonal Gradient Descent for Continual Learning
question: Can catastrophic forgetting in sequential training be reduced by constraining each new-task gradient step to be orthogonal to gradient directions that change previous-task predictions, without storing data?
mechanism: Previous-task subspace S = span of the model's logit gradients grad f_k(x; w*_A) over previous-task samples and ground-truth logit indices k (Eq. 8), orthogonalized with Gram-Schmidt. Algorithm 1: for each new-task minibatch gradient g, g_tilde = g - sum_{v in S} proj_v(g), then w <- w - eta * g_tilde. After a task, the gradients of its samples are added to S. Variants: OGD-ALL (all logits), OGD-AVE (gradient of the averaged logits), and a ground-truth-logit variant.
training: Yes: gradient training with projected gradients. No data stored, but a basis of gradient directions is stored. Training-set sizes not in the packet.
inference_cost: None at inference. The stored basis S grows with the number of tasks, which the authors list as a downside.
setup: Permuted MNIST, Rotated MNIST and a third continual-learning benchmark, with network classifiers rather than LLMs.
limits: Storage grows with the number of tasks (Sec. 3). Effectiveness depends on the learning rate keeping the gradient neighbourhood valid. Adam and principal-component reduction of S are left as future work. Numeric table cells were not reliably extracted from the packet or full text, so no numbers are recorded.

title: Neural Networks Remember More: The Power of Parameter Isolation and Combination
question: Can continual learning avoid catastrophic forgetting and task-ID routing by training one PEFT module per task and combining the task vectors afterwards by task arithmetic?
mechanism: Backbone frozen (RoBERTa-large as the PLM). For each task n, train an Adapter or LoRA module Phi_n. Task vector tau_i = Phi_i - Phi_pre (Eq. 2). Combined tau = sum_i lambda_i tau_i (Eq. 3), lambda chosen on validation data; final model Theta = Theta_pre + tau (Eq. 4). Knowledge transfer: initialize the next task's PEFT module from the previous one ('pre') or from the mean of the tuned modules ('mean').
training: Yes: one PEFT module per task trained on that task's data with the backbone frozen; lambda chosen on validation data. Sequence of five datasets.
inference_cost: None reported; a single merged model is used at test time.
setup: RoBERTa-large; five-dataset continual text-classification sequence ag news -> yelp -> amazon -> yahoo -> db (full setting).
numbers: Table 3 (average accuracy): LoRA no-init 22.0 vs LoRA pre 75.5; Adapter no-init 30.0 vs Adapter pre 77.2
Intro: 77.2% vs EPI 76.3% average accuracy in the full-shot setting

title: Activation Steering with a Feedback Controller
question: Can activation steering be cast as a control-theoretic feedback loop whose integral and derivative terms remove the steady-state error of existing difference-of-means steering methods?
mechanism: Difference-of-means steering (ActAdd, DirAblate, Mean-AcT) is interpreted as a proportional (P) controller with the steering vector as feedback. PID Steering computes per layer k: u(k) = Kp r(k) + Ki sum_{j=0}^{k-1} r(j) + Kd (r(k) - r(k-1)), where r(k) is the diff-in-means error between contrastive activations at layer k (Eq. 17-18). Layers update as x(k) = f(k)(rho_steer(x(k-1), u(k-1))). The integral term accumulates past error to remove offset; the derivative term damps overshoot. Plugs into ActAdd, Mean-AcT and Angular Steering.
training: No gradient training of the LLM reported. Steering vectors come from contrastive activation sets (refusal directions built from 80% of AdvBench and 512 harmless Alpaca samples). Gains Kp, Ki, Kd are set by a grid sweep (Sec. 5.4, Fig. 6), not learned.
setup: LLMs: Gemma2-2B and -9B, Llama3-8B, Qwen2.5 (3B-14B). Diffusion: SDXL-Lightning, Flux. Benchmarks: toxicity (Table 1, with Wikipedia and Mistral-7B perplexity and MMLU), jailbreak ASR with tinyBenchmarks (Table 2).

Table 1, Gemma2-2B, MMLU: Original 53.1; PID-AcT (Ours) 51.30±0.52
limits: Large Ki without enough Kp is unstable; a small Kd in [0.01,0.05] is needed to suppress oscillations (Sec. 5.4). PI-only control shows large overshoot (Fig. 3). Table 1 shows higher Wikipedia perplexity and lower MMLU than Original for PID-AcT on Gemma2-2B.
evidence_quote: by showing that popular steering methods correspond to the proportional (P) controllers, with the steering vector serving as the feedback signal.

title: ODESteer: A Unified ODE-Based Steering Framework for LLM Alignment
question: Can activation steering be unified as solving an ODE whose vector field climbs a barrier function, giving multi-step adaptive steering that beats one-step activation addition?
mechanism: Activation addition is the single Euler step of the ODE a' = v(a) with step T. Barrier h(a) = log(p+(a)/p-(a)) is estimated as h(a) = w'^T phi(a) + b' + log(N-/N+), where phi is a Polynomial Count Sketch of unit-l2-normalised activations and (w', b') come from logistic regression on positive and negative activations (Sec. 5.1). The steering ODE is a'(t) = J_phi(a)^T w / ||J_phi(a)^T w||, solved numerically from a(0)=a over [0,T] to give the steered activation a(T) (Eq. 13-14).
training: No LLM gradient. The barrier needs a logistic-regression fit (scikit-learn) on contrastive positive and negative activations. Sample counts are in Appendix C, which was not read.
setup: Falcon-7B, Mistral-7B, LLaMA3.1-8B. UltraFeedback (win rate, reward model), TruthfulQA (T x I), RealToxicityPrompts (toxicity, PPL). Baselines RepE, ITI, CAA.

title: When a Conceptor Complement Becomes Gain: Operator Geometry and Behavioral Attribution in Language Models
venue: PMLR 2026 (Symmetry and Geometry in Neural Representations)
question: When a conceptor-complement steering map changes behaviour, does its fitted covariance filter C_t add anything beyond the shared target-specific centre and gain?
mechanism: Conceptor C = R(R + alpha^-2 I)^-1 from centred target-present activations, R = X^T X / n. Deployed map F_{C,t}(h) = m_t + beta (I - C_t)(h - m_t), with target mean m_t and gain beta. Matched control F_{0,t}(h) = m_t + beta (h - m_t) keeps centre and gain and zeroes only C_t, so the difference is exactly -beta C_t (h - m_t) (Eq. 5-6). Per-direction gain is beta(1 - c_i), c_i = lambda_i/(lambda_i + alpha^-2); attenuation needs alpha^2 lambda_i > beta - 1 (Eq. 4).
training: No gradient training reported. Covariance and centre are fitted in closed form from target-present extraction generations (80/20 question folds in the held-out correction analysis). Generated responses are scored by LLM judges (Gemini 2.5 Flash; DeepSeek-V4-Pro for the rescore).
setup: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Seven persona targets from the Persona Vectors construction for spectra and linear accessibility; four targets (Sycophancy, Hallucination, Optimistic, Apathetic) for the matched generation study at beta = 2, alpha = .05.
numbers: Abstract: 'The matrix correction is 0.093%-7.815% of the matched-control displacement on held-out extraction activations.'
Abstract: '285 of 480 paired texts differ.' (Sec. 4)

Abstract: 'In 480 paired comparisons within a 1,920-response study, retaining the matrix changes many individual texts but does not establish a consistent additional target-suppression benefit on the four-target panel.'
limits: Matched panel is four targets, described as exploratory. alpha = .05 was inherited from an earlier GPT-J setting and not tuned here; at alpha = .2 some maps attenuate. Only 195 of 480 complete-vs-control pairs match exactly. Four responses hit the 1,024-token cap. Judges have no human validation. Zero-width intervals do not establish equivalence.
evidence_quote: The matched matrix-removed control F0,t preserves the same target-specific center, β, layer, prompts, seeds, decoding, and response budget.

novelty_note.C: Uses the conceptor matrix R(R + alpha^-2 I)^-1, a regularised covariance-inverse-type filter, as the steering filter. Not a discriminant gate.
novelty_note.D: The positive class is activations generated under an instruction that elicits the target (paired instruction templates); the fitted map is built from those activations. The paper does not turn one system prompt into one weight edit.
novelty_note.G: Shows the matrix term is 0.093%-7.815% of the displacement and that retaining it gives no consistent extra target-suppression, so the behavioural effect is attributed to the shared centre and gain rather than the intended covariance filter.

title: Model Predictive Control on the Neural Manifold
question: Can PID and model predictive control, driven by a learned latent dynamics model, steer the latent dynamics of a spiking network through closed-loop sensory stimuli, and which controller does better?
mechanism: Latent model z_{t+1} = g(z_t, u_t, eps_t), x_t = f(z_t). PID: u(t) = Kp e(t) + KI integral e + Kd de/dt (Eq. 5). MPC: at each step minimise J(x_0) = sum_i l(x_i, u_i) over a horizon T, with x_{n+1} = f(x_n, u_n) and box bounds on x and u; apply only the first input and re-solve (Eq. 6 and following).
training: The latent dynamics model (nVAE plus latent dynamics model, LDM) is trained on activity from a simulated spiking network. The packet does not give the training method or dataset size.
setup: Simulated spiking neural network (n = 80 neurons per ensemble) as a model of a neural circuit, with trajectory-following tasks on latent state and step-function set points. Neuron observability varied from 1% upward.
numbers: Experiment II: 10 independent ensembles sampled from the SNN (n = 80) per observability level; 50 trials per ensemble
Latent-dynamics performance 'saturated at 20% observability' (Fig. 5A)
limits: MPC hyperparameters from Experiment I did not generalise to 1% observability. PID sometimes failed catastrophically and produced oscillatory control signals. MPC is computationally expensive (stated in the introduction).
evidence_quote: The controller uses the dynamical model to simulate T time steps into the future.

title: Theory of gating in recurrent neural networks
question: How do multiplicative update and output gates in an RNN shape its timescales, dimensionality and transition to chaos?
mechanism: Gated RNN: h_i' = sigma_z(z_i)[-h_i + R_i] + I^h_i, with recurrent input R_i = sum_j J^h_ij phi(h_j) sigma_r(r_j); gates tau_x x_i' = -x_i + sum_j J^x_ij phi(h_j) + I^x_i for x in {z, r}; sigma(x) = [1 + exp(-alpha x + beta)]^-1. The update gate sets an adaptive time constant and the output gate scales unit output. Couplings J ~ N(0, 1/N). Analysed by random-matrix and MSRDJ mean-field theory, Jacobian spectra and phase diagrams.
training: none (analytical theory of random-coupling networks; no training procedure in the packet)
setup: Theoretical analysis of N-unit random gated RNNs with phase diagrams; simulations of the dynamics. No LLM or benchmark.
numbers: Fig. 5 caption: purely chaotic state '(c, gh = 3.0)', where input has 'the familiar effect of stabilising the dynamics (d)'
limits: The packet shows no limitations section. Results are mean-field statements for random couplings.
evidence_quote: The gate controlling timescales leads to a novel, marginally stable state

title: AutoHebb: Self-Modifying Neural Networks that Zero-Shot Infer and Continually Learn
question: Can a feedforward plastic network whose neuromodulatory signal is generated internally from its own activity and external feedback achieve zero-shot inference and continual learning?
mechanism: Main net h_i = g((W_i + A_i ⊙ P_i(t)) h_{i-1} + b_i), with fixed W, fixed plasticity coefficients A_i, and plastic weights P_i updated by a 3-factor Hebbian rule. A separate fixed control MLP outputs a scalar neuromodulator m = C(h_L, phi), with phi = 1 for a correct response and 0 otherwise; m gates the plastic-weight updates. The fixed (non-plastic) weights are found by meta-learning.
training: Meta-learning of the fixed weights over task episodes; plastic weights change online without gradients. Episode counts and dataset sizes are not in the packet.
setup: Four ZI/CL tasks (TI, TE, and sequences TI-TE and TE-TI). Baselines: MAML, Reptile, MER, OML, FLP, ANML, 2F-A, 2F-ABCD, EWC, SI, A-GEM, DER.

title: NeuroLoRA: Context-Aware Neuromodulation for Parameter-Efficient Multi-Task Adaptation
question: Can a learned, input-conditioned gate that rescales a frozen sparse random projection improve LoRA expert selection for multi-task merging and continual learning?
mechanism: Frozen sparse random projection (FlyLoRA-style, winner-take-all on projected magnitudes, sparsity 0.25, active rank 8 of 32). Neuromodulation gate m_x = sigma(W2 GELU(W1 x)) ⊙ gamma + beta (Eq. 3), rescaling projection axes per input before expert selection. Contrastive orthogonality loss L_orth (lambda = 0.1) penalises overlap between expert subspaces, using squared inter-expert correlations c_ij^2.

title: Backpropamine: training self-modifying neural networks with differentiable neuromodulated plasticity
question: Can neuromodulated Hebbian plasticity, in which a network decides where and when its connections change, be trained end-to-end with gradient descent?
mechanism: Differentiable Hebbian plasticity: x_j(t) = sigma(sum_i (w_ij + alpha_ij Hebb_ij(t)) x_i(t-1)); Hebb_ij(t+1) = Clip(Hebb_ij(t) + eta x_i(t-1) x_j(t)), with hard clip to [-1,1]. Neuromodulation replaces the per-connection learning rate eta with a neuron output M(t) computed from the layer's previous activations (one neuromodulatory neuron per layer, fan-out equal to the plastic connections). Simple and retroactive (eligibility-trace) variants.
training: End-to-end gradient descent (SGD and backprop through time) on w, alpha, eta and the neuromodulator parameters, over RL and supervised tasks. Training set sizes for the language-modelling task are not in the packet.
setup: Reinforcement learning tasks, a supervised task, and Penn Tree Bank language modelling with small and large LSTMs (Table 1).
numbers: Table 1 (Penn Tree Bank test perplexity): Baseline LSTM 104.26 ± 0.22; LSTM with Retroactive Neuromodulation 102.48 ± 0.28

limits: The packet shows no limitations section. Retroactive neuromodulation gives about 1.7 perplexity improvement over the baseline LSTM on the small model.
evidence_quote: Here we show for the first time that artificial neural networks with such neuromodulated plasticity can be trained with gradient descent.

title: Evolving Decomposed Plasticity Rules for Information-Bottlenecked Meta-Learning
question: Can connection-level Hebbian plasticity rules be decomposed into neuron-level rules, cutting meta-parameters from Θ(n²) to Θ(n) without losing learning performance?
mechanism: Canonical Hebbian plasticity uses 3-4 meta-parameters per connection. Decomposed plasticity makes each rule depend separately on pre- and post-synaptic neurons, so the number of meta-parameters is Θ(n) while the number of plastic connections is Θ(n²). Plastic weights, including recurrent and input connections, start from random initialisation and are updated in the inner loop. One or more neuromodulator neurons gate plasticity. The exact update formula is in the section not in the packet.
training: Outer-loop evolution of the meta-parameters (per the title and baselines); inner-loop plasticity is not gradient-based. Number of generations and dataset size are not in the packet.
setup: 2D random maze navigation (9x9, 15x15, 21x21 mazes; 2,048 test mazes). Baselines: Meta-RNN, Meta-LSTM, Evolving&Merging, PRNN.

title: Gated Linear Networks
question: Can a backprop-free network of gated geometric-mixing neurons learn online with local credit assignment and resist catastrophic forgetting?
mechanism: Each neuron is a gated geometric mixer: GEO_W(1; p) = sigma(w_c(z)^T sigma^-1(p)), where p are input predictions from the previous layer and the context c(z) selects one weight row from side information z (halfspace gating: a hyperplane test on z). Each neuron takes online gradient descent on its own log-loss, with gradient (GEO - x) logit(p). Layers stack; the last neuron gives the prediction.
training: No backpropagation. Each neuron does online gradient descent (online convex programming) on its own convex log-loss in one pass over the data stream. Dataset sizes for the benchmarks are not in the packet.
setup: Permuted-MNIST continual learning (one-vs-all GLNs with [100, 25, 1] neurons per layer, context dimension 6), standard classification, regression and density-modelling benchmarks. Compared with MLP with dropout and EWC.
numbers: Appendix, Permuted-MNIST: GLN 'one-vs-all GLNs composed of [100, 25, 1] neurons per layer and a context dimension of 6'
Abstract: GLN 'performing comparably to a MLP with dropout and Elastic Weight Consolidation on standard benchmarks'
limits: The packet gives no limitations section. The abstract claims comparability with dropout-MLP and EWC on standard benchmarks.
evidence_quote: Each neuron receives inputs from the previous layer as well as the broadcasted side information z.

novelty_note.B: Halfspace gate computed from side information z with no separate classifier, used to select which weight vector applies. It selects weights, not a steering vector, and the input is side information rather than a hidden state.

title: Dynamic Manifold Hopfield Networks for Context-Dependent Associative Memory
question: Can a Hopfield network whose interactions are learned from data reshape its attractor manifold by context, giving higher associative capacity than classical and modern Hopfield networks?
mechanism: Continuous Hopfield dynamics with a learned symmetric static weight matrix, plus a cue-dependent term, so the energy landscape changes with the cue. The decomposition into cue-independent (static) and cue-dependent (dynamic) energy terms is shown in Fig. 1h. Retrieval starts from x(0) = E(u) and runs T = 10 steps. Training loss: retrieval loss plus lambda times reconstruction loss (lambda = 5). Weights are projected to symmetry and spectrally bounded. The exact dynamic-term form is in the omitted section.
training: Backpropagation with AdamW (LR 5e-4) for 10,000 steps (binary patterns) or 20,000 steps (CIFAR-10 latent model). Encoder and decoder are two-layer MLPs for CIFAR-10.
setup: Random binary patterns (N = 100), MNIST binary (N = 784), CIFAR-10 continuous latent space (N = 1000). Compared with classical (CHN) and modern (MHN) Hopfield networks.
numbers: Abstract: 'when storing 2N patterns in a network of N neurons, DMHN attain reliable retrieval with an average accuracy of 64%, compared with 1% and 13% for classical and modern variants, respectively.'
limits: The packet gives no limitations section.
evidence_quote: continuous dynamical models in which contextual modulation dynamically reshapes attractor geometry

title: "More Is Different" in Neural Circuits: Algebraic Emergence of Effective Theories in Canonical Recurrent Motifs of Biological Neuronal Networks
question: Do composed canonical circuit motifs (divisive normalisation and winner-take-all) generate non-aperiodic group-like structure from individually aperiodic primitive updates?
mechanism: Each motif is a finite transformation system whose states are acted on by input-conditioned maps. The transition monoid is the closure under composition. Krohn-Rhodes and holonomy decomposition (SgpDec) test for group components. Compositions are compared across four couplings (independent product, DN-to-WTA and WTA-to-DN cascades, recurrent coupling). Interfaces are swept exhaustively, so the composite cycle can be predicted from the coupling structure before running the dynamics.
training: none (finite-state algebra; no learning)
setup: Three- and four-state divisive-normalisation models; a winner-take-all circuit with two excitatory populations and a shared inhibitory pool; joint-state compositions.
numbers: Fig. 5 caption: 'over all 48 = 65 536 maps' for the winner-to-normalisation interface psi (panel a)
Fig. 5 caption: update schedule over 'the full grid of 50 331 648 (φ , ψ) pairs' (panel c)
Fig. 5 caption: 'the biological winner-pooling interface sits at the 95.7th percentile' (panel d)
limits: The author says these are 'probes of the computational repertoire of the cortex, not replicas of cortex'. Results are for small finite models.
evidence_quote: Recurrent circuits are compositional transformation systems; their algebra constrains what they can be programmed to compute.

novelty_note.E: Predicts from the interface structure whether composing motifs yields a composite cycle, algebraically and before running the dynamics. This is interaction prediction for composed components, not interference between many patches.

title: PolyGLU: State-Conditional Activation Routing in Transformer Feed-Forward Networks
question: Does letting each FFN neuron route among several activation functions through input-conditioned gating produce useful depth-dependent specialisation?
mechanism: PolyGLU(x) = sum_k g_k sigma_k(x W_gate) ⊙ (x W_up), with K = 4 activations (ReLU, Tanh, SiLU, GELU). Routing logits l_k = alpha_k + beta_k f(h̄)_k, where alpha is a per-neuron static preference (zero-initialised), f is a gate MLP on the mean-pooled hidden state (W1 in R^{32 x d_model}), and g = GumbelSoftmax(l, tau) with tau annealed linearly from 1.0 to 0.1.
training: Trained end-to-end from scratch on about 10B tokens (single A100), then supervised fine-tuning for 13,067 steps on math data. No sparsity or entropy loss.
inference_cost: Computes all K = 4 activations per neuron before selecting one, so overhead scales with K (not measured). Parameter overhead 0.23% (about 1.4M of 597M).
setup: PolychromaticLM, 597M parameters, 28 layers, GQA. Benchmarks include MMLU-STEM, ARC-Challenge, LAMBADA and SciQ, compared with Qwen3-0.6B-Base. GSM8K evaluation was not completed.

title: How Linear Is a Transformer Feed-Forward Block? Per-Block Linear Recoverability Is Learned, Not Architectural
question: How linearly recoverable is each trained FFN block, measured by a closed-form least-squares map, and does that predict which blocks can be replaced by a single layer?
mechanism: Cache FFN input-output pairs (x, y) from a frozen model via a forward hook. Fit the closed-form least-squares affine map W* x + b* on the training split; R_lin^2 is its held-out variance explained. Residual probe: a rank-16 bilinear term added to the linear branch, with the linear branch frozen at the closed-form optimum and the bilinear branch trained with early stopping. Replacements are re-inserted into the live LM to measure ΔPPL.
training: None on the host model. The linear ceiling is closed form. The bilinear probe and the dense control are trained on the cached pairs. Corpora: WikiText-2, Gutenberg prose, math/logic puzzles; sizes are not in the packet.
setup: GPT-2, Pythia-160m, llama-160m (all 12 blocks each), TinyLlama-1.1B as a scale probe. Corpora: WikiText-2, Gutenberg, math/logic puzzles.
numbers: Abstract: 'GPT-2's early FFN at ×8 fewer parameters for +0.77 perplexity'
Abstract: adjacent blocks range 'from nearly perfectly linear (Rlin > 0.99) to strongly nonlinear (Rlin < 0.3)'
limits: Small base models and modest English corpora. Perplexity on a capped test slice. Healing introduces an in-domain adaptation confound. The residual probe is one low-rank bilinear form, so the negative result is specific to it. The closed-form baseline is exact only for the linear candidate.
evidence_quote: We then ask whether the residual is low-order multiplicative by fitting a low-rank bilinear probe on top of the optimal linear map.

title: High-rank connectivity scaffolds support precision and generalisation in recurrent neural networks
question: Does higher-rank recurrent connectivity beyond the dominant low-dimensional dynamics contribute to accuracy and generalisation in path-integration RNNs?
mechanism: Low-dimensional activity clamp (LDAC): project hidden activity onto the top-k PCs and invert PCA to clamp higher PCs in the full space. Individual PCs are clamped to test causal roles. Recurrent-weight SVD modes and rank-k approximations of the recurrent matrix are tested, plus zeroing of single neurons ranked by displacement score.
training: RNN agents trained with proximal policy optimisation (PPO) on reward-location tasks (1D and 2D path integration). Packet gives no dataset size; 162 trained models were evaluated.
setup: 1D linear track and 2D navigation tasks; speed inputs drawn from rectified Gaussian distributions, with novel speed distributions at test. RNN agents only, no LLM.

'When tested on novel speed distributions, > 35 PCs were required for >99% reward'

title: Representing Neural Network Layers as Linear Operations via Koopman Operator Theory
question: Can a nonlinear pretrained MLP layer be replaced by a finite-dimensional linear operator, obtained with Koopman/DMD on time-delay coordinates, at a small accuracy cost?
mechanism: Layer scaling: insert k extra Linear+ReLU layers G before the target layer F1 and train G alone (Huber loss between F1 ∘ G_{k-1} and F1 ∘ F0), so ablating G restores F. Activations from the scaled stack form a snapshot matrix D = [F0 G0 ... G_{k-1} F1]. Time-delay coordinates serve as observables. DMD gives a companion-matrix linear operator that replaces the layer.
training: Scaling layers G are trained by gradient descent (AdamW, Huber loss, 10 added layers per hidden layer, search with Ray Tune). The DMD operator is a closed-form fit to the snapshots. Base MLPs trained for 5,000 epochs (Yin-Yang) and 30 epochs (MNIST).
setup: Yin-Yang dataset (2,000 random training samples; 3-hidden-layer MLP, original 98.4% in the abstract). MNIST (784-256-128-64-32-10 MLP, original 97.2%, 60,000 train and 10,000 test).

title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
question: Can a large frozen pretrained model be adapted to downstream tasks by training a low-rank additive update, avoiding full fine-tuning cost and adapter inference latency?
mechanism: For frozen W0, the layer computes h = W0 x + dW x = W0 x + B A x, with B (d x r) zero-initialized and A Gaussian-initialized; dW x is scaled by alpha/r, and alpha is set once rather than tuned. Only A and B are trained. After training, W = W0 + BA is stored or merged, so inference uses the original architecture.
training: Gradient training (Adam) of A and B only, on each task's conditional language-modelling objective over (x,y) pairs; W0 is frozen. Dataset sizes are in the experiment sections, which were not recovered.
inference_cost: Zero added latency once merged (paper claim). Unmerged adapter layers add latency: Table 1 (GPT-2 medium, ms) gives Fine-Tune/LoRA 1449.4, 338.0, 19.8 with AdapterL +2.2%, +5.0%, +20.7% and AdapterH +3.0%, +8.4%, +30.3% at batch 32, 16, 1.
setup: GPT-3 175B (headline case); RoBERTa, DeBERTa, GPT-2; NLG tasks summarization, MRC and NL2SQL (Sec. 2). Latency study on GPT-2 medium.
numbers: LoRA can reduce the number of trainable parameters by 10,000 times and the GPU memory requirement by 3 times (Abstract).

training: LAT is unsupervised (PCA over stimulus differences; no LLM gradient). The LoRRA baseline trains low-rank adapters on attention weights with a representation loss. Training data sizes for LAT stimulus sets are task-specific and not extracted.
inference_cost: Contrast-vector control needs two extra forward passes per contrast pair at inference, per the authors' own description ('computational overhead required during inference'); no FLOP figure given.
setup: LLaMA-2-Chat 7B/13B/70B; TruthfulQA MC1 and other honesty, harmlessness, power-aversion, fairness and emotion tasks.
numbers: TruthfulQA MC1 average over 7B/13B/70B: standard evaluation 32.3 vs zero-shot LAT with stimulus set 3 at 60.7 (Table 1).
Table 1 7B row: standard 31.0 vs LAT stimulus 3 58.2.
limits: Reading vectors are stimulus-independent (same direction for every input), which the authors say 'may render it a less effective control method'.
Contrast-vector control adds inference-time computation; LoRRA removes that cost but requires training.
Authors' Section 6 applications are shown as case studies rather than benchmarked against all baselines (not verified in detail).
evidence_quote: Our experiments indicate that pairing neural activities and applying PCA to the set of difference vectors can yield superior results when the stimuli in each pair share similarities except for the target concept or function.

title: Towards Unifying Interpretability and Control: Evaluation via Intervention
question: Do interpretability methods (SAEs, logit lens, tuned lens, probes) support causal intervention that changes model outputs in the intended way, and how does that compare with steering vectors and prompting?
mechanism: Unifying encoder-decoder framework: an explanation encoder maps the latent x to interpretable features z = xD; intervention edits z to z'; decoder x' = z' D^-1 reconstructs a counterfactual latent. Two metrics: intervention success rate (desired output change) and coherence-intervention trade-off. Logit lens uses the unembedding; tuned lens adds a learned affine map; SAEs and probes use their own encoder/decoder; steering vectors and prompting are baselines.
training: Existing trained artifacts are used (pretrained SAEs via SAELens, tuned lenses, linear probes); the paper proposes no new training. Amount of data not extracted.
setup: GPT2-small, Gemma2-2b, Llama2-7b, Llama3-8b; open-ended prompt dataset of simple topics and more complex concepts; baselines steering vectors and prompting.
numbers: Logit lens and tuned lens: 'intervention success rates of around 0.5 and 0.6 respectively for outputs within one point of deviation from the mean coherence score of the clean model' (Results, Figure 3 text).
On more complex concepts 'prompting generally outperforms interpretability-based interventions, particularly for the French language concept' (Section 4.4 text).
SAEs, probes and steering vectors 'require significantly larger edits in order to achieve reasonable intervention success' (Section 4 text).
limits: Intervention often reduces output coherence; at high intervention strength outputs degrade into incoherent repetition for all methods (Figure 5).
Prompting, a training-free baseline, matched or beat most interpretability-based interventions.
Only 30 generated tokens were used, which the authors note may understate prompting's success rate.
No method was consistent across models and features.
evidence_quote: we can intervene on the interpretable feature activations generated by each method

novelty_note.G: Authors report SAE feature labels are often erroneous and speculate that SAEs, probes and steering vectors may bias toward representing past tokens and information rather than the target concept; this is speculation plus label-error evidence, not a direct test.

title: Control Illusion: The Failure of Instruction Hierarchies in Large Language Models
question: How reliably do LLMs prioritise system-level over user-level instructions when two individually valid, verifiable constraints conflict?
mechanism: Evaluation framework, not an edit: pairs of mutually exclusive IFEval-style constraints (e.g. English vs French; at least 300 words vs under 50 words) are placed as primary and secondary across system and user roles under separation configurations (Pure, Task, Emph.). Metrics: primary obedience rate R1, secondary rate R2, explicit-conflict acknowledgement rate (ECAR), priority adherence ratio PAR = R1/(R1+R2) (Eq. 1; denominator extracted), and constraint bias CB between constraint types.
training: None (evaluation only; models used as provided).
setup: Six state-of-the-art LLMs (including GPT-4o variants, Claude, Llama and Qwen models; Table 6); 100 base tasks x 6 constraint pairs x 2 priority designations = 1,200 test points, plus enriched 'rich' prompts.
numbers: 'Most models show dramatically lower performance (9.6–45.8% average R1) when handling conflicting constraints' (Section on priority adherence).
'ECAR ranging from 0.1% (Qwen-7B) to 20.3% (Llama-70B)' (Table 3 discussion).
Societal hierarchy framings (authority, expertise, consensus) shift obedience more than the system/user role (Section on advanced metrics).
limits: System/user prompt separation does not reliably establish an instruction hierarchy in these models.
Models show inherent constraint-type biases regardless of priority designation.
Models rarely acknowledge conflicts explicitly (ECAR 0.1-20.3%).
Only six constraint types and simple formatting conflicts; the authors call the result a limitation of current instruction-tuning paradigms.
