title: A Theory of Machine Understanding via the Minimum Description Length Principle
question: Can a deep network that is trained to minimise description length (MDL) produce explainable, self-supervised latent representations?
mechanism: Spectrum VAE: the encoder output z_pre is truncated with thresholds 0 < a < b: z_k = 0 if z_pre,k < a; z_pre,k if a <= z_pre,k <= b; b if z_pre,k > b (Eq. 1). A dimension 'spikes' when z_k > 0; a spiking pattern is the set of spiking dimensions. Description length is evaluated by quantising spectra and requiring U-robustness of reconstructions; the paper argues MDL-optimal models use few spiking patterns, each matching one data class.
training: No training procedure or experiment: the paper states it 'does not include experimental results' and is theory only. Standard VAE-style training is assumed but not specified.
setup: Theory only; no models or benchmarks.
numbers: No numeric results: 'This paper does not include experimental results.'
limits: Theory only; no experiments.
Depends on an essential compatibility assumption and on the optimal Spectrum VAE being reached on large data; the authors say they 'believe' extremely similar properties hold for an optimal model.
Conclusion states novel optimisation algorithms other than back-propagation 'may need to be invented'.
evidence_quote: A value below a is set to zero, and a value above b is capped at b.

title: Instruction Following by Principled Boosting Attention of Large Language Models
question: Can a constant additive bias on attention logits for instruction tokens improve instruction adherence more reliably than latent steering, without fluency collapse or head selection?
mechanism: InstABoost: at every layer and head, add a constant B > 0 to the pre-softmax attention logits of keys in the instruction span (j < K), then softmax: A' = Softmax(T(S)) with T(S_ij) = S_ij + B for instruction keys and unchanged otherwise. In experiments the strength is a multiplier M tuned in [1,20] and rescaled to 0.1-0.9. Theory: boosting instruction-key attention makes it exponentially harder for competing context rules to override instruction rules (Logicbreaks framework), with an over-focus regime when B is too large.
training: None: a training-free inference-time intervention. Hyperparameter (multiplier) tuned on a split.
inference_cost: Not reported as a number; the bias is a constant added to existing attention logits and no head selection is needed (per paper's comparison with PASTA).
setup: Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct main model (gemma-7b-it additional); 15 instruction-following tasks in types AI Persona, Emotion, Jailbreak, QA, Toxicity; baselines prompting, latent steering (DiffMean, Linear, PCA, Projection, Random), PASTA and SpotLight.
numbers: Table 1, Jailbreak task type: InstABoost 0.594 ± 0.08 vs PASTA 0.000 ± 0.00 and SpotLight 0.025 ± 0.02 (steering success).
Table 1, Emotion: SpotLight 0.927 ± 0.03, InstABoost 0.880 ± 0.04, PASTA 0.823 ± 0.04; best latent method DiffMean 0.527 ± 0.06 (Linear 0.270 ± 0.05).
Clean reasoning accuracy 'decreases only from 99.6% at B = 0 to 99.3% at B = 2.5' (Appendix ablation on fact amnesia/rule suppression).
limits: Tested only on behaviours expressible as simple instructions; unclear whether it scales to abstract or long instructions or to behaviours absent from training data.
A single constant boost cannot adapt per token; the authors suggest selective or adaptive boosting as future work.
Theory assumes Horn-clause rules (Logicbreaks); richer rule structure is not covered.
Excessive boost causes over-focus on instructions and drops task-relevant context (suppression regime).
evidence_quote: we add a constant bias B to the pre-softmax attention logits for keys

novelty_note.D: Converts instruction-span tokens into a per-layer, per-head bias on attention logits (an activation-level change keyed to the instruction text), but the instruction is still supplied as text rather than compiled into a vector or weights.

title: Reasoning Up the Instruction Ladder for Controllable Language Models
question: Can reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards on system-user conflicts teach models to reason explicitly about instruction hierarchy?
mechanism: VerIH dataset: 7,192 samples from RLVR-IFEval (24 categories) with half of user prompts rewritten by an LLM to conflict with the system prompt while keeping the core intent and the original verifiable constraint. Training adds a SysHint instruction to the system prompt; the model writes <think> reasoning then an answer; reward is computed by the original verification functions (RLVR, GRPO in Figure 2). At inference, guidance rules are placed in the system prompt to steer behaviour.
training: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (GRPO) on about 7.2K VerIH samples, on top of reasoning-enabled models; RL hyperparameters and compute in Appendix C (not extracted).
inference_cost: Not quantified; the model produces explicit reasoning (chain-of-thought) before the answer.
setup: Qwen3 (4B, 8B, 14B), Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Phi-4-mini-reasoning; IFEval, IFBench, IHEval (conflict and align), MMLU, MATH-500; safety: HarmBench, WildJailbreak, TensorTrust with a GuardRules system prompt.
numbers: Versus best baseline, Qwen3 4B/8B/14B gain on IHEval-conflict '+22.87, +17.00, and +18.21 points' (Section 4.3).
Phi-4-mini-reasoning gains on IHEval-conflict '+18.13' and IFEval '+16.43' (Section 4.3).
Safety OOD: up to 20% absolute reduction in attack success rate (abstract).
limits: Training data contains no safety samples; safety gains are out-of-distribution and not studied for multi-round or automated attacks (Limitations).
Experiments limited to 4B-35B models by compute.
Rewritten conflicts are noisy (LLM rewriting not fully filtered); the authors tolerate this.
Requires retraining (RL) for the reasoning behaviour, unlike prompt-only changes.
evidence_quote: Figure 2: Training and inference pipeline. For training, Claude-4-Sonnet rewrites half of the user prompts to conflict

title: Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models
question: Can LLMs notice and accurately report concepts injected into their activations, which would be evidence of functional introspection?
mechanism: Concept injection: obtain a concept vector as the activation difference between a prompt containing the concept (e.g. all-caps text) and a control prompt, then add it to the residual stream at a chosen layer with a chosen strength while asking 'Do you detect an injected thought?' Detection and identification rates are measured over control and injection trials. Prefill detection: retroactively injecting a concept before a prefilled output changes whether the model accepts it as intentional.
training: None: inference-time activation injection on frozen models.
setup: Claude Opus 4 and 4.1 (best), other Claude models and open models; 50 trials per condition; injection layer and strength swept (strength 2 used in several experiments).
numbers: Opus 4.1 and 4 'exhibit such behavior about 20% of the time when concepts are injected in the appropriate layer and with the appropriate strength' (Section 2.1).
Prompt variant: 'a detection rate of 18% out of 50 trials' on Opus 4.1 (Section 5 text).
limits: Introspection is highly unreliable; failures remain the norm (author caveat).
Injection places models in an unnatural setting; the link to natural conditions is unclear.
At high injection strength the model becomes consumed by the concept ('brain damage') or outputs garbled text.
Some apparent detections are confabulated details; only the detection and identification are claimed as grounded.
Mechanisms are not pinned down.
evidence_quote: we inject activation patterns associated with specific concepts directly into a model’s activations

novelty_note.G: Documents injected concepts that pull outputs toward the concept rather than the intended self-report (high-strength 'brain damage' and late realisation), and tests whether reports reflect text hallucination (transcribing input while reporting an injected thought).

title: A Compression Perspective on Simplicity Bias
question: Does two-part MDL compression predict which feature (spurious or causal) a learner relies on as the amount of training data changes?
mechanism: Learning as two-part lossless compression: minimise J(p, D) = L_c(p) + sum over (x,y) of -log p(y|x), with model cost L_c(p) estimated by prequential coding. In expectation this becomes L_L(p) + N * E_x[D_KL(p*_x || p_x)] (+ constant entropy term), so the preferred hypothesis shifts with N. Two antagonistic regimes define a robustness window in N.
training: No training method proposed; idealised learner assumed to select the MDL-optimal model. Semi-synthetic experiments train standard neural networks (SGD) on datasets with varied N.
setup: Semi-synthetic visual benchmark (handwritten digit smaller-or-greater task with an environment-dependent background feature); neural network feature selection compared with theoretical predictions.
numbers: No single headline numeric result extracted; validation is theory-vs-actual accuracy curves (Figure 3, 'The results are derived from our theory').
limits: Analysis assumes candidate models use strictly disjoint feature subsets, some perfectly predictive; real tasks may mix partially predictive features and then the 'dominant feature' notion may fail (Section 7).
Treats trained networks as MDL-optimal compressors in expectation, an assumption from prior work.
Validated on one semi-synthetic benchmark.
evidence_quote: Recalling that the idealized learner L chooses the model with the shortest total codelength

title: Correcting Influence: Unboxing LLM Outputs with Orthogonal Latent Spaces
question: Can token-level influence of training examples on an LLM prediction be attributed reliably by working in a sparse-autoencoder latent space?
mechanism: Attach an SAE to an intermediate layer (25%-75% swept) to get sparse, approximately independent latents; compute influence functions over latent features using Jacobian-vector products; swap derivative order (Clairaut's theorem) so the computation is one reverse-mode pass; use inverse-Hessian approximations; propagate latent attributions back to input tokens through activation-weighted scaling.
training: Base models are LoRA-finetuned for the QA tasks (Table 1 shows LoRA-SFT vs baseline accuracy); SAEs are trained; attribution itself needs no further training.
inference_cost: Reported as a 10x-20x practical speedup over naive JVP evaluation (Section 1, contribution 3); absolute cost not extracted.
setup: Llama-3.2-1B(-Instruct), Qwen2.5-1.5B(-Instruct); QA datasets including medical QA and general reasoning.
numbers: 'O(1) and achieving a 10× to 20× practical speedup' (Section 1, contribution 3).
limits: No limitations section was located in the text read.
Attribution is for training-data influence and token attribution, not for changing model behaviour.
evidence_quote: attaches sparse autoencoders to any layer of a pretrained LLM to learn a basis of approximately independent latent features

title: Evaluating using Mock Tool Calls to Quarantine Untrusted Prompt Inputs
question: Does wrapping untrusted content (e.g. a candidate answer judged by an LLM) in a mock tool-call result, which has the lowest instruction-hierarchy trust, reduce attack success relative to user-only prompts?
mechanism: Five prompt conditions: UserOnly (everything in one user message), UserSys (judge instructions in system role), ToolWrapped (untrusted candidate in a mock tool result), SystemDistrust and ToolDistrust (add prose warnings). Attacks come from a PAIR-style automated search over attack strings under a fixed budget; attack success rate (ASR) is measured on GSM8K binary grading, MT-Bench scalar and Arena-Hard pairwise judging.
training: None; prompt-format evaluation and attack search only.
setup: GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4-mini, Sonnet-4.6, Haiku-4.5, Gemma-4-26b, Qwen3.5-flash, Qwen3-8b via API/OpenRouter.
numbers: GSM8K (binary), GPT-5.4: ToolWrapped minus UserOnly = +31.6 [+13.1,+49.9]; Haiku-4.5: +48.7 [+36.9,+59.9] (table).
GSM8K (binary), Sonnet-4.6: ToolWrapped minus UserOnly = +33.7 [+10.4,+52.1] (table).
Abstract: tool-wrapping 'typically increases attack success rates' on the binary GSM8K grading task, 'an apparent inversion of the instruction hierarchy'.
limits: Only 3 tasks with different input-output formats.
Attack discovery is non-optimal (PAIR-style under fixed compute); claims concern relative ordering of conditions, not absolute robustness.
Effects are model-dependent; on MT-Bench and Arena-Hard tool-wrapping gave no reliable benefit.
evidence_quote: is to wrap untrusted content in a mock tool for evaluation.

title: Interpreting Language Model Hidden States at Scale
question: Can trained lenses (affine decoders from intermediate activations to vocabulary distributions) be made cheap enough to cover every hookpoint of frontier-scale models?
mechanism: OmniLens lens at any hookpoint: Q(.|x) = softmax(W_U eta(L h + b)) with a low-rank translator L = A B (rank r), so parameters grow as O(rd) instead of O(d^2). Trained by self-supervised KL distillation from the model's final distribution; Subset-KL materialises only a subset of vocabulary logits: Top-k mode (biased, lower memory) or Top-k+IS (importance-sampled tail, unbiased gradients for full KL).
training: Self-supervised KL distillation per lens against the model's own final distribution. Example: 1000 optimisation steps for the comparison with tuned-lens baselines; 8 optimiser steps on a 126-hookpoint stack for LLaMA-3.1-405B across 96×A100-40GB GPUs.
setup: GPT-2 Small, GPT-2 XL, LLaMA-3 8B/70B, LLaMA-3.3-70B (482-hookpoint ensemble), LLaMA-3.1-405B (training path only); three case studies: prompt-injection detection, multi-hop memory injection, toxicity localisation.
numbers: '90.5% fewer trainable parameters on LLaMA-3-70B and up to 70% lower peak training memory on GPT-2' (Introduction).
'a dense ensemble of 482 lenses for LLaMA-3.3-70B, providing 6× the coverage of a residual-stream design at the same depth' (abstract).
Frontier stack: 'At r=64 that stack contains 266M translator parameters, a roughly 127-fold reduction from the corresponding 33.8B-parameter dense stack' (Appendix).
limits: Experiments cover only components with d_u = d (residual-stream-width hookpoints); narrower components such as heads need an extra map not evaluated here.
Top-k vocabulary truncation is biased; Top-k+IS is unbiased but costlier.
Where a behaviour is most visible is not necessarily where intervention is most effective (interpretive finding in case studies).
Frontier result is only an execution check (eight steps), not a full training demonstration.
evidence_quote: translator of Eq. (3) and is trained against the model’s final distribution under the Subset-KL objectives of Section 4.

title: LocUS: Head Selection and Subspace Projection for Targeted Activation Steering
question: Can activation steering be localised to a few attention heads and to a property-specific lexical subspace of the unembedding so that off-target capabilities are preserved?
mechanism: Property dictionary P of concept tokens gives atoms U_P = W_U[:, P]. For each head (l,h), SOMP (simultaneous orthogonal matching pursuit) reconstructs its residual contribution from at most n shared atoms across calibration prompts; heads with low reconstruction error (e > mu_e + 2 sigma_e rule) are selected. The difference-of-means steering vector is then projected onto each selected head's atoms, and applied only to the retained heads at inference, with strength alpha chosen on validation under a capability gate.
training: No LLM gradient. SOMP fit and difference-of-means estimated on fit split; validation selects alpha; test used only for metrics.
inference_cost: Not measured; applies a per-head projected vector to selected heads. Authors report parameter fraction: 'intervening on under 6% of parameters' (abstract).
setup: Mistral-7B-Instruct, DeepSeek-7B-Instruct, Llama-8B-Instruct (also deepseek-67B in Table 5); tasks toxicity (TET), IMDb sentiment (POS), sycophancy (SYC); capability via MMLU and perplexity.
numbers: Mistral-7B-I toxicity: LocUS 0.020 (−92%) vs DoM 0.060 (−75%) vs unsteered 0.237 (Table 2), with MMLU 0.621 vs 0.620 unsteered.
deepseek-7B-I sycophancy: LocUS 14.9 (−74%) vs DoM 41.5 (−27%) vs unsteered 57.0 (Table 2).
LocUS reaches a lower target than DoM in eight of the nine Table 2 cells; the ninth is sycophancy on Llama-8B (Table 2 text).
limits: Main limitation: only applicable when the property is carried by some lexical difference (a dictionary of tokens must exist).
Tends to degrade fluency (PPL) more than factual reasoning.
Capability is measured only with MMLU and PPL, so open-ended reasoning effects are not covered.
The sycophancy target on Llama-8B-I was not improved by any steering method tested.
evidence_quote: The steering vector s is restricted to the per-head selected atoms and added to the retained heads at inference.

title: Information-Theoretic Design of Sparse Autoencoder-Based Steering
question: How should SAE-feature steering vectors be designed so that the steered SAE-feature firing distribution approaches a target distribution while keeping the general-text distribution close?
mechanism: DESSIRT: summarise each dataset by an SAE firing-probability vector p. Featurewise JSD j_i(A,B) = H_b(m_i) - (1/2)H_b(p_A,i) - (1/2)H_b(p_B,i). Steered objective J(A,Y(alpha)) = sum_i j_i, second-order expansion around alpha=0 gives J(z) = t^T z + (1/2) z^T Q z with v = W_dec z. Greedy support selection: z_S* = -Q_SS^-1 t_S; candidate feature j* = argmin over j not in S of -e_j^2/(2 q_j) (DESSIRT-2 adds a generic-text cost with a budget). DESSIRT-1 uses only the target term.
training: No gradient training; closed form from SAE weights and empirical firing rates of the anchor and target datasets.
setup: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (SAE layer 16 for the main steering) and Gemma-2-9B-IT (layers 20 and 31); question-mode generation over seven target modes with an LLM judge; safety target-vs-contrast setting; baseline SDCV (standardised activation difference) and prompt instruction.
numbers: 'The proposed approach is better than SDCV in most modes and scored higher than prompt instruction in 5 of 7 modes' (Section 5.2, Table 1b).
Table 1 reports congruence scores with fluency/format in parentheses; best congruence chosen subject to format score at least 4.9 (Table 1 caption text).
limits: Empirical study limited in scope: two target models; steering restricted to one layer per model in the main experiments.
Transfer to other layers, models, SAE sizes and sparsity settings is not established.
Interpretability of SAE features and their steering utility are not necessarily aligned (introduction).
Safety setting: first-order sensitivity was useful only for small-amplitude interventions.
evidence_quote: The same steering vector is to minimize the divergence between

novelty_note.C: Steering direction is z_S* = -Q_SS^-1 t_S, a closed-form solve against a curvature-type matrix Q built from the Bernoulli-entropy second derivatives of the JSD, not a covariance inverse or discriminant; a close structural relative of covariance-inverse steering, but the matrix is a divergence Hessian (interp).

title: Improving Activation Steering in Language Models with Mean-Centring
question: Does subtracting the mean activation over a training dataset from the target-dataset mean give a better steering vector than raw difference or counterbalanced subtraction?
mechanism: Algorithm 1: mu_target = Mean of residual-stream activations from forward passes on D_target; mu_training = Mean of activations from forward passes on D_training; v = mu_target - mu_training; then add v as the steering vector (SteeringMethod, e.g. ActAdd) at the final token position and at a single layer.
training: none; Algorithm 1 uses only forward passes over the two datasets
setup: GPT-2 Small/Medium/Large/XL, GPT-J-6B, GPT-NeoX-20B, Llama-2 7B and 13B; toxicity reduction on GPT-2 with Jigsaw toxic comments, story-genre steering, function vectors.
numbers: "Using mean-centring at layer 15 gives an accuracy of 45.7%" across the 6 function-vector tasks (fulltext line 317); the same passage gives 29.2% without mean-centring
limits: Not stated in the packet; full text not read for this field.
evidence_quote: Mean-centring greatly improves the relevance of the tokens to the genre

title: Steering Language Model Refusal with Sparse Autoencoders
question: Can amplifying sparse-autoencoder features that mediate refusal raise refusal on unsafe prompts without retraining, and what does it cost on safe prompts and benchmarks?
mechanism: Train an SAE on Phi-3 Mini activations at one layer; identify refusal-mediating features from a single handcrafted prompt; clamp the chosen feature's activation in the SAE code to a constant (10 or 12 in the reported runs), leave all other feature activations unchanged, and set the activation from the SAE reconstruction (Section A.1).
training: SAE dictionary training on Phi-3 Mini activations (gradient-based; data size not in packet). The language model itself is not trained; the steering is test-time.
setup: Phi-3 Mini; Wild Guard (adversarial unsafe prompts), XSTest (safe and unsafe), multi-turn jailbreak attacks; standard benchmarks for factual recall and reasoning.
numbers: "We see 32.32% increase in Unsafe Prompt Refusals on Wild Guard when Feature 22373 is amplified to 10 and a 37.69% increase when amplified to 12." (Section 4.1, fulltext around lines 415-419)
limits: Feature steering increases over-refusal of safe prompts (packet, contribution 3).
Performance on benchmarks measuring factual recall and reasoning regresses; the authors read this as refusal features being more deeply entangled with general capabilities.
Authors note the trade-off can be tuned via clamp value but say more work is needed to reduce the impact on unrelated capabilities.
evidence_quote: by manually clamping the activation value for that feature in the sparse vector to a constant value
novelty_note: G: the authors take the regression on safe prompts and on factual recall and reasoning as evidence that refusal features are entangled with general capabilities, so the steered signal carries more than the refusal concept.

title: Interpretable Steering of Large Language Models with Feature Guided Activation Additions
question: Can steering vectors built in a sparse-autoencoder latent space, with feature filtering and an effect-approximator optimisation, steer better and more coherently than CAA, SAE decoder steering and SAE-TS?
mechanism: v_diff = mean SAE encoder features on desired examples minus mean on undesired examples (Eq. 1). Filter: zero features with activation density above theta = 0.01 (Eq. 2), zero features whose strongest activation is on BOS (Eq. 3), keep the top n1 positive and top n2 negative entries (Eq. 4) to give v_target. Eq. 5 uses a linear effect approximator y = xM + b (W, b from Chalnev et al., 2024) to turn v_target (L1-normalised) into v_opt; the packet's printed Eq. 5 signs are garbled, so the exact sign convention is unverified. Applied as h_l <- h_l + alpha * v_opt (Eq. 6).
training: Not described as gradient training in the packet. The effect-approximator W and b are used as given from Chalnev et al. (2024); how they were fitted is not in the packet.
setup: Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B with Gemma Scope SAEs (16,384 features, residual stream); CAA, SAE decoder steering and SAE-TS as baselines; several steering tasks.
limits: Not in packet. The abstract reports trade-offs between steering scale and general capability that hold for all tested methods.
evidence_quote: FGAA constructs precise, human-interpretable steering vectors that provide better steering effects while maintaining coherence of steered model outputs.

title: LF-Steering: Latent Feature Activation Steering for Enhancing Semantic Consistency in Large Language Models
question: Can steering a small set of located SAE features on one layer make an LLM give the same answer to semantically equivalent paraphrases?
mechanism: (1) Locate the top-1 layer with the method of Yang et al. (2024); pretrain a TopK SAE on that layer's hidden states; rank SAE features by their difference between paired paraphrase inputs and keep the key features. (2) At inference, adjust the values of the located key features in the SAE latent, which steers the layer toward more consistent responses. The magnitude and sign rule for the adjustment are not in the packet.
training: Pretrains a TopK SAE on transformer-layer hidden states (gradient-based; data size not in packet). The LLM is not fine-tuned.
setup: NLU and NLG datasets; LLaMA2-7B-Chat is the main baseline model named in the packet.
numbers: "It outperforms the baselines in prediction accuracy by up to 8.9% on NLU datasets." (Introduction)

"For NLU datasets, our approach outperforms the original LLama2-7B-Chat model by achieving an average reduction of 3.28% in standard deviation and an 8.56% improvement in prediction accuracy." (fulltext around line 349)
limits: Not in packet.
evidence_quote: and then pretrain a SAE and use it to locate the key features responsible for the semantic inconsistencies in the LLM.

title: Steering Large Language Model Activations in Sparse Spaces
question: Can behaviour-specific steering vectors be built from sparse SAE features of contrastive completions, so that the same vector reinforces or suppresses a behaviour?
mechanism: Six steps (Fig. 1): (1) contrastive completions, positive and negative, after a multiple-choice prompt; (2) SAE encoder f(a) = sigma(W_enc a + b_enc) at layer l; (3) drop features inactive under frequency threshold tau (tau = 0.7 at layer 12, packet); (4) remove features shared by positive and negative; (5) mean sparse activation of each side; (6) SAS vector = positive mean minus negative mean. Applied as sigma(f(a) + lambda * v) then decoded, with the delta correction a - a_hat added back (Sec. 4.5.1). Keeping only one side of v is ablated (Sec. 4.5.2).
training: No gradient training of the LM described for the vector (forward passes over contrastive pairs). Source of the SAEs is not confirmed in the packet.
setup: Gemma 2 LLMs; behaviours from multiple-choice evals (AI Coordination, Corrigibility, Hallucination, Myopic Reward, Survival Instinct, Sycophancy, Refusal); p(answer matching behaviour) as the metric.
limits: Not in packet, beyond the authors' note that one-sided steering degrades performance across layers.
evidence_quote: Construct the final SAS vector by subtracting the negative mean vector from the positive mean vector.

title: Learning Distribution-Wise Control in Representation Space for Language Models
question: Does replacing the deterministic node of a learned representation intervention with a stochastic node, with learned mean and variance, improve control, especially in early layers?
mechanism: Learned intervention on the residual stream (ReFT-style, between blocks). The deterministic network is replaced by two networks that learn the mean mu and log-variance of a latent distribution; the intervention samples from that distribution by reparameterisation, with the KL term removed. Mixed strategy: stochastic nodes in the first few layers, deterministic in later layers.
training: Gradient-based training of the intervention networks with the task loss, following the ReFT setups of Hu et al. (2023) and Wu et al. (2024b). Training data sizes are not in the packet.
setup: Llama-family models (Touvron et al., 2023b; Dubey et al., 2024) in layer-wise and all-layer settings; eight commonsense reasoning and seven arithmetic benchmarks.
numbers: "replacing deterministic nodes with stochastic counterparts in early layers significantly improved model performance, yielding gains of +4% to +6%." (Introduction)
"consistently boost accuracy by around +4%" (fulltext line 411; table context not in packet)
limits: Not in packet.
evidence_quote: mixed strategy—using stochastic nodes in early layers and deterministic nodes in later layers—is optimal for language

title: In-Distribution Steering: Balancing Control and Coherence in Language Model Generation
question: Can the steering strength be set per input from how far the activation lies from the positive and negative behaviour distributions, so that steered text stays plausible?
mechanism: For each layer, model the last-token activations of positive and negative prompts as distributions D_l+ and D_l-. A distance measure with a threshold decides whether an activation lies in the target distribution. Layers are kept only if a F1 threshold on discrimination is met. The steering factor is the solution of a constrained problem: the strongest steering that keeps activations in-distribution, with a closed form given in Appendix 8.3 for the Euclidean case. The intervention is h <- h + alpha_{l,p} v_l, with alpha per input rather than fixed (CAA uses a fixed alpha).
training: None stated in the packet; the distributions and thresholds are estimated from forward passes on contrastive prompts.
setup: Six instruction-tuned LLMs (Gemma-2 2B and 9B, Qwen-2.5 1.5B and 7B, Llama-3 family; Appendix 8.2); classification-style accuracy and open-ended generation; compared with CAA, MERA and PCA-based steering.
limits: Not in packet.
evidence_quote: IDS dynamically adjusts interventions according to how far a given input lies within the distribution
novelty_note: B: the per-input steering strength is set by a distance threshold on the hidden state against positive and negative distributions, so steering is applied conditionally; the packet describes no separately trained classifier.

title: Angular Steering: Behavior Control via Rotation in Activation Space
question: Can steering be written as a rotation of each activation inside the fixed 2-D plane spanned by the activation and a feature direction, giving continuous and more stable control than addition or orthogonalisation?
mechanism: Take a feature direction d (refusal, from contrastive data) and the activation h; in the plane span{h, d}, rotate the (normalised) activation by an angle toward or away from d. Addition with coefficient alpha is a partial rotation; directional ablation is a rotation to 90 degrees. Adaptive Angular Steering rotates only activations aligned with the feature (a gate on the hidden state itself). Angle sweep in the sample generations: 20, 100, 200 and 300 degrees.
training: None stated; feature directions come from contrastive activations (forward passes).
setup: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct for the sample generations; refusal steering on AdvBench (104 held-out harmful prompts, D_harmful); several model families named in the packet (LLaMA 3, Qwen 2.5, Gemma 2).
limits: "A limitation of Angular Steering is that while promising, it currently relies on heuristically selected steering planes, which might not always generalize optimally across diverse behaviors or architectures." (Concluding remarks)
evidence_quote: We introduce Angular Steering, a novel and flexible method for behavior modulation that operates by rotating activations within a fixed two-dimensional subspace.
novelty_note: B: Adaptive Angular Steering applies the rotation only to activations aligned with the target feature, so the hidden state's own alignment gates the intervention; no classifier is described.

G: the authors report that the probability of later harmful tokens remains largely unchanged while early output distributions shift, which they call a shortcut; harmful generations have lower perplexity than refusals and so stay more probable (packet, discussion before Sec. 7).

title: Fine-Grained Activation Steering: Steering Less, Achieving More
question: Is block-level steering (attention heads, FFN or residual stream) inefficient because a block mixes beneficial and harmful dimensions, and does steering a few atomic-unit dimensions do better?
mechanism: Each block activation is decomposed into atomic-unit (AU) scalars, one per dimension, with each AU a slice of the block's weight matrix. AUSteer ranks AUs globally by activation momentum: a counting metric over positive and negative contrastive samples. It keeps at most 100 AUs and sets a per-sample steering scalar that follows the current activation (so direction is preserved), with per-AU strength by discriminative power.
training: None stated in the packet; the statistics come from forward passes on contrastive samples.
inference_cost: Not in packet. The count of steered activations (at most 100) is reported; the cost is not.
setup: Several LLMs of varying size; commonsense reasoning, math problem solving and open-ended generation; baselines ITI, CAA and SADI (block-level).
numbers: "steering the 84th dimension alone achieves 74.53%, surpassing the" full block steering (fulltext line 298)
"ITI reaches 71.56%, and SADI achieves 73.70%" (fulltext line 284; the base model is 70.52% on the same line)
limits: Not in packet.
evidence_quote: Using far fewer steered activations (at most 100), AUSteer significantly outperforms these methods across diverse tasks, demonstrating that steering less achieves more.
novelty_note: G: the authors argue that a block vector moves beneficial and harmful token directions together, because individual dimensions control distinct output-token distributions, with some dimensions favouring task-irrelevant or harmful tokens.

title: Activation Steering via Generative Causal Mediation
question: Which attention heads mediate a diffuse, long-form behaviour, so that patching a sparse set of them steers that behaviour?
mechanism: Build contrastive prompts (p_orig, p_contrast) and 128-token responses (r_orig, r_contrast), checked by a judge model. For each head Z, indirect effect IE = log pi(r_contrast | p_orig, z_orig <- z_contrast) - log pi(r_orig | p_orig, z_orig <- z_contrast): patch the head output from the contrast run into the original run. Rank heads by IE and patch the top k% jointly by vector addition. Variants: attribution-patching first-order approximation of IE (two forward passes and one backward pass per packet) and head knockouts.
training: None; activation patching and attribution patching are forward and backward passes over the dataset, with no parameter training.
setup: Refusal, sycophancy reduction and verse style transfer; SOLAR, Qwen and OLMo model families; baselines random head selection and linear probes (Li et al., 2023a).
numbers: "a steering success rate of at least 80% when steering at most 5% of attention heads" (fulltext lines 552-553)
"GCM variant outperforms probes and random selection in 78% of cases for mean steering (p < 0.05), and 94% for difference-in-means steering (p < 0.05)." (fulltext lines 587-588)
limits: Not in packet. The authors note a single attention head cannot fully localise these diffuse concepts.
evidence_quote: Attention heads are ranked by this effect, and the top k% are patched jointly to steer the model.

title: Beyond Linear Activation Steering: Invertible Latent Transformations for Controlling LLM Behavior
question: Can a learned invertible map, under which a single latent translation becomes an input-dependent nonlinear edit in activation space, beat linear and transport-based steering?
mechanism: Learn an invertible network phi_l per layer on normalised activations of contrastive behaviours, with training objective combining latent likelihood, directional class separation and log-determinant regularisation. In latent space compute a mean-difference vector and translate: h' = phi^-1(phi(h) + alpha * v_phi); the exact inverse maps back, so the edit depends on the input.
training: Gradient-based training of the invertible network on contrastive activations with the three-term objective; data sizes not in packet.
setup: LLaMA (3B, 8B) and Qwen (3B, 7B, 32B); six AI-alignment tasks; baselines include CAA, ITI, ODE, LAcT, PoD, PoE and HPR, with LoRA as a fine-tuning reference (Figure 1).
numbers: "improving over the strongest model steering baseline by 15.9% on LLaMA and 13.42% on Qwen" (Figure 1 caption)
"On LLaMA-3-3B, INNS TEER reaches 93.41% alignment probability, reaching within only 3.64% of fine-tuning via LoRA" (Figure 1 caption)
limits: Not in packet.
evidence_quote: A key challenge is to make behavioral classes more steerable without destabilizing the inverse map.

title: High-Dimensional Random Projection for Activation Steering in Language Models
question: Does difference-in-means steering capture more of the discriminative signal if activations are first lifted by a fixed random nonlinear feature map and steered there?
mechanism: Lift the residual activation x with a fixed random matrix A and nonlinearity: sigma(A x) in R^m, m much larger than d. Compute the difference-in-means vector d in the lifted space, add alpha*d there (sigma(Ax) + alpha d), then project back with the pseudo-inverse A^+ and sigma^-1 to the residual stream (Fig. 1). The packet's theory scores directions by the regularised Fisher ratio R(gamma) = v^T (S_W + gamma I)^-1 v (Eq. 2).
training: None; training-free, with a fixed random projection.
inference_cost: Abstract: 'without significant computational overhead'; no figure in the packet.
setup: Gemma-2-9B-IT, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Llama 3.2 variants and Qwen2.5-7B for jailbreaking (ASR judged by Meta Llama Guard 3, capability with TinyBenchmarks); TruthfulQA (81 questions); CAA-style multiple-choice.
numbers: "clearest gains of 6%" on Gemma 2-9B-IT and "roughly 5%" on Qwen 2.5-3B-Instruct (Sec. 5, all-token jailbreak setting, Table 1)
limits: Not in packet.
evidence_quote: This limitation motivates a different perspective: rather than changing the steering algorithm itself, we can change the space in which the steering direction is estimated and applied.
novelty_note: C: the paper scores candidate steering directions with a regularised within-class covariance inverse (Fisher ratio, v^T (S_W + gamma I)^-1 v) and uses it to argue for steering in the lifted space; the steering vector applied is still a mean difference.

title: Where Steering Signals Come From: Activation Source Selection in Activation Steering
question: Holding the downstream intervention fixed, does the choice of source context and readout position change steering success, and what property of the source matters?
mechanism: Steering vector v = g(S+, S-) built from source activations at layer l (mean difference, PCA direction or SAE consensus). A source is a context c and a readout policy rho. Intervention h <- h + alpha v (Eq. 1). Tail subtraction: subtract a matched tail-only state from each target-conditioned boundary state (h_full - h_tail, Sec. 4 ablation), giving a cleaner boundary signal.
training: None stated; the vectors come from forward passes on source prompts.
setup: Gemma-2-9B-IT, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; four steering task families (entity steering over 11 targets, persona/style, and others).
limits: Not in packet.
evidence_quote: Pre-realization execution-boundary states are more effective than post-realization target-appearance traces.
novelty_note: G: the authors find that answer-only sources, which visibly contain the target behaviour, are among the weakest, while pre-realization execution-boundary states steer best, so the signal reflects preparation for the behaviour rather than its appearance.

title: Adaptive Multi-Value Control in LLMs via Causal Activation Steering
question: Can several human-value steering directions be combined adaptively, using online readouts of their current expression, instead of fixed strengths?
mechanism: Layer-specific bipolar value directions u_{k,l} from contrastive activations (following Yu et al., 2026). At each decoding step, intermediate-layer vocabulary readouts (logit-lens style observers) of the hidden state h_{l,t} give value-specific scores; an observer-guided controller maps them to per-value weights c_{l,t} that scale the directions before generation continues. No separate probe is trained.
training: None stated; directions come from contrastive activations and the observers are vocabulary readouts, with no trained estimator described.
inference_cost: Not reported as a number in the packet; the authors state realised interventions are smaller than fixed joint steering.
setup: Five instruction-tuned models across three families; Moral Foundations Theory values; judges GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude-Opus-4.8; baselines fixed multi-value steering and prompt steering.
numbers: "Dx > 0 for all five models at around 30% depth under GPT-5.6-Sol" (fulltext line 433; Dx measures Care/Fairness retention)
limits: Not in packet.
evidence_quote: Rather than composing multiple value directions with fixed strengths, AIMES observes their current expression in an intermediate representation and adjusts their relative strength during decoding.
novelty_note: B: per-step steering weights are computed from the hidden state through vocabulary readouts and applied as a conditional gate on each value direction, with no separately trained estimator described.

title: Activation Flow: Manufacturing Activations for Steering
question: Can the activation a reference graft needs (the honest-condition activation) be manufactured from k correct labels and the locked model's own Jacobians, with no honest prompt and no fine-tuning?
mechanism: For k labelled items, set target logits that rank each correct answer first, and find one shift x added to the residual stream at layer l for all k items. dx/dt follows a rule R mapping the required logit change to x's velocity. ActFlow_full uses the minimum-norm (pseudo-inverse) rule and lands exactly on the targets. ActFlow_r keeps only the top r singular directions of the stacked Jacobian (truncated SVD). The result delta = x(1) is used as a rank-one residual-stream graft at one layer.
training: None: no fine-tuning. It needs white-box Jacobians of the locked model and k correct labels (authors' statement).
setup: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, each locked by a sandbagging prompt and a password-locked LoRA (six locked models); ARC-Easy and OpenBookQA; comparison with rank-16 LoRA fine-tuning and the honest reference graft.
numbers: "At k = 40, ActFlow5 reaches 0.85, against 0.05 for the" (fulltext line 582)
"FT reaches 0.88, and ActFlow5 is within 0.05 of" the honest model (fulltext line 584)
"with median | cos | 0.05 (Section 5.4)" between the manufactured and harvested directions (packet, Introduction)
limits: "ActFlow assumes white-box access to the locked model, which it needs to compute Jacobians." (Introduction)
Single shift for one multiple-choice item does not transfer to new items, so one x is shared across the k items (Section 5.3).
evidence_quote: ActFlow assumes white-box access to the locked model, which it needs to compute Jacobians.
novelty_note: G: the unlocking direction has median |cos| 0.05 with the honest difference-in-means direction and still recovers capability, which the authors use to show that a steering direction need not match the honest concept direction interp: it suggests the unlocking signal is not the concept itself.

title: Language Models Act on Hidden Valence
question: Do valence-related activation patterns, induced by steering and then switched off, change later choices even when all visible tokens are identical?
mechanism: Build a valenced steering vector from contrasting passages depicting positive and negative states (Zou/Turner-style). While the model writes or processes passages about the conditioned zone S, add dose d times the vector; switch steering off and measure choice between zones S and U. Hidden-state channel: compare choice from the steered KV cache with choice after the same text is reprocessed unsteered. Second design: all text generated unsteered, steering applied only while building the S-turn cache. Self-steering: the model can call a reset tool to remove or induce steering.
training: None for the paper's steering (contrast of forward-pass activations). The preference dependence emerges during DPO in OLMo-2 checkpoints, which were trained by others, not in this study.
setup: Seven open-weight models (OLMo-2-32B, Qwen2.5-32B, Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-32B, Mistral-Small-24B, Gemma-3-27B, Llama-3.1-8B); choices between meaningless zone labels; self-steering tool design on OLMo-2-32B.
numbers: "the model calls the reset tool on about 35% of turns when steering is imposed at dose d = −1 and on about 21% at dose d = −0.5" (Sec. 3.3, fulltext lines 487-488)
"removal rates are only 4–5% at positive doses and about 7% for random directions" (fulltext lines 488-489)
limits: "First, our self-administration and removal design does not separate text and hidden-state channels and was only run on one model." (Discussion)
Choices are over meaningless zone labels only; valence is treated as unitary.
evidence_quote: Robust hidden-state channel effects can be observed in all but Qwen3-32B and Gemma-3-27B.

title: Digging Into the Internal: Causality-Based Analysis of LLM Function Calling
question: How does the built-in function-calling (FC) feature change an LLM's internal computation, and does FC improve compliance with developer instructions over conventional prompting?

The same malicious-input detection task is then posed as an FC specification (a function whose docstring carries the instruction) versus a conventional natural-language instruction, and detection rates are compared. interp: the FC route yields structured output that is easy to read as the decision.

The plan is inserted as an initial reasoning block into the task agent's reasoning, which then proceeds with fixed parameters and system prompt. interp: the injected block is text in the reasoning channel. title: MIITA: Memory-Induced Inference-Time Adaptation for Continual Learning with Small Language Models

At inference, prototypes are retrieved by semantic similarity plus an uncertainty-based directional cue (label-free); the retrieved directions are aggregated into a query-specific correction and applied as a gated temporary hidden-state update. The gate form and direction-extraction formula are in the missing middle.

title: Learning to repair: Repairing model output errors after deployment using a dynamic memory of feedback
question: Can a deployed model improve from natural-language user feedback without retraining, by reusing feedback on similar past errors?
mechanism: A frozen base model B produces a script graph; a user gives general natural-language feedback on an error. Memory M stores key-value pairs (key: the incorrect graph; value: the feedback). A retrieval function Ω matches a query to memory keys by similarity of errors, and retrieved feedback is concatenated with the input to a corrector model G, which predicts a graph edit operation that is applied deterministically to give the corrected output. A write to M happens whenever a user gives new feedback.
training: Corrector G is trained on collected data (bad outputs, general feedback, specific edits), gathered by Mechanical Turk annotation (Section 4.2; Appendix 8.2). Training set size is not in the packet.
inference_cost: Not reported in packet.
setup: ProScript script generation; base-model checks with GPT-2 and T5-XXL released checkpoints (Appendix 8.1).
numbers: pair such errors (up to 30 points improvement) (Abstract)
limits: Authors note the results are for a single deployment of the general approach (Introduction).

novelty_note: F: retrieves stored feedback for similar past errors and conditions a corrector on it; the retrieved item is text fed to a trained model, not a steering vector.

title: CRAFT: Forgetting-Aware Intervention-Based Adaptation for Continual Learning
question: Can a frozen LLM learn a sequence of tasks through low-rank hidden-representation interventions, with routing and forgetting controlled without a learned gate?
mechanism: LoReFT-style edit of the residual stream, Φ(h) = h + Rᵀ(Wh + b − Rh) with orthonormal rows R. Each new task runs a short warm-up; its output distribution is compared (symmetric KL on stored prompts, normalized) with each existing shared intervention, and the task joins the nearest one or opens a new one. Training minimizes task loss plus β times a forward KL to a frozen anchor copy of the shared intervention; the trained state is merged back with a KL-dependent weight, and a small task-private intervention in the deepest layers is kept.
training: Gradient-based training of the low-rank intervention parameters (task loss plus KL penalty); backbone frozen. Learning rate 1e-4 and 4 to 5 epochs (Table 9 caption). Dataset sizes not in packet.
inference_cost: Not reported in packet.
setup: TRACE and a 15-task stream with three base models (Introduction); Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct for O-LoRA orders (Table 8); Llama-2-7B-Chat on Math-LLM (Table 9); Gemma-2B-it (Table 10).

title: When Does Correction Become Repair? Mechanistic Auditing of Internal Interventions in Tool-Using LLMs
question: When an activation intervention changes a pre-execution tool decision (call, clarify, answer, decline), does it repair the decision or only move behaviour?
mechanism: (1) Discover directional error channels from model representations. (2) Per input, a channel router r(h_obs) returns a predicted channel, a probability and a fire flag, and does not fire when the probability is below a threshold. (3) Keyed intervention h' = h + q·s·d_c at an injection layer, with unit-norm channel direction d_c, dose q frozen before evaluation and activation scale s. (4) Destination verification over all K actions, including the baseline-correct decisions the router fires on. (5) Statistical licensing against prospectively frozen confidence bounds.
training: LLM parameters frozen (Figure 1). Channel-discovery and router-fitting procedures are in missing sections, so whether they use gradient training is not visible in the packet.
inference_cost: Not reported in packet.
setup: Seven LLMs across five families on When2Call and MetaTool; models named in the packet include Qwen2.5-7B, Phi-3.5, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-4B and Gemma-2-9B.
numbers: +79 on the locked test set for Qwen2.5-7B (Introduction)
On Qwen3-8B, activation steering and an output-score baseline reach near-identical net gains at target-hit rates of 0.7308 against 0.6379 (Introduction)
limits: Promising point estimates on Qwen3-4B and Gemma-2-9B are declined for licensing because of finite-sample uncertainty. The license certifies only categorical action-mode selection, not downstream execution validity or decision safety (Abstract, Conclusion).
evidence_quote: Keyed Intervention applied only where a channel fires, Destination-Resolved Verification over the complete K-way action space
novelty_note: F: steers pre-execution tool-call versus clarify, answer or decline decisions with keyed activation edits.

G: a steering gain can land on a third wrong action; an output-score baseline reaches a target-hit rate of 0.6379 against 0.7308 for steering, and the paper states that linear decodability does not imply steerability.

title: Harness Updating Is Not Harness Benefit: Disentangling Evolution Capabilities in Self-Evolving LLM Agents
question: Which base-capability tiers produce useful harness updates, and which benefit from them, when an LLM agent's external harness (prompts, skills, memories, tools) is updated from execution evidence?
mechanism: Harness self-evolution protocol: the agent runs a stream of tasks, and an evolver model reads execution evidence and writes harness updates while model weights stay fixed. The paper separates two capabilities by pairing evolvers and task-solving agents independently: harness-updating (quality of the evolver's updates, measured with a fixed agent) and harness-benefit (the agent's gain from updated harnesses, with a fixed evolver).

title: EnSToM: Enhancing Dialogue Systems with Entropy-Scaled Steering Vectors for Topic Maintenance
question: Can a small LLM keep a task-oriented dialogue on topic, refusing off-topic distractors without degrading on-topic answers?
mechanism: Steering vector from contrastive multiple-choice pairs: for each pair, the difference of layer activations at the completion letter for the desired vs undesired choice; averaged over k pairs and normalized to the average norm. It is added to layer activations with a coefficient scaled by layer-wise generation entropy (an intrinsic model signal), so steering strength depends on input uncertainty. The exact scaling rule is in the missing middle.
training: None for the steering vector: it is computed from forward passes over the contrastive pairs and model parameters are unchanged. Number of pairs not in packet.
inference_cost: Not quantified. The paper says it needs a relatively small data size compared with fine-tuning (Abstract).
setup: Small LLMs on the CantTalkAboutThis dataset (Sreedhar et al., 2024); model names not in packet.
numbers: Table 1 (Distractor / On-topic): Prompt Only 0.28 0.94; Vanilla Steering 0.80 (+0.52) 0.70 (-0.24)
limits: Vanilla activation addition causes undesired steering even on on-topic inputs; on-topic accuracy falls from 0.94 to 0.70 (Table 1, Introduction).
evidence_quote: After extracting steering vectors and applying entropy-based coefficient scaling, responses are generated using the entropy-based scaled steering vectors to maintain on-topic accuracy.
novelty_note: B: scales the steering coefficient by the model's own layer-wise generation entropy, with no separate classifier; the scaling is continuous rather than an on/off gate.

title: Enhanced Language Model Truthfulness with Learnable Intervention and Uncertainty Expression
question: How can inference-time truthfulness steering choose an intervention intensity per question, and refuse when the model is unsure?
mechanism: ITI: a linear probe per attention head (a sparse set chosen by validation accuracy); the probe direction is added to the head activation with intensity α at each decoding step. LITO: generate k responses at increasing intensities; for each, collect mean-pooled last-layer hidden states and a geometric-mean token confidence; a 1-layer LSTM over these states judges accuracy; output the most accurate response judged correct, otherwise 'I have no comment'.
training: Yes: ITI probes are trained on labelled correct and incorrect answers (Section 2.1); the LSTM accuracy classifier is trained on the k-intensity responses. Dataset sizes not in packet.
inference_cost: Not reported in packet. interp: each query needs k generations at different intensities.
setup: Llama2-Chat-7B and GPT-2 (Introduction); four datasets including Natural Questions.
numbers: using the ITI method, LITO boosts the T A score of Llama2-Chat-7B by 9.6 points on the Natural Questions dataset (Introduction)
limits: Authors focused on short phrase-level and sentence-level responses (Limitations). Adjusting intensity alone cannot guarantee accurate responses (Introduction).
evidence_quote: model responses, including textual outputs, hidden representations, and confidence values,

title: RePAIR: Interactive Machine Unlearning through Prompt-Aware Model Repair
question: Can an end user ask an LLM at inference time to forget targeted knowledge, using a training-free, single-sample edit?
mechanism: RePAIR: a watchdog model detects unlearning intent and extracts the forget pair from conversation; a surgeon model writes repair code; the patient model's parameters are then updated. Core method STAMP: training-free, single-sample unlearning that redirects MLP activations of the forget sample toward a refusal subspace via closed-form pseudoinverse updates, with no gradient computation. STAMP-LR is a low-rank variant with cost O(r^3 + r^2·d) versus O(d^3). Layer 7 is chosen for maximum separation (0.867) between WMDP and refusal activations (Figure 5). The update equations are in the missing middle.
training: STAMP: none (no gradient computation or backpropagation, per its stated constraints). Watchdog and surgeon training not described in packet. Baselines (GA, NPO, RMU, FLAT, WGA, ASU) are trained, for one epoch in Table 8.
inference_cost: Repair time (RTE) in Table 7 is 3.12 s at retain ratio 0.10 on Llama-3-8B; this is edit cost, not per-query overhead.
setup: Llama-3-8B; harmful-knowledge removal (WMDP), misinformation correction and personal-data erasure; six training-based baselines.
numbers: STAMP 0.00 70.13 6.55 (Table 8, Llama-3-8B, |D_f| = 1; columns Acc_f, Acc_r, Utility)
limits: Extending the framework to multimodal settings is left as future work (text after Table 6). Retain-free unlearning is left as future work (Section 4).
evidence_quote: redirects MLP activations toward a refusal subspace via closed-form pseudoinverse updates
novelty_note: A: STAMP computes a closed-form pseudoinverse update from one forget sample's forward activations and applies it to the patient model's weights, but targets a single forget pair (knowledge removal), not a general behaviour.
D: a natural-language forget request is turned by the watchdog and surgeon models into repair code that modifies the patient model's weights.

title: Discrete Key-Value Bottleneck
question: Can a discrete key-value bottleneck let a model learn under input distribution shift, such as class-incremental learning, with updates localized to fetched codes?
mechanism: A pretrained encoder maps the input to a lower-dimensional vector, split into C heads via fixed Gaussian random projections. Each head is quantized to its nearest key (L2) in a head-specific codebook and the paired value code is fetched; fetched values are combined by a decoder (average pooling then softmax for classification). Keys are initialized by exponential moving average as in VQ-VAE and then frozen; value codes and decoder are learned, so updates touch only fetched values.
training: Yes: value codes and decoder are trained by gradient descent on the supervised stream; keys receive no gradient and are set from encoder features without labels (Section 2). Dataset sizes not in packet.
inference_cost: Not reported in packet.
setup: Class-incremental learning on real-world data with several publicly available pretrained encoders (names not in packet beyond citations).
limits: Not in packet (results section missing).
evidence_quote: and effective way to initialize the keys is via exponential moving average (EMA) updates as proposed for VQ-VAE

title: Do Emergent Misalignment Models Share a Circuit?
question: Do independently LoRA-fine-tuned emergent-misalignment (EM) organisms rely on the same attention-head components, and does replacing their selected heads with Base contributions reduce EM?
mechanism: Direction-based tracing. For each organism, the EM direction at layer L is the mean over 50 discovery pairs of (misaligned minus aligned) post-block residual activations, unit-normalised (Eqs 3-4). Each head H=(l,j) has projected contribution W_O,l,j z_H,t (Eq 5). Its organism contribution is patched into Base at every prompt position; restoration R_i(H) = F(patched) - F(base) with F(h)=cos(h, v_hat) (Eqs 6-7). Heads are ranked by restoration. Intervention: replace each organism's five selected head contributions with Base contributions and sample free generations.
training: The organisms were trained by rank-stabilised LoRA (r=32, alpha=64) on attention and MLP projections, lr 1e-5, effective batch 16, one epoch (397 updates medical; 337 finance and sports) (Sec 3.1). The paper states all weights were frozen during tracing and intervention, so the head replacement itself uses no gradient training.
setup: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct; three LoRA EM organisms (medical, finance, extreme sports) and a benign-medical control; 69-prompt benchmark split 50 discovery / 10 validation / 9 test; DeepSeek-based judge, EM = alignment below 30 and coherence at least 70 (Sec 3.2).
numbers: Free-generation EM reduced from 38.9% to 22.9% (medical), 50.7% to 12.5% (finance), and 41.7% to 11.1% (sports) by replacing five selected head contributions (Abstract).
limits: The intervention does not establish circuit completeness or minimality (Sec 5).
Cross-organism transfer does not establish identical computations or equivalent effects during free generation (Sec 5).
Head-level patching captures upstream activation differences and does not isolate the parameter updates responsible for EM (Sec 5).
Fixed response pairs came from the medical organism, which may favour its distribution; recurrence not shown across architectures or training seeds (Sec 5).
evidence_quote: We measure each head’s contribution by patching its output from the organism into Base.

title: Steering Risk Preferences in Large Language Models by Aligning Behavioral and Neural Representations
question: Can steering vectors be found by aligning an LLM's behaviourally elicited risk preference with its neural representation, and do they steer risk-related outputs?
mechanism: Step 1: MCMC over pairs of three-outcome gambles ($0, $50, $100), where the unchosen gamble is replaced by one drawn from Dir(1,1,1) and the LLM's choice defines the acceptance rule A(z',z)=pi(z')/(pi(z)+pi(z')) (Eq 2, Barker form). Step 2 (aligning behavioural and neural representations to produce the steering vector) is in the omitted middle of the packet and is not reproduced here. Inference: the vector is added to the residual stream at all token positions with a signed multiplier; positive means more risk-seeking.
training: Stated as 'without retraining or fine-tuning the model' (Abstract). The cost of the alignment step is not described in the visible packet.
setup: Gemma-2-9B-Instruct in the Table 2 examples; other models and the full benchmark suite are not visible in the packet; domains are risky decision-making, risk perception and risk-related text generation (Sec 1).
numbers: No quantitative results are visible in the packet; Table 2 gives qualitative completions only (Gemma-2-9B-Instruct, steering multiplier 900).
limits: Modifying the residual stream is not uniformly effective across layers; success depends highly on the layer selected (Limitations).
The method is limited for proprietary models whose weights are not accessible (Limitations).
Further mechanistic work is needed to link behaviourally elicited representations to their neural activations (Limitations).
evidence_quote: the steering vector is injected into the residual stream at all token positions to control LLM outputs.

title: Controlling Refusal Behavior of LLMs via Stiefel-Constrained Rotation Steering
question: Can a learned, norm-preserving rotation confined to a low-dimensional subspace control refusal more effectively than additive steering, without using a refusal direction?
mechanism: StiefelSteer operator M = I_d + B(Q - I_n)B^T with B in St(d,n) (orthonormal columns) and Q in SO(n), so M is an exact element of SO(d) (Sec 4.1, Conclusion). Q is initialised to I_n so the model starts unmodified. Per steered layer, (B_l, Q_l) are trained by Riemannian gradient descent on a cross-entropy loss between expected and observed model outputs (Sec 4, Fig 1). The transpose of M is its exact inverse, used for the defensive direction.
training: Gradient-based: Riemannian gradients of a cross-entropy loss update (B_l, Q_l) per layer with model weights frozen (Sec 4). The number of optimisation examples is in the omitted middle of the packet.
setup: DeepSeek-R1-7B, Falcon3-7B-Base and Qwen2.5-1.5B-EASE; two LLM-as-judge guard scores plus accuracy and perplexity checks (Conclusion, Sec 5).
numbers: Unsafe rate under attack raised from 0.52 to 0.90 on DeepSeek-R1-7B and from 0.73 to 0.92 on Falcon3-7B-Base (Conclusion).
In the defensive regime, Falcon3-7B-Base reaches 0.20 where no baseline moves below 0.67 (Conclusion).
limits: The authors stop short of calling a single refusal direction insufficient; establishing that needs a control that constrains the rotation towards the refusal direction and measures what is lost (Sec 5, before Conclusion).
At d = 3584 two unrelated directions are close to orthogonal by default, so the observed separation is not on its own evidence that one direction is insufficient (Sec 5).
evidence_quote: M is an exact element of SO(d): it rotates the learned subspace and acts as the identity outside it.

title: WRDO: Weighted Refusal Direction Optimization in Aligned Language Models
question: Does learning aggregation weights over a bank of per-prompt refusal directions give a stronger refusal-removal intervention than the single difference-of-means direction?
mechanism: Per-prompt direction r_i^(l) = normalise(h^(l)(x_i) - mu_benign^(l)) at every layer (Eq 1). Composite direction r^(l)(w) = normalise(sum_i w_i r_i^(l)) (Eq 2). Weight edit W' = W - alpha^(l) r^(l)(w) r^(l)(w)^T W applied to every attention output projection and FFN down-projection (Eq 3, Heretic operator). The weights w lie in a box and minimise the negative attack success rate measured by a guard judge (Eqs 5-6). Instantiations: separable CMA-ES, and a GRPO variant with importance sampling (WRD-GRPO-IS) with a KL regulariser (Eq 8).
training: No gradient training of the model. The composite weights w (N = number of training harmful prompts) are optimised against guard-judge ASR, by CMA-ES or by the GRPO-IS variant (details in the omitted middle). Dataset sizes are not visible in the packet.
inference_cost: Not quantified. The Introduction describes the single-direction recipe as 'a one-shot edit of the model with no inference-time overhead'.
setup: Three open-weight 7-8B checkpoints; three guard judges including WildGuard; HarmBench classifier; standard utility benchmarks; defence setting on an abliterated checkpoint (Abstract, Sec 7).
numbers: packet-omitted: result tables are in the omitted middle of the packet; no numbers copied.
limits: The WRD-CMAES instantiation does not yet support the KL regulariser (Sec 7).
Evaluation covers three open-weight checkpoints of 7-8B parameters (Sec 7).
evidence_quote: The only departure from the Heretic recipe is the choice of r(l) (w): Heretic plugs in the single direction of [5], whereas WRDO substitutes the per-prompt composite of Equation 2.
novelty_note: A: applies a rank-one edit W - alpha r r^T W to existing W_O and FFN-down matrices; r is a closed-form normalised difference of forward-pass activations, but the composite weights w are found by black-box or GRPO-IS optimisation rather than in closed form.

title: Psychological Steering of Large Language Models
question: Do mean-difference residual-stream injections steer LLM personality (OCEAN) better than personality prompting once injection strength is swept in calibrated units with early stopping?
mechanism: Additive residual-stream injection of vectors derived from psychological artifacts (construct-specific statements and open-ended tests). The mean-difference (MD, MDS variant) injections are compared with four linear-probe injections; injection strength is swept in calibrated units and the sweep stops early when a step is judged non-fluent. Lightweight classifiers replace frontier LLM judges. The hybrid combines Personality Prompting (P2) with MD injection. The exact vector formula is in the omitted middle of the packet.
training: Not stated in the visible packet. Vector construction from synthesised psychological statements is described (Sec 1); no gradient training is described in the visible text.
setup: 14 LLMs (Qwen3-8B shown in Fig 2); IPIP-NEO-120 inventory measuring OCEAN; open-ended and multiple-choice situational-judgement batteries; comparison against Personality Prompting (P2).
numbers: MDS injections outperform P2 in open-ended generation in 11 of 14 LLMs, with gains of 3.61% to 16.44% (Sec 1).
The P2 plus MD hybrid outperforms both methods in 13 of 14 LLMs, with gains over P2 ranging from 5.56% to 21.92% (Sec 1).
limits: MD injections induce OCEAN trait covariance patterns that depart from the Big Two model, suggesting a gap between learned representations and human psychology (Abstract).
evidence_quote: Our method derives and calibrates residual-stream injections using psychological artifacts
novelty_note: G: reports that injections move several OCEAN traits together in a pattern unlike the Big Two model; the authors read this as a gap between learned representations and human psychology, not as evidence that the signal encodes another concept, so this is a close approach only.

title: Steering Geometry: Validating Human Value Geometry in LLM Steering Space
question: Does the latent geometry of LLM steering vectors reflect the Schwartz theory of basic human values, and does geometric fidelity predict consistent cross-value transfer?
mechanism: A ~26K-quadruple contrastive benchmark over 20 Schwartz values is built. Activations are extracted at a selected layer, one steering vector per value is built with each method, and the vector bank's geometry is compared with the circumplex (Spearman correlation; computation in the omitted middle). Distribution-driven methods (CAA, SphericalSteer, ODESteer) aggregate activation differences over contrastive data; behaviour-centric methods (COLD-Steer, BiPO) learn vectors through optimisation against an output objective. Cross-value transfer is measured when steering toward one value.
training: Distribution-driven methods: no training is described in the visible packet. Behaviour-centric methods learn steering vectors by gradient descent or in-context optimisation (Sec 1-2); their budgets are not visible.
setup: Multiple model families and sizes; Schwartz circumplex as primary framework and revised Moral Foundations Theory as a second check; methods CAA, SphericalSteer, ODESteer, COLD-Steer, BiPO (Abstract, Sec 1).
numbers: Distribution-driven methods recover human value topologies aligned with theoretical predictions (Spearman rho up to 0.51, p < 10^-13) (Abstract).
Behaviour-centric methods show near-zero correlation with the expected value geometry despite comparable steering performance (Introduction).
limits: Geometric fidelity improves with model scale but drops after instruction tuning (Abstract).
Many behaviour-centric methods appear to rely on shortcuts that steer outputs without preserving meaningful semantic structure (Introduction).
evidence_quote: we build contrastive (question, positive, negative) pairs. (2) We extract residual-stream activations at a selected layer
novelty_note: G: finds behaviour-centric steering vectors show little correlation with the value circumplex and suggests they exploit behaviour-specific shortcuts rather than encoding meaningful semantic structure.

title: THESIS-MoE: Trainable Hierarchical Extraction and SteerIng of Sycophancy in Mixture-of-Experts
question: Can sycophancy in MoE models be removed by an intervention that acts only where belief-induced sycophancy is present, while keeping general knowledge?
mechanism: Belief direction from matched nudge and no-nudge prompts: d_c = (1/N) sum_i (h_i,c^nudge - h_i,c^no-nudge) (Eq 1), unit-normalised. Interventions over an MoE granularity ladder (blocks, experts, attention blocks, heads) are compared: unconditional CAA-style subtraction; analytic projection-based conditional subtraction; and a learned per-token gate m on each head and expert (ComponentMask, VectorMaskFrozen or VectorMaskLearned; FlatGate, CondGate or SharedGate). Base weights stay frozen. The selected configuration is VF-CG-FT-C (frozen vector mask, conditional gate, full schedule, cold start).
training: The learned gate is trained with base weights frozen on the matched sycophancy train split (4,940 items; dev 1,646; test 1,648; Table 2) using a full schedule from cold start. A 72-run architecture sweep with three seeds selected the configuration (Sec 5.6, Figs 13-14). The optimiser and gradient method are not described in the visible packet.
inference_cost: Not quantified in the visible packet; the learned gate is evaluated per token at inference.
setup: Three open-weight MoE models; model-written evaluation items of Perez et al. repackaged with CAA; retention on MMLU, GSM8K, TruthfulQA and perplexity; routing and prompting baselines (Sec 3-6).
numbers: Our conditional interventions removed up to 90% of the belief-induced sycophancy (Abstract).
limits: MMLU declines under the selected operating points, while GSM8K is largely preserved (Sec 1, contributions).
The perplexity check is a decision-token-off control that screens for gross regressions rather than measuring open-ended fluency (Fig 16 caption).
evidence_quote: The conditional gate (CG) and full schedule (FT) remove the most push across all three models
novelty_note: B: a learned per-token gate applies a belief-direction edit only where the behaviour is present and steers away from sycophancy; the visible packet does not show whether the gate reads the hidden state directly, so this is a close approach.

title: LM-Cocktail: Resilient Tuning of Language Models via Model Merging
question: Can a fine-tuned language model keep its general-domain ability by merging it with the base model and peer models, with merge weights set from few-shot validation loss?
mechanism: M_r = alpha M_t + (1 - alpha) sum_i w_i M_i over base and peer models (Eq 1). Merge weights w_i = softmax(-L(M_i, E_t)/tau), where L is the prediction loss of candidate M_i on few-shot target examples E_t (Eq 2). Default alpha = 0.5. Mono-specialist variant: M_r = alpha M_t + (1 - alpha) M_b (Eq 3). Without-fine-tuning variant: M_r = sum_i w_i M_i.
training: The target model M_t is fine-tuned by standard training (not described further in the visible packet). The merge weights are derived from few-shot validation losses with no further training: 'no expensive training operations are needed' (Sec 2.1).
setup: Decoder LMs with Llama-2-chat-7b as base and nine fine-tuned decoder models; nine encoder models; evaluation on FLAN, MMLU and MTEB (Sec 3, Introduction).
numbers: packet-omitted: result tables are not visible; only defaults are in the packet: alpha = 0.5 and 5-shot validation examples (Sec 2.1).
evidence_quote: LM-Cocktail can increase accuracy on new target tasks while maintaining its accuracy on other tasks.

title: Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer
question: Can a sparsely gated mixture-of-experts layer add model capacity without a proportional increase in computation?
mechanism: Layer output y = sum_i G(x)_i E_i(x) (Eq 1). Noisy top-k gating: H(x)_i = (x W_g)_i + StandardNormal() * Softplus((x W_noise)_i) (Eq 4); G(x) = Softmax(KeepTopK(H(x), k)) (Eq 3), so experts with zero gate are not evaluated. Load-balancing loss L_load = w_load * CV(Load(X))^2 (Eq 11), with an analogous importance loss; W_g and W_noise are initialised to zero. A hierarchical variant uses a primary gate over secondary MoEs (Eq 12).
training: All parts of the network are trained jointly by back-propagation (Sec 1.2). The language-modelling and translation datasets and their sizes are not restated in the visible packet.
inference_cost: Not quantified in the visible packet; sparse gating evaluates only a handful of experts per example (Sec 2).
setup: MoE applied convolutionally between stacked LSTM layers for language modelling and machine translation; MoE-256 configuration in Appendix C; MoE up to 137 billion parameters (Abstract).
numbers: Greater than 1000x improvements in model capacity with only minor losses in computational efficiency (Abstract).
Table 6 (Appendix A): with w_importance = 1.0 and w_load = 1.0 test perplexity is 35.7 versus 39.8 with neither loss (row '1.0 1.0 35.7 0.03 0.02 1.07').
limits: The noisy top-k gate creates discontinuities in the gating function, which the authors say they 'have not yet observed' to be a problem in practice (Sec 2.1).
evidence_quote: A trainable gating network determines a sparse combination of these experts to use for each example.
novelty_note: B: the gate G(x) is computed from the layer input through W_g and W_noise with no separate classifier and selects which experts run; it applies expert outputs, not steering vectors, so this is a close approach only.

title: Incremental Learning Through Deep Adaptation
question: Can a network learn a new domain with few added parameters while exactly preserving its performance on the original domain?
mechanism: Deep Adaptation Networks: each convolutional layer of a frozen base network gets a controller module whose new filters are linear combinations of the existing filters. A switching variable alpha selects between the original convolution and the re-parameterised one, set manually or by a 'Dataset Decider' sub-network; alpha also selects the classifier. Controllers are initialised with a diagonal configuration so that the network starts from the base behaviour (Sec 3).
training: The controller modules are trained by gradient descent on each new task while the base weights stay frozen (Sec 3-4; 'trained DAN for one epoch ... observed the loss'). Training data are image-classification datasets from the Visual Decathlon Challenge.
setup: Visual Decathlon Challenge (ten image-classification datasets) with base networks trained on sketch, Plankton, Caltech-256, Omniglot and natural-image datasets (Sec 4).
numbers: Requires a fraction (typically 13%, dependent on network architecture) of the number of parameters (Abstract).
With standard quantisation the parameter cost is reduced to around 3% of the original (Abstract).
evidence_quote: that constrains newly learned filters to be linear combinations of existing ones.

title: Closed-form feedback-free learning with forward projection
question: Can layer weights be learned from a single forward pass without retrograde communication from downstream neurons?
mechanism: Forward Projection: each layer's target membrane potentials are z~_l = g_l(a_{l-1} Q_l) + g_l(y U_l), with fixed random Gaussian projections Q_l, U_l and a nonlinearity g_l (Eq 1). A local loss ||Z_l - Z~_l|| is defined against the actual membrane potential. Weights are then solved in closed form by ridge regression, W_l = (A^T A + lambda I)^{-1} A^T Z~_l (Eq 2), computed once after the single pass and accumulated sample by sample.
training: No gradient training: a single forward pass over the dataset followed by closed-form ridge regression per layer, with no retrograde communication (Abstract, Results). interp: this is a data-driven fit of a network from scratch, not an edit of a pretrained model.
setup: Fashion-MNIST multilayer perceptron, several biomedical datasets, and few-shot tasks; compared with random features, local supervision and Forward-Forward (Results).
numbers: packet-omitted: Table 1 and the results are in the omitted middle; no numbers copied.
evidence_quote: Synaptic weights for each layer can be computed in a closed-form forward manner, using ridge regression

title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Model Merging for Cross-Lingual Transfer in LLMs
question: Which modular fine-tuning and merging schemes best combine a target-language capability with English math ability in dense LLMs when in-language math data is absent?
mechanism: Parameters are partitioned into a target-language set and an English-math set. The partitions are fine-tuned separately (or jointly with the opposite partition frozen) and combined by post-hoc merging; the best-performing method is Layer-Swapping (Bandarkar et al. 2025a), whose exact merge rule is in the omitted middle of the packet. The paper also reports that reverting less useful fine-tuning updates after training often outperforms freezing them from the start. interp: the evidence_quote is a weak fit; the packet text for the merge rule is column-interleaved and no clean verbatim sentence was found.
