title: A Pipeline to Assess Merging Methods via Behavior and Internals
question: How does merging two Qwen2.5 parent models (instruct and math/coder) affect both their behaviour and their internally encoded linguistic competence?
mechanism: A three-stage pipeline: (1) merge two parent models with MergeKit using Linear, SLERP, TIES, DARE-TIES or Task Arithmetic; (2) evaluate parents and merged models on behaviour with LM-Harness benchmarks and on internals with the Holmes probing benchmark (morphology, syntax and other linguistic phenomena); (3) correlate the two rankings.
training: None for the merge step, which combines weights (MergeKit). The parent models were already fine-tuned; their training is not described in the visible packet.
inference_cost: Not quantified. Linear and TIES are described as keeping low power use during inference and merging (qualitative, Sec 3.1).

numbers: packet-omitted: no numeric results are visible; the Abstract reports qualitative findings only.

title: An Empirical Survey of Model Merging Algorithms for Social Bias Mitigation
question: Which model-merging algorithms reduce social bias in LLMs while preserving downstream accuracy?
mechanism: interp: the evidence_quote is a weak fit (title only); the packet text for the bias-inversion steps is column-interleaved. Bias-amplified model theta_bias is made by continued pretraining on a biased corpus; the bias vector is theta_bias - theta_LLM, and the bias-inverted model is theta_inv = 2 theta_LLM - theta_bias (Eq 1). The debiased model is theta_debias = (1 - alpha) theta_LLM + alpha theta_inv (Eq 2), with the merge realised by one of seven algorithms: Linear, Karcher Mean, SLERP, NuSLERP, TIES, DELLA and Nearswap.
training: Continued pretraining on the biased corpus produces theta_bias (gradient training; corpus size not visible). The merge step itself needs no training.
setup: 13 open-weight models from the GPT-2, LLaMA and Qwen2 families; bias benchmarks BBQ, BOLD and HONEST; SuperGLUE for downstream accuracy (Abstract, Sec 3).
numbers: packet-omitted: result tables are in the omitted middle; the Abstract gives qualitative results only, with Linear, SLERP and Nearswap reducing bias while maintaining overall performance.
limits: Methods achieving greater bias reduction degrade accuracy, particularly on tasks requiring reading comprehension and commonsense and causal reasoning (Abstract).
evidence_quote: An Empirical Survey of Model Merging Algorithms for Social Bias Mitigation

title: From Parameter Rebasin to Functional Transfer Across Heterogeneous Transformers
question: Can task-specific behaviour be transferred to a Transformer of different depth or width without transporting source parameters or training?
mechanism: ARIADNE pairs each target block j with a source block pi(j) by relative depth, pi(j) = round(j(D_s - 1)/(D_t - 1)). For each matched block, a local Procrustes map Q_j aligns source and target base residual-stream states, and the source fine-tuning activation displacement is expressed in target coordinates as D_j. A sparse target update is then obtained by closed-form ridge regression so that one residual-writing target component reproduces D_j on a small calibration set (Eq 8).
training: Training-free: closed-form Procrustes alignment and ridge regression on a small calibration set; no gradient training and no target fine-tuned checkpoint (Abstract, Sec 1).
inference_cost: Not reported. The paper states the update needs no inference-time interventions (Sec 1).
setup: Vision Transformer expansion and reduction, and language-model variants (Abstract).
numbers: packet-omitted: results are not visible in the packet; the Abstract gives qualitative claims only.
evidence_quote: Rather than transporting the source task vector, it transfers the observable effect of source fine-tuning
novelty_note: A: a closed-form ridge-regression update to one residual-writing target component, computed from forward-pass activations, transfers a fine-tuned behaviour; the rank of the update is not stated in the visible packet and it is not described as low-rank, so this is a close approach.

title: A Low-Rank Space Captures Linear Alignment Between LLM and Human Neural Activity During Naturalistic Language Listening
question: Which low-dimensional subspace of LLM representations supports linear prediction of human neural responses to natural speech?
mechanism: Ridge reduced-rank regression from word embeddings to neural responses finds the brain-predictive subspace; the rank is swept until performance saturates (99% of maximum across quantiles), and the saturation rank is compared with a PCA subspace of the same embeddings. Leave-one-subject-out tests transfer the projection to held-out participants (Figs 1-2).
training: No training of the language models: embeddings are extracted from pretrained models (Sec 3.3, App A.1.1). The subspace fitting beyond the ridge reduced-rank regression is described in the omitted middle and not visible.
setup: GPT-2, GPT-2 XL, GPT-J 6B, Llama 3 8B and RoBERTa Large, plus a randomly initialised GPT-2 and GloVe; Podcast ECoG (nine participants), Brain Treebank Cars 2 sEEG, and Deep fMRI (eight participants) (Sec 3.1, 3.3).
numbers: Full linear encoding performance can be recovered using only 1-3% of the original embedding dimensionality (Abstract).
limits: The low-dimensional subspaces generalise across held-out participants and, to a lesser extent, across datasets (Abstract).
evidence_quote: full linear encoding performance can be recovered using only 1–3% of the original embedding dimensionality

title: Tool Calling is Linearly Readable and Steerable in Language Models
question: Can the tool a request needs be read from the hidden state before generation, and steered to a chosen tool without retraining?
mechanism: Tool vector h̄_i = mean over 2-3 example requests of the residual stream at the last prompt token (final layer for main results). Read: nearest tool vector by cosine similarity. Steer from tool a to b: h_l <- h_l + alpha*(h̄_b - h̄_a), alpha=0.7 or 1.0, applied once at the last prompt token. Wrong-call flag: gap between the two highest similarity scores; small gaps mean likelier wrong calls.
training: none (forward passes only, 2-3 requests per tool; no gradients)
setup: 8 instruction-tuned models 4B-27B (Gemma 3, Qwen 3/2.5, Llama 3.1); synthetic tool lists; real APIs from tau-bench, ToolBench, BFCL v3.
numbers: Steering changes the generated call to a chosen target tool in 56–78% of held-out tool pairs, depending on the model (Abstract).
Across four models, this signal achieves an AUROC of 0.61–0.78 and outperforms a first-token confidence baseline on three of them (Abstract).
limits: Near-synonymous tools cannot be separated; on ToolBench the direction moves the call to the right domain but rarely to the right API (Introduction).
For four get_ tools at most 165 of 210 ordered pairs can be switched, because last-layer steering only changes the first output token (Section 2).
evidence_quote: For each tool, we average the model’s hidden states from a few example requests to obtain a tool vector.

novelty_note.F: Steers which tool is called (tool choice, not call/no-call) with a difference of averaged hidden states.
novelty_note.G: Compares the steering direction with an output-weight direction layer by layer; in middle layers the steering direction switches more calls, which the authors use to argue the effect is more than raising the target name's score (interp: partial evidence the signal is not only the output score).

our_questions.a: Not call/no-call: this is tool identity via nearest-centroid readout; per-layer readout accuracy not extracted.
our_questions.b: Steering switches calls to the target tool in 56-78% of pairs; accuracy cost not extracted.

title: Tunable Tool-Call Rates in LLM Agents via Representation Steering
question: Is the binary decision to call a tool at all controlled by a single linear direction in the residual stream, and can it be steered without training?
mechanism: Propensity s(q)=log p(<tool_call> token at first generated position) (Eq. 1). Direction v_l = mean of h_l(q) over high-propensity set minus mean over low-propensity set at the last prompt token (Eq. 2). Inference: h'_l = h_l + alpha*v_l at every position (Eq. 3); layer and alpha chosen on a held-out set. Also clamping and directional-ablation projections.
training: none (no labels, gradients or sparse autoencoders; a few thousand queries suffice for extraction)
inference_cost: one vector addition per position at the chosen layer; overhead not quantified in sections read
setup: Multi-tool harness; PopQA (lowest-popularity decile, 200 per evaluation), GSM8K, BIG-Bench Hard word sorting and date understanding; dense, MoE and multimodal models; held-out tools.
numbers: Adding the direction moves the call rate monotonically from near 0% to over 90% while keeping calls well-formed (Abstract).
With live tool execution, a single sweep of the steering nearly doubles open-domain QA accuracy (0.29 → 0.56) (Abstract).
limits: Limitations section not read; the abstract reports no failure cases beyond the cost/accuracy frontier.
evidence_quote: We show that whether an instruction-tuned model calls a tool can be controlled by a single linear direction in its residual stream

novelty_note.F: Steers whether a tool is called with a difference-of-means direction added to the residual stream, with no training and no prompt change.

our_questions.a: Call/no-call is controlled by the direction; a probe accuracy is not the reported metric. Layer picked on a held-out proxy.
our_questions.b: Yes: call rate near 0% to over 90%; QA accuracy 0.29 to 0.56 at about one search call per question; projection and ablation controls also reported.
our_questions.d: Partly: steering is knowledge-selective (adds calls on questions the model cannot answer; subtracting removes needless calls on questions it can solve).

title: How Do Agentic LLMs Decide to Call Tools? A Tool-Call Vector Shaped by Suppression
question: What internal mechanism decides whether an agentic LLM calls a tool or answers directly?
mechanism: Minimal contrastive prompts in which an execution verb (write) versus an analysis verb (discuss) flips the call decision. The decision is traced to a vector mu_Delta, described as the inverse of a suppression signal written by transcoder features that signal tool use is unnecessary. Downstream attention heads and MLP features read the state. Tested by behavioural ablation, full-state patching and vector interventions.
training: not stated in the sections read
setup: 500 paired prompts across Python, Java, C++ (300 analysis, 200 held out); native multi-turn tau2-Bench trajectories; seven models from the Qwen, Mistral and Granite families.
numbers: Full-state patching recovers calls on 93.5–100.0% of analysis prompts. Vector interventions yield normalized sufficiency scores of 0.81–1.03 and necessity scores of 0.61–1.04 (results section; section number not recorded).
limits: Scope is the binary call-or-no-call decision under a fixed scaffold; the authors do not evaluate whether the call selects the right tool or completes the task (Section 10, Limitations).
evidence_quote: Full-state patching recovers calls on 93.5–100.0% of analysis prompts. Vector interventions yield normalized sufficiency scores of 0.81–1.03 and necessity scores of 0.61–1.04.

novelty_note.G: Ties the call-decision vector to a suppression signal written by features that encode tool use being unnecessary (interp: the vector tracks a necessity judgement, not only the scaffold prior).

our_questions.a: Not a linear-probe readout; the vector is characterised by intervention.
our_questions.b: Yes: patching and vector interventions move the call decision (sufficiency and necessity scores above); accuracy cost not reported.
our_questions.d: Partly: analysis verbs signal that tool use is unnecessary given the request; not a test of information already in context.

title: LLM Agents Already Know When to Call Tools -- Even Without Reasoning
question: Is tool necessity linearly decodable from the pre-generation hidden state, and can a probe-gated prefill reduce unnecessary calls without hurting accuracy?
mechanism: A linear probe on the hidden state at the last input token, before generation, predicts whether a tool is necessary. Probe&Prefill: if the probe predicts the call is unnecessary, the response is prefilled with a steering sentence (soft or hard prefill; threshold chosen on single-hop tasks). Probe overhead under 1 ms.
training: a linear probe trained on 900 labelled training examples; training takes seconds on CPU
inference_cost: <1ms overhead for the probe (Abstract)
setup: 18 environments (15 single-hop, 3 multi-hop) across computational scale, knowledge boundaries and execution reliability; six models (names not extracted); Qwen models in multi-hop results.
numbers: Probe&Prefill reduces tool calls by 38% with only 1.7% accuracy loss, while the best baseline at comparable accuracy only reduces 4.2% of tool calls (Abstract).
The probe achieves AUROC 0.89–0.96 across all six tested models (Table 3, probing section).
limits: Out-of-distribution transfer holds within a category only (Appendix D); Prompt-only suppresses necessary calls alongside unnecessary ones (Abstract).
evidence_quote: This reveals that models already know when tools are needed, but fail to act on this knowledge during generation.

our_questions.a: Yes: linear probe at the last input token before generation; AUROC 0.89–0.96 across six models; layer selection in Appendix E.
our_questions.b: Yes: prefill gated by the probe cuts calls 38% at 1.7% accuracy loss; up to 75% on multi-hop Qwen (Appendix C).
our_questions.c: Yes, explicit: the probe reads necessity that generation fails to act on.
our_questions.d: Not addressed directly beyond knowledge-boundary tasks.
our_questions.e: A labelled probe (900 examples) is trained; no weight training.

title: Model-Adaptive Tool Necessity Reveals the Knowing-Doing Gap in LLM Tool Use
question: Where does the mismatch between a model's tool necessity and its tool calls arise: in cognition (whether it believes a tool is needed) or in the action?
mechanism: Model-adaptive necessity label from each model's own empirical performance. Two supervised linear probes per (token, layer): w_c for necessity (cognition) and w_a for the tool-call action. Cosine similarity CosSim(w_c, w_a) at each position tests whether the two share a direction. Appendix C flips the action with activation steering.
training: supervised linear probes on labelled hidden states (dataset size not extracted)
setup: Four models including Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct; arithmetic and factual QA (TruthfulQA in figures).
numbers: substantial mismatches of 26.5–54.0% and 30.8–41.8%, respectively (Abstract, arithmetic and factual QA).
limits: Limitations section not read.
evidence_quote: By tracing the trajectory of samples in the two-stage process, we further discover that the majority of mismatch is concentrated in the cognition-to-action transition, not in cognition itself.

novelty_note.G: Checks whether the necessity probe direction coincides with the action probe direction; they are near orthogonal in late layers, which bears on whether the probe reads the intended concept (interp: partial evidence).

our_questions.a: Yes: both cognition and action are linearly decodable; probe directions nearly orthogonal in late-layer, last-token positions; per-layer accuracy not extracted.
our_questions.b: Yes, qualitatively: the action can be flipped by activation steering (Appendix C); magnitudes not extracted.
our_questions.c: Yes, explicit knowing-doing gap: most mismatch lies in the cognition-to-action transition.
our_questions.d: Partly: necessity is defined relative to each model's own capability, not whether the answer is in context.
our_questions.e: Supervised probes on labelled hidden states.

title: Amplitude-Only FFN Intervention for Tool-Structured LLM Inference: Method, Gated Evaluation Protocol, and Cross-Model Empirical Results
question: Can multiplicative rescaling of FFN activations repair tool-call and structured outputs without changing pretrained weights?
mechanism: Amplitude Gating: magnitude- and entropy-based multiplicative masks on FFN activations at six SwiGLU sites, with a Newton-Schulz windowed ranking variant; a random-forest selector refit over six tasks chooses settings.
training: pretrained weights kept fixed; a random-forest selector refit on six tasks (training data size not extracted)
setup: Three Qwen checkpoints (Qwen3.5-9B among them), six text/tool endpoints including two function-call endpoints, static ToolBench in- and out-domain, and JSON.
numbers: Qwen3.5-9B non-NS configurations improve two function-call endpoints by +2.61/+2.67 percentage points (Abstract).
the six-task random-forest refit improves native score by +0.46 pp (Abstract).
limits: Scores measure lexical or answer/action-name agreement, not executed-tool success (Abstract).
Causal mechanisms, equal-budget advantages, repeated-run uncertainty and serving cost require further evaluation (Abstract).
evidence_quote: Scores measure lexical or answer/action-name agreement, not executed-tool success. Under the current experimental conditions, the six-task random-forest refit improves native score

novelty_note.B: interp: the masks are computed from FFN activation magnitude and entropy and applied per token, with no separate classifier for the mask itself; a random forest selects settings separately.
novelty_note.F: Steers tool-structured generation (function calls and tool names) by rescaling activations.

our_questions.b: Gains of +1.6 to +2.8 pp on tool benchmarks; call-rate or accuracy cost not reported.
our_questions.e: Random-forest selector refit on six tasks; model weights untouched.

title: Internal-State Probes Read the Situation, Not the Action: Three Negative Results for Pre-Action Misalignment Monitoring
question: Can internal probes detect misaligned tool actions before they are generated, or do they only read the situation?
mechanism: Three probe families, all difference-of-means or PCA-style directions in the residual stream: a fine-tune-minus-base disposition direction (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B), probes at the last token of unsafe prefills (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), and emotion-concept vectors (Gemma-3-27B-IT). Tested with scenario/action controls and cross-domain transfer.
training: directions fitted from labelled contrast sets; no training of the monitored model (sizes not extracted)
setup: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct fine-tune and base; Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; Gemma-3-27B-IT; Petri-style multi-turn red-team scenarios.
numbers: observed misaligned behavior in 11 of 17 audited automated multi-turn red-team scenarios (65% transcript-level) (Section on red-team audit).
limits: Sparse-autoencoder feature decompositions are not evaluated (Limitations).
Negative results are scoped by clustering, sampling and measurement choices (Limitations).
evidence_quote: Emotion and content directions are all learned by the same difference-of-means plus neutral-PCA pipeline

novelty_note.G: Shows that probe directions track the prompt domain or construction contrast rather than the upcoming action (interp: the signal reflects the situation, not the intended concept).

our_questions.a: Probes read the situation; layer-wise accuracies not extracted; transfer across domains is poor.
our_questions.c: Partly: the situation is readable, but it does not predict the action.
our_questions.d: Yes, as a confound: the probes pick up prompt or construction contrast present in context.
our_questions.e: Fitting probes on labelled prefills; no model training.

title: Constraint Tax in Open-Weight LLMs: An Empirical Study of Tool Calling Suppression Under Structured Output Constraints
question: Do JSON-schema output constraints suppress tool calls, and why?
mechanism: JSON Schema constraints are compiled into grammar-based token masks that make tool-call tokens unreachable during decoding. Constraint Priority Inversion (CPI) hypothesis: schema satisfaction dominates action selection. Mitigation, Transparent Two-Pass Execution: run tool execution separately from schema-constrained response generation.
training: none (inference-time strategy; 'without requiring model retraining')
inference_cost: two passes (qualitative; not quantified in sections read)
setup: Open-weight models across several families and deployment settings (names and counts not extracted).
limits: CPI is presented as a behavioral hypothesis rather than a verified internal mechanism (Abstract).
evidence_quote: We present CPI as a behavioral hypothesis consistent with the observed evidence rather than a verified internal mechanism.

our_questions.b: Two-pass execution restores tool invocation while keeping structured output; cost not extracted.
our_questions.d: Not addressed; the schema is in context but acts through decoding masks, not knowledge.

title: To Call or Not to Call: A Framework to Assess and Optimize LLM Tool Calling
question: Are LLM tool-calling decisions aligned with true need and true utility, and can hidden states predict them better?
mechanism: Decision-theoretic framework over necessity, utility and affordability; normative (true need and utility) versus descriptive (self-perceived need and utility) lenses. Trains lightweight latent need estimators (LNE) and latent utility estimators (LUE) from model hidden states that predict true need and utility; LNEs are then used as controllers.
training: lightweight estimators trained on hidden states with labels of true need and utility (sizes not extracted)
setup: Six open models and one proprietary model (GPT-5.5), two tools (web search, calculator), six tasks.
numbers: tool calls cost $0.94 and $5.80 for the whole task (Abstract; column text interleaved in the extraction).
limits: LUEs give smaller improvements than LNEs (Abstract, as read in text).
evidence_quote: S ELF - DECISION and LNE are compared within the natural setting and at each tool-call budget.

our_questions.a: Yes in spirit: LNEs trained on hidden states predict true need better than the model's self-report; layer and accuracy numbers not extracted.
our_questions.b: Used as controllers at a tool-call budget; control results not extracted.
our_questions.c: Partly (interp): the model's perceived need is misaligned with its true need.
our_questions.d: Partly: need is defined against the model's counterfactual performance with and without tools.
our_questions.e: Yes: estimators trained on labelled hidden states.

training: not stated in the sections read
setup: LoCoMo long-term conversational QA benchmark.
numbers: around 4 iterations, as 97.73% questions are finalized by then (Section on iteration analysis).
limits: Not extracted.

title: Adaptive Retrieval helps Reasoning in LLMs -- but mostly if it's not used
question: Does letting an LLM agent decide when to retrieve help mathematical reasoning on GSM8K and MATH-500?
mechanism: Behavioural comparison of CoT, static retrieval and adaptive retrieval where the agent decides in-trace whether to query a knowledge base. No hidden-state analysis.
training: none stated
setup: GSM8K and MATH-500 with an LLM agent (model details not extracted).
numbers: Adaptive Retrieval–CoT consistently achieves the highest accuracy, exceeding the CoT baseline by 1.1 percentage points(pp.) on GSM8K and by 6.4pp. (Section 3.1).
On the GSM8K benchmark, the agent invoked retrieval in only 7.0% of cases, relying primarily on its parametric knowledge (Section 3.1 analysis).

title: When to Retrieve: Teaching LLMs to Utilize Information Retrieval Effectively
question: Can an LLM learn to decide when to use an external retriever, instead of always or never retrieving?
mechanism: Fine-tune the LLM (ADAPT-LLM) to generate a special token <RET> when it does not know the answer; retrieval is invoked only when the token is produced. Compared with always-retrieve, never-retrieve and a popularity-threshold rule.
training: supervised fine-tuning on existing open-domain QA data with RET labels (size not extracted)
setup: Llama-2 models; PopQA.
numbers: A DAPT-LLM decreases the usage of IR down to 83.99% while improving performance over vanilla retrieval (Section 4 results; table not recorded).
limits: Not extracted; the authors note the IR system is the primary bottleneck (Discussion).
evidence_quote: able to generate the ⟨RET⟩ token when it determines that it does not

our_questions.a: Not a probe: the call decision is a learned output token.
our_questions.b: Not steering; IR use falls to 83.99% with improved performance.

title: MICE for CATs: Model-Internal Confidence Estimation for Calibrating Agents with Tools
question: Can model-internal confidence, read from intermediate layers, calibrate whether a tool call is correct, so the agent knows when to call?
mechanism: Decode each intermediate layer with the logit lens; features compare each layer's decoded output with the final output (BERTScore-style similarity, raw confidence); a learned probabilistic classifier (logistic regression or random forest with 1000 trees) estimates whether the call is correct; the call decision is taken on expected tool-calling utility at a risk level.
training: learned classifiers on labelled simulated tool-calling data (STE set); sample efficiency measured (300 examples reach NWKR on full data)
setup: Llama3-8B-Instruct and Llama 3.1 and 3.2 models; simulated trial-and-error (STE) tool-calling dataset; unseen APIs for zero-shot.
numbers: MICE models show clear improvements in the medium and high risk regimes (Section 5).
limits: MICE conditions on model internals, so it cannot be applied to closed models (Limitations, as read in text).
evidence_quote: MICE models show clear improvements in the medium and high risk regimes.

our_questions.a: Partly: confidence from layer-wise features predicts call correctness; a linear probe accuracy is not reported.
our_questions.b: No steering; calls gated by calibrated confidence at risk levels.
